About the Authors

C R Rene Robin received his M.E. and Ph.D. (both in Computer Science and Engineering) from the College of Engineering, Guindy, Anna University. He is currently working as Professor in the Department of Computer Science and Engineering, and as Dean (Innovation) at Sri Sairam Engineering College, Chennai. His areas of specialization are data science, ontological engineering, knowledge management, e-learning, and the semantic web. He is a recognized supervisor of Anna University to guide Ph.D. scholars in Computer Science and Engineering. He is also a doctoral committee member of Anna University and other universities and a senior member of IEEE, lifetime member of Indian Society for Technical Education (ISTE), and member of several professional bodies. He has published three books and has written over 100 articles in both national and international conferences and journals. He has created an innovation ecosystem that integrates with the UN’s Sustainable Development Goals.

![](Images/image1.jpeg)

Doreen Robin is Founder and Director of Computational Intelligence Research Foundation (CIRF), Chennai. A skilled data scientist and an experienced trainer in Machine Learning and Deep Learning, she is also a renowned keynote speaker. She earned her B.Tech. in Information Technology from the University of Madras, M.E. in Computer Science and Engineering from Anna University, and Ph.D. in Computer Science and Engineering from the same institution. Her research interests encompass parallel and distributed computing, peer-to-peer computing, grid computing, cloud computing, cybersecurity, blockchain technology and big data analytics.

With over 500 keynote addresses, conference presentations, and hands-on training sessions delivered to corporations, faculty, and students, Doreen Robin has shared her expertise on topics such as data engineering, blockchain, software testing, cybersecurity, cloud computing, and digital educational tools for teaching and learning. She has published approximately 40 papers in both national and international journals and conferences and is a life member of the Indian Society for Technical Education (ISTE).

![](Images/image2.jpeg)

Chandra Mouli P V S S R has been associated with the Department of Computer Science, Central University of Tamil Nadu since 2019. Prior to that, he worked at the National Institute of Technology, Jamshedpur, and VIT University, Vellore. He received his M.C.A. from Osmania University, Hyderabad in 2000. He obtained his Ph.D. in Computer Science from the National Institute of Technology (NIT), Tiruchirappalli in 2010. His research interests include digital image processing, digital watermarking, pattern classification, machine learning and deep learning. He has around 35 papers published in SCI/SCIE/Scocpus-indexed journals and around 30 papers in international conferences. He is the resource person for various Faculty Development Programmes conducted under the ATAL scheme introduced by AICTE. He has given many talks and lectures on machine learning and deep learning with practical demonstration using Keras and TensorFlow.

![](Images/image3.jpeg)

Preface

Machine Learning is how computers learn from data and experience without being explicitly programmed. It is very important in the modern world because it can help us solve many problems that are too complex or too large for humans to handle. Machine learning is a fascinating and powerful technology that can improve our lives in many ways. However, it also has some challenges and limitations we must be aware of.

This book is a comprehensive guide to machine learning, covering the theoretical and practical aspects of the field. It is intended for students, researchers, and practitioners who want to learn the fundamentals and applications of machine learning. At the end of this book, you will have a deep understanding of machine learning and be ready to apply your knowledge to real-world problems.

The book is organized into 14 chapters, each covering a different topic or aspect of machine learning. This structure is designed to provide a comprehensive understanding of the field, starting from the basics and gradually progressing to more advanced topics. This approach allows readers to build a solid foundation and then apply their knowledge to real-world problems.

Chapter 1 introduces you to the basic definitions, types, and challenges of machine learning, as well as some examples and applications. Chapters 2, 3, and 4 provide the mathematical background and tools that you will need to understand and implement machine learning algorithms. They introduce the basic concepts and tools of probability theory and statistics, which are essential for understanding and analyzing data. The book also covers linear algebra, algorithms, and complex optimization, which are the foundation of many machine-learning algorithms and models.

Chapter 5 explores computational learning theory, which includes its definition, objects, history and importance as well as the main methods used. Chapter 6 discusses different machine learning model types and highlights different feature types. It also introduces concept learning in a detailed manner, briefly introduces artificial neural networks, multilayer perceptrons, and linear discriminant analysis, and introduces regression types and logistic regression.

Chapters 7, 8, and 9 cover two major machine learning categories: unsupervised and supervised learning. Unsupervised learning is the process of finding patterns and structures in unlabeled data, while supervised learning is the process of learning from labeled data. You will learn to discover patterns and structure in data without labels using clustering, dimensionality reduction, and association rules. You will also learn how to train models that can predict outcomes or labels from data using linear and non-linear regression, classification, and ensemble methods.

Chapter 10 introduces the most potent and popular of machine learning models: artificial neural networks. You will learn how to build and train neural networks using various architectures, activation functions, optimization algorithms, regularization techniques, and loss functions. You will also learn how to use neural networks for tasks such as image recognition, natural language processing, and reinforcement learning.

Chapter 11 discusses trends in machine learning, including reinforcement learning, multitasking learning, online learning, sequence learning, prediction, bagging, and boosting. Chapter 12 focuses on machine learning applications in various industries, such as Retail, Logistics, Manufacturing, Energy and Utilities, Travel, Banking, Finance, and Insurance.

Chapters 13 and 14 cover practical aspects of machine learning, including capstone projects in Python and R, Jupyter notebook-based programs, and various assignments.

This book is intended for anyone who wants to learn about machine learning, whether you are a student, a researcher, a developer, or a hobbyist. You do not need any prior knowledge or experience in machine learning, but you should have some basic familiarity with programming (preferably Python) and mathematics (especially algebra). The book is designed to be self-contained, but it also provides references and links to further reading for those who want to dig deeper into any topic. The book is also interactive, with exercises and questions at the end of each chapter to help you test your understanding and practice your skills.

We hope it inspires readers to explore machine learning’s potential for solving real-world problems and creating value for society.

C R Rene Robin

Doreen Robin

Chandra Mouli P V S S R

Learning Objectives

At the end of this chapter, you will be able to:

•Define the fundamental concepts of machine learning and explain its historical context

•Explain the significance of machine learning in computer science and its role in problem solving

•State the principles of supervised learning and its subcategories, regression and classification

•Elaborate on the concepts of unsupervised learning, including clustering and association

•Explain the process and objectives of reinforcement learning

•Elucidate the concepts of transfer learning and meta learning and their relevance in machine learning

•Recognize real-world problems that have been solved using machine learning

•Discuss the disadvantages and limitations of data-driven solutions

•Define well-posed machine learning problems

•Outline the life cycle of a machine learning system, from design to deployment

[1.1Introduction](#07_Contents.xhtml#sub-1)

In the real world, we are surrounded by people who can learn from their experiences, thanks to their capacity for learning; we also have computers or other machines that carry out our orders. However, can a machine learn from past data or experiences, like humans? The answer is “Yes,” and it is called machine learning. Machine learning (ML) is a powerful tool in computer science and problem solving because it enables computers to learn from data and make predictions or decisions without being explicitly programmed. Complex problems that would be impossible or difficult for traditional algorithms to solve can be worked out using this type of learning. For instance, ML can determine the best route you can take to a destination, the best time to drive, and even provide updates as you drive. Numerous fields, such as robotics and natural language processing, use machine learning.

[1.2What is Machine Learning?](#07_Contents.xhtml#sub-2)

Machine learning is a branch of computer science and artificial intelligence (AI) that focuses on using statistical methods to create intelligent computer systems that can learn from databases that are already available. ML systems are designed with advanced algorithms that enable them to identify patterns and forecast outcomes with limited necessity for human intervention.

In addition, they can automatically learn from data, improve performance based on experience, and make predictions. This refers to devices that can comprehend a text written in natural language, identify a visual scene, or carry out a physical action. ML focuses on emulating human learning processes through data and algorithms, gradually increasing their accuracy.

Arthur Samuel coined the term ‘machine learning’ in 1959 and described it as, “the scientific field that enables computers/machines to learn without being explicitly programmed.” Data such as numbers, images, or text is the foundation of machine learning. Examples of data sources include:

•Bank transactions

•Photos of people or specific objects

•Bank statements

•Profit and loss statements

•Time series data from sensors

•Sales reports

First, a machine learning model will be trained on the data ([Fig. 1.1](#09_Chapter1.xhtml#fig1-1)), which has been collected and prepared for use as training data. The next step is for programmers to choose a machine learning model to employ, provide the actual data, and then sit back and watch as the computer model learns to spot patterns or predict outcomes. Finally, the human programmer can adjust the model over time, including changing its parameters, to help it produce more accurate results.

A machine learning system’s function can be descriptive, in which case it makes use of the data to explain what has happened; predictive, in which case it uses the data to forecast what will occur; or prescriptive, in which case it uses the data to suggest possible courses of action.

![](Images/f1-1.jpg)

[Figure 1.1](#09_Chapter1.xhtml#fig-1-1)  Simple flow of a machine learning program

A portion of the training data is stored and used as evaluation data to determine how accurate the ML model is when exposed to new data. The outcome is a model that can be applied in the future to analyze different data sets. Without being explicitly programmed, ML algorithms build a mathematical model using historical sample data, or ‘training data,’ to help with predictions or decisions.

Computer science and statistics are combined with machine learning to create predictive models. ML uses algorithms to go through vast amounts of data in search of patterns and learn in an iterative process. Ideally, decisions are made based on these insights that impact essential growth metrics in applications and businesses. Recent technological advancements in storage and processing power have made it possible for ML-based products like Netflix’s recommendation engine and self-driving cars.

An advanced concept of ML, called deep learning, teaches computers to mimic natural human abilities, such as learning from examples. As a result, compared to traditional ML algorithms, it offers better performance parameters. While ML is not new – it was used in the Second World War to crack the Enigma code – the ability to automatically perform complex mathematical operations on the expanding quantities and diversity of available data is a more recent innovation. With the growth of big data, internet-of-things (IoT), and universal computing, ML is crucial for finding solutions to issues in various fields.

Normal programming involves writing code (the program) for a computer to execute instructions given by the programmer ([Fig. 1.2](#09_Chapter1.xhtml#fig1-2)). This code is often written to perform tasks such as sorting numbers, adding two values, or printing something on the screen. The instructions are written so that when they are followed, it will result in an expected outcome. For example, if you write code telling the computer to add two numbers and store them in memory, when the program is run, it will do that regardless of what those two numbers are.

![](Images/f1-2.jpg)

[Figure 1.2](#09_Chapter1.xhtml#fig-1-2)  Normal programming versus machine learning programming

ML programming, on the other hand, works differently from regular programming. Instead of writing instructions in code for the computer to follow exactly, ML programs use algorithms that help teach the computer how to think and make decisions without being explicitly told what to do by a programmer – this is why we call it ‘machine learning’ and not ‘programming.’ For example, if you have a program designed with ML capabilities and give it an image with different colored shapes – circles and squares – then this program could be taught how to recognize which shapes are circles and which are squares without ever being explicitly told how many sides each shape has or what color each shape is supposed to be.

[1.3History of Machine Learning](#07_Contents.xhtml#sub-3)

Machine learning was once considered science fiction, but today it is a reality in our daily lives. Machine learning is aiding our daily lives, from self-driving cars to the Amazon virtual assistant Alexa. The concept behind ML, however, is ancient and has a long history.

The history of ML can be traced back to the mid-1950s, when researchers began to explore algorithms that could learn from data. In the 1950s and ’60s, researchers developed algorithms that used numerical input and output data to learn to make predictions. By the late 1960s and early ’70s, researchers began exploring algorithms that could learn from more complex data. Another significant milestone in ML’s history was the development of the backpropagation algorithm. This algorithm allowed neural networks to process data and make predictions by adjusting the weights and bias values of the network. Backpropagation quickly became the standard for training neural networks.

Arthur Samuel’s paper was the first significant turning point in machine learning history; Samuel proposed a computer program that could learn from its own experience to play checkers. In addition, his program was the first to use a feedback loop, allowing it to improve its play as it gained experience.

Some significant events in the history of machine learning are listed below ([Fig. 1.3](#09_Chapter1.xhtml#fig1-3)):

•1952: This year saw the invention of a program by ML pioneer Arthur Samuel that assisted an IBM computer in a game of checkers. The more it played, the better it played.

•1959: Arthur Samuel first used the phrase ‘machine learning.’ Using an adaptive filter to eliminate echoes over phone lines, the first neural network came into use.

•1967: An article titled ‘Nearest Neighbor Pattern Classification’ was published by Cover and Hart. This article postulated that machine learning is a technique of inductive logic that divides input objects into two groups. The classification pattern assigns items to the same categories as their closest neighbors. With the help of this technique, objects can be categorized according to various attributes, many of which are categorical or numerical and may have values that overlap.

•1979: The ‘Stanford Cart,’ created by Stanford University students, could autonomously move around obstacles in space.

•As the 1980s began, researchers began to explore how machines could learn without being explicitly programmed with rules.

•1981: Explanation-based learning (EBL), which Gerald DeJong introduced, used a computer to analyze training data and generate a general rule it could apply by ignoring irrelevant data.

•1985: Terry Sejnowski and Charles Rosenberg created NETtalk, a neural network that learned how to pronounce 20,000 words correctly in a single week.

•1986: Geoffrey Hinton and David Rumelhart proposed a new algorithm called the backpropagation algorithm. This was the first to use an artificial neural network to learn from input data.

•1997: A computer defeated a human chess expert for the first time when IBM’s Deep Blue defeated chess master Garry Kasparov.

•2006: Geoffrey Hinton, a computer scientist, renamed neural network research ‘deep learning.’ Since then, it has emerged as one of the most popular technologies.

•2010: People could interact with computers by moving and making gestures, thanks to Microsoft Kinect’s ability to track 20 human features at a rate of 30 times per second.

•2011: Watson from IBM defeated human opponents on Jeopardy.

•2012: Google developed a deep neural network that learned to identify images of people and cats in YouTube videos.

•2014: The chatbot Eugene Goostman passed the Turing test. About 33% of the event’s judges thought that Goostman was human. Facebook developed a deep neural network called DeepFace that the company claimed could recognize people as precisely as humans.

•2016: Google’s artificial intelligence algorithm defeated a professional Go player, in what is regarded as the world’s most challenging board game that is many times more complex than chess. In the Go competition, the AlphaGo algorithm created by Google DeepMind won all five games.

•2017: Waymo began testing driverless vehicles in the US, but only with backup drivers in the back. They rolled out fully autonomous taxis in Phoenix later that year.

•2017 to the present: Building neural networks and deep learning algorithms has advanced many sectors from 2017 to 2024. The industry prioritized ethical AI and explainability in 2020 to improve algorithm fairness, transparency, and accountability. Generative models dominated content production and simulation by 2022, as the ML business grew. AI outperformed humans in image categorization, visual reasoning, and language interpretation. However, it lacked advanced cognitive skills like competitive mathematics and common sense logic. The ML market is predicted to reach $21 billion by 2024, illustrating its rapid growth and AI investment.

![](Images/f1-3.jpg)

[Figure 1.3](#09_Chapter1.xhtml#fig-1-3)  History of machine learning

The principles of learning observed in animals also inspired the development of ML algorithms. Experiments such as bait shyness and Skinner’s pigeon superstition provide examples of how animal behavior can be related to machine learning concepts such as sampling data and empirical risk minimization. By understanding these principles, ML researchers can develop more effective algorithms that can learn from data and improve their accuracy over time.

The bait shyness experiment involved rats and their learning behavior. The experiment showed that rats tend to eat small quantities of food before consuming a full meal. This behavior is akin to the concept of sampling data in machine learning. In ML, sampling data involves selecting a subset of data from a larger data set to train a model. This process helps to reduce the computational complexity of the model and improve its accuracy.

Skinner’s pigeon superstition experiment involved pigeons and their behavior in response to a reward. The experiment showed that pigeons developed superstitious behavior when they received a reward randomly, even if the reward was not related to their behavior. This behavior is like the concept of empirical risk minimization in machine learning. Empirical risk minimization involves minimizing the difference between the predicted output of a model and the actual output of the data. This process helps to improve the accuracy of the model and reduce the risk of overfitting.

ML Today: Machine learning has made significant strides in its research, permeating every aspect of our lives. Examples include self-driving cars, Amazon’s Alexa, chatbots, recommender systems, and many more. It combines clustering, classification, decision trees, and supervised, unsupervised, and reinforcement learning techniques. For example, while the rest of the world was dealing with the pandemic in 2020, OpenAI unveiled GPT-3, a revolutionary natural language processing algorithm that had the remarkable ability to produce text that resembled human speech in response to a prompt. The GPT-3 language model, which employs 175 billion parameters and Microsoft Azure’s AI supercomputer for training, is currently regarded as the most sophisticated and extensive language model in the world.

In 2022, ChatGPT employing GPT-3.5 as a free research preview revolutionized AI chatbot accessibility and utility. This major release gave developers and AI enthusiasts a vital tool. OpenAI launched ChatGPT Plus in 2023, a premium membership with less downtime and new capabilities, showing demand for advanced AI. In the same year, Microsoft added ChatGPT-powered Bing features to conversational AI. Developers might use the API to add ChatGPT capabilities to their apps, expanding its use cases. The rapid growth of AI is astonishing and encouraging, with OpenAI’s GPT-4 in ChatGPT and Bing promising better reliability, inventiveness, and problem-solving. While outages and data privacy concerns raise questions about AI accountability, ChatGPT is being improved to meet ethical difficulties. How we utilize AI and interact with machines may change.

Machine learning is an interdisciplinary field that combines computer science, mathematics, and engineering to develop computers and software that can learn from data, identify patterns, and make data-driven decisions. This allows for increasingly sophisticated applications to perform tasks, such as intelligent search engines that can sort through massive amounts of information to find the most relevant results, self-driving cars that can navigate roads without human intervention, medical diagnosis systems that can diagnose diseases before they become too severe, and facial recognition systems that allow for secure access control in many settings.

[1.4Role of Machine Learning in Computer Science and Problem Solving](#07_Contents.xhtml#sub-4)

Computer science and machine learning have formidable problem-solving capabilities. ML enables computers to learn from data and make decisions without directly programming them. This form of technology aids in the resolution of a range of problems that are too complicated or time-consuming for people to handle alone.

ML employs techniques that may be used to solve various problems, including classification, grouping, prediction, and search optimization. These algorithms teach computers to recognize patterns in massive data sets and utilize them to make predictions or judgments.

ML is widely employed in computer science when dealing with massive data sets or issues that require substantial computational power, such as picture recognition or natural language processing (NLP). For example, suppose a group of photos requires labeling based on their content. An ML algorithm may be created to detect specific aspects within the images, such as color composition and texture.

This algorithmic technique is significantly faster than human labeling since it does not require human experience; it only requires training on relevant data sets to identify photos reliably based on their content. Furthermore, once trained on one type of data set, the same algorithm can frequently be reused for similar types of image recognition tasks without requiring additional training, leading to more efficient results.

Another example where ML shows its worth is in predicting user behavior by analyzing historic trends pointed out by big data analytics companies such as Google Analytics. This helps businesses better understand how users interact with their services/products so they can tailor their offerings to maximize user engagement while also minimizing the costs associated with development/marketing.

Due to its versatility and scalability, ML has been widely embraced by both industry professionals and academics alike. Although there remain challenges when developing these algorithms (ease of interpretability, avoiding overfitting), ML continues to revolutionize how we look at problem solving, provide more significant opportunities than ever before, analyze situations accurately, and arrive at meaningful conclusions.

[1.5Why Machine Learning?](#07_Contents.xhtml#sub-5)

One of the reasons why machines need to learn is to perform tasks that are beyond the capability of human beings. For example, machines can process and analyze large amounts of data that humans cannot, such as the results of thousands of scientific experiments. Machines can also learn from their own experiences and improve their performance over time, which is called experiential learning.

Let us consider an example of a scientific experiment that involves testing different combinations of chemicals to produce a desired reaction. A human scientist may conduct several trials and record the outcomes, but it would be very difficult and time-consuming for the scientist to analyze all the possible patterns and correlations among the variables. However, a machine can use data mining techniques to discover hidden insights and generate hypotheses from the data. The machine can also use ML algorithms to test and refine its hypotheses and optimize its results.

Another reason why machines need to learn is to emulate human abilities, such as voice recognition and image recognition. These tasks require machines to understand and interpret natural language and visual information, which are unstructured and complex forms of data.

Let us consider an example of a voice recognition system that can transcribe speech into text. A human listener may be able to understand what a speaker is saying, but it would be very challenging for them to write down every word accurately and quickly. However, a machine can use speech recognition techniques to convert the sound waves into digital signals and extract features from them. The machine can also use NLP techniques to parse the sentences and assign meanings to the words. The machine can learn from its own errors and feedback and improve its accuracy and speed over time.

The growth of ML has been fueled by the virtually infinite amount of accessible, affordable data storage options, accessibility and affordability of computational power, development of less expensive and more powerful processors, and accessibility of high-speed internet. Thanks to these digital transformation factors, one can quickly and automatically create models that can quickly and accurately analyze extensive and complex data sets ([Fig. 1.4](#09_Chapter1.xhtml#fig1-4)).

Another way ML enables companies to stay competitive is by automating complex processes such as manufacturing assembly lines or customer service chatbots. Automation can improve efficiency while also reducing costs related to labor expenses and improving time-to-market speeds for new products or services.

ML may be the key to unlocking the value of corporate and customer data and making decisions that keep a business ahead of the competition. Many industries are now creating more powerful models that can analyze more significant and complex data sets and produce faster, more precise results on a large scale. In addition, many of the largest organizations in the world today, including Facebook, Twitter, and Google, rely heavily on machine learning for their daily operations. As a result, it has become an essential competitive differentiator for many businesses worldwide.

![](Images/f1-4.jpg)

[Figure 1.4](#09_Chapter1.xhtml#fig-1-4)  Why machine learning?

ML’s practical applications use data to drive business outcomes, significantly impacting an organization’s bottom line. Organizations have adopted ML as the best method for creating models, strategizing, and planning, and they need a system to analyze it effectively and accurately. It is significant because it helps companies develop new products and gives them insights into consumer behavior trends and business operating patterns. In addition, automation with machine learning capabilities helps remove the bias associated with manual tasks where human error may occur due to unintentional prejudices or oversight during decision-making processes involving subjective criteria such as hiring practices.

ML can quickly and accurately identify complex relationships in data quickly and accurately, whereas doing so manually would take a lot of time and effort. As a result, organizations can more quickly spot lucrative opportunities and potential risks, thanks to ML tools.

Finally, machine learning helps enable personalized experiences in sectors like retail by leveraging behavior analysis data collected from customers’ interactions with websites and mobile apps so that companies can tailor their offerings based on individual preferences while at the same time providing more efficient customer service options through AI-driven automated conversations using chatbots; this provides customers with quick resolution times as they do not have to wait for a human representative’s response which could take hours or even days.

[1.6Adaptivity of Machine Learning](#07_Contents.xhtml#sub-6)

Adaptivity is the ability of a machine learning system to adjust its decisions according to the current state of the environment, without requiring human intervention or retraining from scratch. For example, an adaptive machine learning system for spam detection may learn to identify new types of spam emails that emerge over time by updating its model based on feedback from users or the email server. Another example is self-driving cars, which may learn to cope with different road conditions, traffic patterns, or weather situations, by adapting its behavior based on sensory inputs and rewards from the environment.

Adaptivity of machine learning can be achieved in different ways, depending on the type and degree of change in the environment. Some of the common methods are as follows:

•Online learning: This is a form of incremental learning, where the ML system updates its model continuously as new data arrives, without storing or revisiting the previous data. Online learning can handle gradual or moderate changes in data distribution or the task, but may suffer from catastrophic forgetting if the change is abrupt or drastic.

•Active learning: This is a form of selective learning, where the ML system queries the most informative or uncertain data points from a pool of unlabeled data, and obtains their labels from an oracle (such as a human expert or a simulator). Active learning can reduce labeling cost and improve model accuracy, especially when the data is scarce or noisy. Active learning can also handle changes in data distribution or the task, by focusing on the most relevant or novel data points.

•Reinforcement learning: This is a form of interactive learning, where the ML system learns from its own actions and their consequences in an environment, without requiring explicit labels or supervision. Reinforcement learning can optimize a long-term goal or reward, which may depend on the state of the environment and the actions of other agents. Reinforcement learning can handle changes in feedback or the reward function, by exploring different actions and exploiting the best ones.

[1.7Designing versus Learning](#07_Contents.xhtml#sub-7)

Designing and learning are two different aspects of machine learning. The method used to solve problems is the main distinction. Developing predictive models that can precisely predict future outcomes by learning from historical data is the main focus of learning. Creating novel algorithms or architectures that can be used to address challenging real-world issues like image recognition, natural language processing, and autonomous driving, on the other hand, is the focus of designing.

Designing calls for originality and frequently entails the creation of new algorithms or architectural frameworks. This may entail modifying already-in-use algorithms or building entirely new models from scratch. Working with subject-matter experts to comprehend the issue being addressed and generate solutions may also be a part of the design process. Designing is creating models using algorithms or templates with specific parameters or assumptions about the input data. This includes designing a deep neural network (DNN), a type of AI model composed of multiple layers connected by neurons. Designers need to define what types of layers will be used in the network (such as convolutional layers), how those layers are connected (such as skip connections), and what values will be used for each layer’s weights (which determine how strongly one neuron influences another).

Designing entails creating new methods or techniques for achieving a desired result. In contrast, learning can be thought of as applying current algorithms or architectures to data to infer a result.

Unsupervised learning and supervised learning are additional categories of learning. Labeled data is necessary for supervised learning, which means that the input data must have labels that specify the desired output before the model is created. The model is then trained using the labeled data to discover an input–output mapping. Unsupervised learning makes an effort to identify patterns directly from the data and does not require labeled data. In this process, algorithms refine their internal parameters to better model relationships between inputs/outputs to accurately predict future outcomes, given new inputs not seen during training sessions. Using techniques like backpropagation helps ensure accuracy when dealing with large amounts of data or complex problems where traditional approaches may fail due to their inability to optimize things like hyperparameters faster than manual optimization techniques like the hill climbing approach.

Designing and learning are closely related but distinct concepts in ML development projects. Designers create machines with appropriate architectures (design) while learners use those designs plus existing data sets to refine them further until accurate results are presented. By understanding both concepts, developers can build solutions quickly, adaptively, and efficiently since designers focus on constructing models while learners work on optimizing them over time. In conclusion, designing entails developing new algorithms or architectures, whereas learning is applying current algorithms or architectures to input data to make predictions.

[1.8Training versus Testing in Machine Learning](#07_Contents.xhtml#sub-8)

Training and testing are two vital components of the ML process that work together to produce reliable models. Training and testing are two distinct phases of the model building process. While testing involves assessing the model’s performance on new data, training involves building a model from training data. In other words, testing is validating the model using data that has not been seen before, whereas training is learning from the data.

Training: Training is the process of providing the model with input data to learn how to recognize patterns or identify relationships among variables. This can be done using supervised or unsupervised methods, depending on the problem being solved. Different algorithms are applied to the input data during training, and parameters are adjusted until an optimal solution is found. The main goal of training is to make sure that the model performs well on unseen examples or test sets. Thus, it involves tweaking parameters such as weights and hyperparameters until satisfactory results are applied to a subset (training set) of the provided examples/data points/inputs.

The process of training a model involves several steps:

1.Data preprocessing: This involves transforming the raw data into a form the model can use. Techniques such as normalization, scaling, transformation, imputation, and encoding are applied to prepare the data for ML algorithms. Statistics and mathematics help us understand the properties and distributions of the data and to choose appropriate methods for data manipulation.

2.Feature engineering: This involves creating new features or variables from the existing data that can improve the performance of ML algorithms. Statistics and mathematics help to identify relevant features, measure their importance, and apply techniques such as dimensionality reduction, feature selection, feature extraction, and feature construction.

3.Model selection: This involves selecting the best model to use for the given data set. This requires understanding the type of data and the type of model that will best solve the problem. The best ML algorithm needs to be chosen for a given problem and data set. Statistics and mathematics help to compare different algorithms based on their assumptions, complexity, accuracy, generalization, and robustness. They also help to tune the hyperparameters of the algorithms using methods such as cross-validation, grid search, random search, and Bayesian optimization.

4.Model fitting: This involves optimizing the model parameters to fit the data. This is done using an optimization algorithm such as gradient descent, which adjusts the model parameters to minimize the prediction error. Gradient descent is a powerful optimization technique that can be used to find the optimal values of parameters that minimize a loss function. In ML, the loss function measures how well a model fits the data, and the goal is to minimize the error between the model’s predictions and the actual outcomes. Gradient descent works by iteratively updating the parameters in the direction of the steepest descent of the loss function, using a learning rate that controls the size of each update. One of the challenges of gradient descent is choosing an appropriate learning rate. If the learning rate is too small, the algorithm will take a long time to converge to the optimal solution. The algorithm may overshoot the optimal solution and diverge if the learning rate is too large. Another challenge of gradient descent is that it may get stuck in a local minimum, where the loss function has a lower value than any nearby point but not necessarily the lowest value overall. To avoid this problem, some variants of gradient descent have been developed that use different strategies to explore the loss function landscape and escape from local minima. Some of the common types of gradient descent are given below:

●Batch gradient descent (BGD): This is the simplest form of gradient descent and it ensures that the algorithm converges to the global minimum, but it can be very slow and computationally expensive when the data set is large. BGD is an iterative optimization approach that involves moving in the direction of the steepest descent, which is determined by the negative gradient of the function. In ML, this function typically serves as the loss or error function, which quantifies the degree of fit between the model and the data. The model parameters can be acquired from the data by minimizing the loss function. BGD involves calculating the gradient utilizing the complete data set at each iteration. An advantage of BGD is the assurance of convergence to the global minimum of the loss function, provided that the learning rate is sufficiently small. Another benefit is that BGD may be readily parallelized and dispersed across numerous machines or processors. A limitation of BGD arises when the data set is extensive since it can result in sluggish performance and high computing costs. In addition, in the event of data set modifications or the inclusion of new data points, the algorithm must recalculate the gradient by utilizing the complete data set, resulting in potential wastage and inefficiency. Another disadvantage is that BGD might be susceptible to outliers and noisy data points. This can result in inadequate performance and less-than-ideal solutions.

●Stochastic gradient descent (SGD): SGD employs a modification whereby, instead of utilizing the entire data set, it randomly chooses a single data point (or a small group of data points) throughout each iteration and calculates the gradient based on it. This minimizes the computational expense and enables quicker updates. In addition, when the gradient is calculated from a random subset, the algorithm provides inherent variability and randomness. This characteristic prevents the algorithm from becoming trapped in suboptimal local minima or saddle points. SGD can adjust to varying data distributions and effectively manage noisy or redundant data, surpassing the performance of traditional gradient descent methods. Nevertheless, SGD also presents certain limitations and obstacles. One issue is that the gradient derived from a random sample might exhibit significant noise and inaccuracy, leading to fluctuations and instability in parameter updates. Another obstacle lies in the fact that SGD can be highly responsive to the arrangement and choice of data points, impacting its convergence and overall efficiency. Numerous variations and extensions of SGD have been developed to address these difficulties and to enhance its efficiency and resilience. One such technique is momentum, which incorporates a fraction of the previous parameter update into the current update to expedite convergence and mitigate oscillations. Another technique is adaptive learning rate methods, such as AdaGrad, RMSProp, and Adam, which dynamically adjust the learning rate for each parameter based on its historical gradients.

●Mini-batch gradient descent: This is a method that merges the benefits of BGD and SGD for optimizing the parameters of an ML model. Mini-batch gradient descent divides the training data set into smaller subsets, known as mini-batches. It then utilizes each mini-batch to calculate the gradient and modify the parameters during each iteration. Implementing this technique can mitigate the noise and variability inherent in SGD while enhancing the velocity and effectiveness of batch gradient descent. The ideal mini-batch size is contingent upon several aspects, including the data distribution, the model’s architecture, and the hardware’s setup. Mini-batch gradient descent can be enhanced by employing distinct learning rates for each parameter or by utilizing adaptive learning rates that dynamically adjust based on the prior gradients. These strategies can be used to prevent being stuck at local minima or saddle points and to achieve faster convergence towards the global minimum of the loss function. Several examples of these techniques are momentum, RMSProp, Adam, and AdaGrad.

●Momentum-based gradient descent: This is an alternative form of gradient descent that helps accelerate the optimization process and prevent it being trapped in local minima. This incorporates a momentum component that monitors and includes prior parameter adjustments into the current update using a scaling factor. By following this approach, the algorithm may effectively build up speed in areas where the gradient remains steady and smooth while decreasing speed in areas where the gradient frequently changes direction. This can facilitate the algorithm’s escape from regions with low gradients or local minima more rapidly and mitigate oscillations around the optimal point. Momentum-based gradient descent is a prevalent optimization approach in machine learning and deep learning. It is widely utilized due to its ability to enhance the performance and efficiency of neural networks and other intricate models.

●Adaptive gradient descent: This is a family of algorithms that adaptively adjusts the learning rate for each parameter based on its historical gradients. This means that parameters with large and frequent updates will have a lower learning rate, while those with small and infrequent updates will have a higher learning rate. This way, the algorithm can avoid overshooting the optimal value or getting stuck in a local minimum. Some examples are AdaGrad, Adadelta, RMSProp, and Adam. AdaGrad is a learning rate scaling algorithm that is inversely proportional to the square root of the sum of squared gradients. This means that the learning rate decreases as the gradient accumulates over time. This can be beneficial for sparse features but can also cause the learning rate to become too small and stop the learning process. Adadelta is an extension of AdaGrad that addresses the problem of diminishing learning rates. Instead of a cumulative sum, it employs a moving average of squared gradients. In addition, it provides a decay rate parameter to regulate the speed at which the average diminishes. This way, the algorithm can adapt to changing gradients and maintain a more robust learning rate. RMSProp is another AdaGrad extension that uses a moving average of squared gradients but with a different formula. The average’s square root splits the learning rate, and a momentum parameter is included to incorporate a percentage of the previous update into the current one. By employing this method, the algorithm can expedite the convergence process and overcome stagnant points in the optimization process. Adam is a popular algorithm that combines the ideas of Adadelta and RMSProp. It uses both moving averages of gradients and squared gradients, and it also introduces two parameters called beta1 and beta2 that control the decay rates of these averages. In addition, it performs bias correction to account for the initial values of these averages. This way, the algorithm can achieve fast and stable convergence with minimal hyperparameter tuning.

5.Model evaluation: This involves assessing how well the model performs on unseen data. This means assessing the quality and validity of the machine learning models using metrics such as accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, ROC curve, AUC, confusion matrix, MSE, MAE, R2-score, etc. Statistics and mathematics help to interpret these metrics, test the significance of the results, and diagnose potential problems such as overfitting, underfitting, bias and variance.

6.Model interpretation: This involves explaining how the ML models work and why they make certain predictions or decisions. Statistics and mathematics help to understand the logic and mechanisms of the algorithms, and to visualize or quantify their outputs using methods such as feature importance, partial dependence plots, SHAP values and LIME.

7.Testing: Testing refers to assessing how well an ML algorithm performs on unseen data points or inputs compared to its performance when trained (estimation). This evaluation helps assess whether the predictions made by a given algorithm match up with those made by humans for similar inputs (validation). Testing typically consists of splitting available input into two subsets: one for training purposes and the other for testing purposes; this helps ensure unbiased results since both sets contain randomly distributed examples from the provided data set (cross-validation). The testing phase also allows us to measure performance metrics like accuracy rate, recall score, and precision score, which can then be compared against benchmark values or those achieved during earlier iterations while tuning parameters to improve them further, if needed. Moreover, it indicates overfitting/underfitting problems associated with our approach towards solving the given problem(s). In addition, some ML algorithms utilize cross-validation techniques wherein multiple tests are conducted using different combinations/splits between ‘training’ versus ‘testing’ data sets; this further assists in ensuring better estimates while making predictions about future outcomes/scenarios.

[1.9Machine Learning versus Automation](#07_Contents.xhtml#sub-9)

Machine learning and automation are two related but distinct concepts that are often used interchangeably in the context of artificial intelligence. However, they have different meanings and implications for various domains and applications.

ML is a branch of computer science that deals with creating systems or algorithms that can learn from data and improve their performance over time. It can be used for tasks such as classification, regression, clustering, recommendation, natural language processing and computer vision. It can also be seen as a form of automation, since it enables computers to perform tasks that would otherwise require human intelligence or intervention.

Automation, on the other hand, is a broader term that refers to the use of technology to control or operate processes or systems without human input. Automation can be applied to various fields such as manufacturing, transportation, agriculture and healthcare. Automation can also involve machine learning, but not necessarily.

The main difference between ML and automation is that ML involves learning from data, while automation involves executing predefined rules or instructions. Machine learning can enable automation to adapt to changing conditions or situations, while automation can enable machine learning to scale up or speed up its operations. ML and automation can also complement each other in various ways. For example, ML can be used to optimize or improve the performance of automated systems, while automation can be used to collect or label data for ML models.

ML and automation are both important and powerful technologies that have the potential to transform various industries and domains. However, they also pose some challenges and limitations that need to be addressed. For instance, ML may require large amounts of data or computational resources, while automation may require careful design or regulation. Moreover, ML and automation may have ethical or social implications that need to be considered, such as the impact on human jobs, privacy, security, and accountability. Therefore, it is essential to understand the differences and similarities between ML and automation and use them wisely and responsibly.

[1.10Predictive and Descriptive Tasks in Machine Learning](#07_Contents.xhtml#sub-10)

Predictive and descriptive tasks are two of the major types of tasks that are performed in machine learning. Predictive tasks involve predicting future events or behaviors based on data from the past, while descriptive tasks involve describing the characteristics of existing data.

Predictive tasks create a model that can predict future events or behavior based on prior data. For example, predictive models in financial forecasting may be used to estimate future stock prices or exchange rates. Forecasting client demand for certain products and services, anticipating fraudulent behavior before it occurs, and recommending content to social media platform users are some more examples.

Descriptive tasks entail using techniques like grouping or segmentation analysis to explain aspects of current data sets without making future predictions. Descriptive analysis can frequently uncover previously unknown or poorly understood correlations between elements.

Finally, it is vital to remember that ML algorithms may also be used for productive tasks, such as making new digital photographs, in which machines create something new rather than merely evaluating what already exists (as is seen with predictive and descriptive analytics). Such techniques enable machines to learn from previous experiences and develop new material with some degree of uniqueness – essential skills when used appropriately!

[1.11Some Terminology Related to Machine Learning](#07_Contents.xhtml#sub-11)

Let us use examples to explain the terminology. To buy good quality lady’s fingers, one should look for the following:

•The color should be bright green, without any brown or black spots.

•The texture should be firm and crisp, not soft or mushy.

•The size should be medium, not too small or too large.

•The shape should be straight and slender, not curved or twisted.

These factors are examples of a domain set, which is a collection of possible values for a certain attribute or feature. A domain set defines the range and type of values that an attribute can take.

A label is a value that represents the category or class of an object or an observation. For example, in a classification problem, the label can be yes or no, positive or negative, spam or not spam, etc. A label is usually the output or the target variable that we want to predict or learn from the data.

A domain point is a specific value or instance of an attribute or feature. For example, if the attribute is color, then a domain point can be green, red, blue, etc. A domain point is usually the input or independent variable that we use to predict or learn the label.

A mapping function is a mathematical function that relates the domain points to the labels. For example, if we have a mapping function f(x) = y, then x is the domain point and y is the label. A mapping function describes how the input affects the output, or how the features influence the target.

A learner is an algorithm or a model that learns the mapping function from the data. For example, a learner can be a decision tree, a neural network, a logistic regression, etc. A learner tries to find the best mapping function that fits the data and minimizes error.

A predictor is a function that uses the learned mapping function to predict the label for a new domain point. For example, if we have a predictor p(x) = f(x), then p(x) is the predictor and f(x) is the learned mapping function. A predictor applies the mapping function to a new input and outputs the predicted label.

[1.12Types of Machine Learning](#07_Contents.xhtml#sub-12)

The algorithms and techniques used in machine learning are used to build models that can learn from data and make predictions or decisions. Following are the types of machine learning: supervised learning, unsupervised learning, reinforcement learning, transfer learning, and meta learning ([Fig. 1.5](#09_Chapter1.xhtml#fig1-5)).

![](Images/f1-5.jpg)

[Figure 1.5](#09_Chapter1.xhtml#fig-1-5)  Types of machine learning

1.12.1Supervised Learning

Supervised learning is ML in which machines are trained using well ‘labeled’ training data, and they predict the output based on that data. ‘Labeled data’ means some input data that is already tagged with the correct output. Although this method requires accurate data labeling, supervised learning is compelling and yields excellent results when applied appropriately. The supervisor instructs the machines to predict the output using the training data correctly.

The training data set provides the algorithm with the labeled parameters necessary for the problem and shares many characteristics with the final data set. It provides the algorithm with information about the issue, the solution, and the various data points to be handled. To establish a cause-and-effect relationship between the variables in the data set, the ML algorithm then finds relationships between the input parameters. For example, a supervised learning algorithm aims to find a mapping function to map the input variable (x) with the output variable (y). It applies the same concept as a student learning under a teacher’s supervision.

When the training and processing are complete, we test the model by supplying sample data to see if it accurately predicts the output. The system builds a model using labeled data to understand the data sets and learn about each data. In the real world, supervised learning can also be used for risk assessment, image classification, fraud detection and spam filtering. When we play a film or episode on Amazon Prime Video, we are also informing the ML algorithm to find similar shows based on our preference.

Supervised learning can be further grouped into two categories of algorithms ([Fig. 1.6](#09_Chapter1.xhtml#fig1-6)): regression and classification. Classification and regression are two fundamental types of ML problems that are used to solve a wide range of real-world problems. In essence, classification is a type of problem where the goal is to predict a categorical outcome, while regression is a type of problem where the goal is to predict a continuous outcome. To illustrate this concept, let us consider the example of an average person’s needs and how they can be grouped into classification and regression problems.

For instance, if a person is concerned about whether their son will get a job or not, this is a classification problem. The outcome is binary: either the son will get a job or he will not. Similarly, if a person is interested in knowing at what age their son will get married, this is a regression problem. The output will be a numerical value, such as 28 or 30. Another example of a regression problem is when a person wants to know which area the bride will come from. The answer will be in the form of a city or area name, which is a continuous variable.

![](Images/f1-6.jpg)

[Figure 1.6](#09_Chapter1.xhtml#fig-1-6)  Types of supervised learning

1.12.1.1Regression

Regression algorithms are used if there is a relationship between the input variable and the output variable. It is used for prediction of continuous variables, such as in weather forecasting, market trends and stock values. Some popular regression algorithms that come under supervised learning are linear regression, regression tree, Bayesian linear regression, and polynomial regression.

Linear Regression:Here, a mathematical equation describes the relationship between two or more variables. For example, the ‘dependent variable’ and additional variables (‘independent variables’) are investigated. Regression uses independent variables to model a target prediction value. These models vary according to the number of independent variables they use and the type of relationship they take into account between the dependent and independent variables.

Consider a scenario where you wish to forecast your monthly salary based on your years of experience and educational background. Monthly salary can be the dependent variable in linear regression, whereas years of experience and education can be considered as independent variables. A line that best matches these points is then estimated using the linear regression model.

To make predictions with fresh observations that fall within the range of values in our data set, we need to identify the mathematical equation that best captures the data. Ordinary least squares (OLS), the most popular type of linear regression, determines the line with the fewest squared distances between each point and its corresponding value on our estimated line. This method provides us with an estimate for our model’s unknown parameters, which we can use to make predictions with new data points outside the data set range using extrapolation techniques.

Regression Tree: A continuous target variable is predicted using a regression tree. Based on the values of the input features, it recursively divides the data into various branches, and the target variable is predicted using the mean or median of the values in each leaf node. Each internal node in a decision tree or regression tree represents a feature, and each leaf node in a tree-like structure represents a predicted value or class. The type of target variable that a regression tree and a decision tree are used to predict is their primary distinction.

The root of a regression tree, the first node, contains all of the training data. The data set is then divided into two sections using criteria like the mean or median value of the target variable, creating right and left child nodes.

Bayesian Regression: When the data set has too few or poorly distributed data, Bayesian regression can be very helpful. In contrast to conventional regression techniques, where the output is only derived from a single attribute value, a Bayesian regression model’s output is derived from a probability distribution. The result y is produced by a normal distribution (where mean and variance are normalized). Bayesian linear regression aims to identify the ‘posterior’ distribution for the model parameters rather than the model parameters themselves. Therefore, it is assumed that the model parameters will follow a distribution in addition to the output y.

Polynomial Regression: This models the relationship between a dependent variable (y) and an independent variable (x) as an nth-degree polynomial. Like linear regression, polynomial regression seeks the optimal path through the data points by utilizing the relationship between the variables x and y. For instance, it is frequently used to forecast the rate at which COVID-19 and other infectious diseases will spread. Numerous varieties of polynomial regression exist because a polynomial equation’s degree has no upper bound and can go up to the nth value. For instance, the second degree of a polynomial equation is typically expressed as a quadratic equation. As stated, this degree can reach the nth value, and you can create as many equations as you like.

1.12.1.2Classification

The second category of supervised learning methods uses classification models to draw conclusions from observed categorical values. It predicts the likelihood that new data will fall into one of the predetermined categories using the input training data. Filtering emails into ‘spam’ or ‘non-spam’ is one of the most popular uses of classification.

In ML, there are two different classification types. When there are only two possible classes for a problem, it is said to be in the binary classification category (as in ‘cat or dog,’ ‘yes or no’). If there are more than two potential classes, the problem is a multi-class classifier.

Some classification algorithms are K\-nearest neighbor, decision tree, random forest, support vector machine (SVM), and linear classifiers.

K\-Nearest Neighbor (KNN): KNN is classified as a lazy learner because it does not create any predictive models. Instead, it stores all the training data and uses it to make predictions about new data points based on their similarity to stored points. This technique groups the closest objects in a data set and identifies the most common or average traits. It determines a data point’s likelihood of joining any of the groups based on which group the data points closest to it belong to.

Decision Tree: A decision tree is best utilized to solve classification problems; it can also be used to tackle regression difficulties. It divides data points into two similar groups at a time, starting with the ‘tree trunk,’ moving through the ‘branches,’ and ending with the ‘leaves,’ until the groups are more closely related to one another. This method is similar to a flow chart. Internal nodes in a tree-structured classifier stand in for a data set’s features, branches for the decision-making process, and each leaf node for the classification result. They do not require feature scaling and are simple to understand. In addition, compared to other algorithms, data cleaning requirements are lower. It also leaves out insignificant features.

Random Forest: A random forest is a collection of many decision trees drawn from randomly selected data subsets, and it may be able to predict outcomes more accurately than a single decision tree.

Support Vector Machine (SVM): This well-known ML algorithm is frequently used for classification and regression tasks. Specifically, it is employed to address classification issues. Finding the best decision boundaries in an N\-dimensional space that can divide data points into classes is the primary goal of SVM, and the best decision boundary is referred to as a hyperplane. Support vectors are the extreme vectors that SVM chooses to locate the hyperplane. SVMs use a hyperplane to group objects based on shared characteristics and generate coordinates for each object in an N\-dimensional space.

Linear Classifiers: These categorize objects based on the value of a linear combination of their attributes. The characteristics of an object are also referred to as feature values, and they are usually displayed to the machine in a feature vector. Such classifiers achieve accuracy levels comparable to non-linear classifiers while requiring less time to train and use, making them an excellent solution for real-world issues like document classification and, more generally, for issues with many variables (features).

1.12.2Unsupervised Learning

Unsupervised learning, as the name suggests, has no data labels and is the process of learning patterns from unlabeled data without any supervision.

For example, suppose we have a data set of the sales transactions from a shop, and we want to find out which items are sold more frequently than others. We do not need to tell the computer what the items are. We can simply feed the data to an unsupervised learning algorithm, such as clustering or association rule mining, and let the computer discover the patterns and relationships among the items. The output of the unsupervised learning algorithm can help us understand customer behavior and preferences, and optimize the inventory and marketing strategies of the shop.

The training is provided to the machine with the set of data that has not been labeled, classified, or categorized, and the algorithm needs to act on that data without any supervision. The goal of unsupervised learning is to find the structure and patterns in the input data, group that data according to similarities, and represent that data set in a compressed format. Compared to supervised learning, unsupervised ML services are not very popular because they have fewer applications in day-to-day life. Unsupervised learning creates hidden structures. Relationships between data points are then perceived by the algorithm randomly or abstractly, with absolutely no input required from humans. Instead of a specific, defined, and set problem statement, unsupervised learning algorithms can adapt to the data.

Suppose the unsupervised learning algorithm is given an input data set containing images of different types of bulls and cows. The algorithm is not trained upon the given data set, which means it does not have any idea about the features of the data set. The task of the unsupervised learning algorithm is to identify the image features on it own. The unsupervised learning algorithm will perform this task by clustering the image data set into groups according to similarities between images.

In unsupervised learning, we do not have a predetermined result. The machine tries to find useful insights from the huge amount of data. It can be further classified into two categories: clustering and association ([Fig. 1.7](#09_Chapter1.xhtml#fig1-7)). Anomaly detection and dimension reduction are also other types. We will discuss these in detail in Chapter 6.

![](Images/f1-7.jpg)

[Figure 1.7](#09_Chapter1.xhtml#fig-1-7)  Types of unsupervised learning algorithms

1.12.2.1Clustering

The process of grouping objects into clusters so that those with the most significant similarity stay together and share little to no similarities with those in other groups is called clustering. A cluster is a collection of related items or individuals that are situated or placed close to one another. Because every point in a cluster typically exhibits similarities in those characteristics, ML could be used to identify traits and distinguish between these clusters. Clustering serves as the foundation for numerous ML applications that address data issues in various industries. In a perfect world, machines would be able to recognize various objects and distinguish between them based on their physical characteristics. Therefore, clustering algorithms can be widely used in tasks such as image segmentation, statistical data analysis, classifying diseases in medical science, and customer classification in marketing research. Some commonly used clustering algorithms are K\-means, MeanShift clustering, and DBSCAN.

K\-Means Clustering:This is a popular unsupervised machine learning technique for data exploration and analysis. It is used for grouping or clustering data points into distinct clusters or categories. It aims to divide the data set into meaningful subgroups based on specific characteristics. The algorithm examines each data point and assigns it to one of several groups based on attribute similarities.

The K\-means algorithm can analyze data containing discrete, continuous, numerical entities. However, this algorithm has flaws, including difficulties with categorical data, outliers, and non-linear data. Furthermore, it would help if we decided how many data clusters we want. Finally, K\-means is best applied to smaller data sets because it iterates over all the data points. As a result, if a data set contains many data points, it would take longer to classify them.

Consider the following example. Assume a company makes sports shoes and wants to divide its customers into two distinct groups: male and female. We would begin by gathering customer information such as age, gender, shopping preferences, and spending patterns, among other things, and then use K\-means clustering to determine distinct criteria to determine who should go where!

For example, suppose the data indicates that consumers between 18 and 25 generally spend more on sports shoes. In that case, this specific age group may be grouped as a cluster, with a centroid representing the higher expenditure. In contrast, clients who are 30 years or older and may have distinct purchasing patterns would form a separate cluster characterized by a centroid representing reduced spending on footwear. This differentiation enables the organization to comprehend and anticipate client conduct by considering their age.

MeanShift Clustering: The MeanShift algorithm does not require us to specify the number of clusters, in contrast to the K\-means algorithm. If we need clarification on the patterns in the data, the algorithm automatically determines the number of clusters, which is a significant advantage over K\-means. Dense data point areas use a sliding window, centroid-based algorithm to locate the center group/class points. All center point candidates are the mean value of the sliding window points. Such windows are then sorted post-processing to remove duplicates and give the final group center points. Image segmentation tasks are where MeanShift clustering is most frequently used. Kernel density estimation is the foundation of the MeanShift algorithm.

MeanShift algorithms iteratively assign each data point to the closest cluster centroid, which is initialized arbitrarily. Then, each point is iteratively moved in the space based on where the most points are, that is, the mode. This is similar to the K\-means algorithm. This method overcomes the selection of groups and cluster centers as the mean values are discovered automatically. The clusters also exhibit data sense due to convergence to the areas having maximum data points intuitively.

DBSCAN: Density-based spatial clustering of applications with noise is a prominent algorithm for identifying clusters in spatial data based on the density of data points. DBSCAN does not require the number of clusters to be specified in advance. It works on the principle that clusters are high-density areas separated by low-density regions. The clusters can therefore be found in any arbitrary shape.

1.12.2.2Association

Association is the second type of unsupervised learning. Association rule mining finds associations based on co-occurrences. It determines the set of items that occur together in the data set.

The association rule makes marketing strategy more practical; for example, people who buy X items (say, a toothbrush) also tend to purchase Y items (say, toothpaste).

Association rule mining is used to identify new and exciting insights between different objects in a set and frequent patterns in transactional data or any relational database. The relationship is usually represented in the form of rules or frequent itemsets. It is used in market basket analysis (where items are bought together), web usage mining, and continuous production.

Market basket analysis examines consumer purchasing patterns by identifying relationships between the various items consumers place in their shopping baskets. Retailers create marketing strategies by analyzing which items users frequently purchase and discovering these associations. Web mining has the unique ability to support a variety of different data types. Many aspects of the web produce various mining methods. These include web pages, hyperlinks between web pages, and web server logs that can be used to track user activity.

Association rule learning can be divided into three algorithms: Apriori, ECLAT and FP Growth.

Apriori Algorithm: The Apriori algorithm uses relational databases to learn association rules and mine frequently occurring itemsets. It assists in identifying products that can be purchased in combination and is primarily used for market basket analysis.

This algorithm efficiently determines the itemset using a breadth-first search and a hash tree. Its ‘join’ and ‘prune’ steps condense the search space. It establishes the strength or weakness of the connection between two objects. Finding the frequent itemsets from a large data set involves an iterative process. The itemsets frequently used are those whose support is higher than the threshold value or the minimum support specified by the user. It means that if A and B together are frequent itemsets, then A and B should also be frequent itemsets separately.

This is the most simple and easy-to-understand algorithm among the association rule learning algorithms. The rules are intuitive and easy to communicate to an end user. However, the disadvantage of this algorithm is that when working with large data sets, it could be faster and more efficient. It uses a lot of resources to scan the database many times, generate many candidate sets, and check each of them.

ECLAT Algorithm: This stands for equivalence class transformation. It uses a depth-first search technique to find frequent itemsets in a transaction database. It performs faster than the Apriori algorithm. The ECLAT algorithm can be applied only to data sets in the vertical format. Since most data sets are in the horizontal format, to apply the ECLAT algorithm, we first have to convert them to the vertical format. Thus, the ECLAT algorithm works better with small and medium-sized data sets. The ECLAT algorithm has low memory requirements compared to Apriori as it uses a depth-first search approach. The result of the ECLAT algorithm is frequent itemsets with their support.

FP Growth Algorithm: The FP (frequent pattern) Growth algorithm is a better version of the Apriori algorithm. Instead of using candidate generations, this algorithm finds frequent itemsets which improve performance. It employs the divide-and-conquer tactic.

1.12.3Reinforcement Learning

A significant drawback of ML is that vast volumes of data are needed to train models. The more complex a model, the more data it may require. The required data may not exist, or we may need access to the correct data. Further, the data collected might need to be more reliable. It may have false or missing values or need to be updated. Learning from a small subset of actions will not help expand the vast realm of solutions that may work for a particular problem. Machines must learn to perform actions alone rather than just learn from humans. These problems are overcome by reinforcement learning (RL).

Reinforcement learning is a sub-branch of ML that trains a model to return an optimum solution for a problem by taking a sequence of decisions. RL differs from supervised learning in that in the latter, the training data has the answer key, so the model is trained with the correct answer itself. In contrast, there is no answer key in reinforcement learning, but the reinforcement agent decides what to do to perform the given task. Without a training data set, it is bound to learn from experience. RL solves a specific type of problem where decision-making is sequential and the goal is long-term, such as game-playing, robotics, etc.

For example, a dog cannot be told directly what to do because he does not understand human language. So, instead, we adopt a different approach. For example, we will reward the dog with food if he behaves in the desired manner. Now, whenever the dog encounters the same circumstance, the dog performs a similar action even more eagerly, anticipating a greater reward (food). This is similar to discovering that a dog learns ‘what to do’ from satisfying experiences. At the same time, the dog also learns what not to do when faced with negative experiences. In this case, the dog is an agent exposed to the environment (house). For example, when your dog is sitting, you ask it to go for a walk using a particular word. The agent responds by moving from one ‘state’ to another through an action. For instance, your dog transitions from lying down to walking.

An agent’s response is an action, and a policy is a way to choose an action given a state in the hopes of better results. After the transition, they may receive a reward or a punishment. Reinforcement comes in two varieties. Positive reinforcement is when a behavior increases in strength and frequency because of an external event. In other words, it influences behavior in a good way. Negative reinforcement is the strengthening of behavior because an adverse condition is stopped or avoided.

The main elements of an RL system are:

•The agent or learner (the dog, in this case)

•The environment the agent interacts with (house)

•The policy that the agent follows to take actions

•The reward signal (food) that the agent observes upon taking actions

The agent gains knowledge through trial and error, and using its experience, it improves its performance. The agent keeps doing these three things – take action, alter his state or remain in it, and get feedback – which helps him learn about and explore his surroundings.

In RL, the agent must be instructed on the surroundings and the appropriate course of action.
