4.2.2Other Definitions

Concave Function: A function *f*:ℝ^(*n*)→ℝ

(4.5)

*f*(*α**x*+(1−*α*)*y*) ≥ *α**f*(*x*) + (1−*α*)*f*(*y*)

A concave function is a mathematical function that takes a convex (upward-facing) shape when graphed. This function has several uses in ML. In supervised learning, where the model aims to predict a target variable based on input features, concave functions can help optimize by making it easier to detect local minima or maxima. When the cost function (which measures how accurate a model’s predictions are) is plotted as a graph, its shape will be either convex or concave, depending on how well the model works. A shallow convex curve indicates that more training would be beneficial, whereas deep curves often indicate overfitting (where models fit too closely to their training data).

A concave cost curve typically indicates better performance than its convex counterpart, allowing for more efficient optimization by helping identify regions with lower values more easily. In addition, some unsupervised learning models (which do not use target variables) also rely on minimizing costs using concave functions.

Strictly Concave Function: A function *f*:ℝ^(*n*)→ℝ

(4.6)

*f*(*α**x*+(1−*α*)*y*) > *α**f*(*x*) + (1−*α*)*f*(*y*)

Note: f is concave if and only if f is convex. Similarly f is strictly concave if and only if -f is strictly convex.

Affine functions *f*(*x*) = *a*^(*T*)*x* + *b*, (*a*∈ℝ^(*n*), *b*∈ℝ) are functions that are both convex and concave.

When using strictly concave functions in ML, one usually looks at changes in objective function values (cost) and aims to reduce them gradually by considering small changes in inputs or parameters at each step. Strictly concave functions allow us to analyze how much impact any change has made on our overall cost quickly and efficiently without having to perform computations for every possible combination of inputs or parameters being tested. The ability of strictly concave functions to rapidly analyze complex data sets also allows them to be used as part of more sophisticated predictive models like neural networks where multiple layers of neurons can be trained simultaneously, with each layer receiving feedback from previous layers about how its output might affect performance downstream; this helps make training faster and more accurate than traditional methods which tend not require such insights into how one layer affects another during training.

Convex Combination: The convex combination of a set of points *x*[1], ⋯*x*[*k*] is defined as $\\sum\\limits\_{i = 1}^{k}\\alpha\_{i}x\_{i}$ such that $\\alpha\_{i} \\geq 0\\forall i = 1\\cdots k\\,\\text{and}\\,\\sum\\limits\_{i = 1}^{k}\\alpha\_{i} = 0$.

The convex combination method combines different models into one, taking a weighted average of all the individual models. The weights assigned to each model are based on how accurate each model is and how well they work together.

For example, suppose you have three different regression models that predict stock prices instead of choosing just one. In that case, you can combine them with convex combinations and get a more accurate prediction from the combined result. The same concept applies to other areas of ML, such as classification or clustering algorithms.

This technique helps create more robust and accurate systems by combining information from multiple sources rather than relying on just one source for all predictions or decisions made by an algorithm or system. In addition, this method allows for greater flexibility when making changes to optimize results since weights can be adjusted easily without having to rebuild the entire model from scratch.

Convex Hull: The convex hull of a set S is the set of all convex combinations of points in S.

(4.7)

$\\left. conv\\left( s \\right) = \\text{\\{}\\alpha\_{1}x\_{1} + \\cdots + \\alpha\_{n}x\_{n}\\text{|}x\_{i} \\in \\text{S},\\alpha\_{i} \\geq 0,i = 1\\cdots n,\\sum\\limits\_{i = 1}^{n}\\alpha\_{i} = 1 \\right\\}$

The convex hull of a set S is the smallest convex set which includes S.

The convex hull is a concept used in mathematics and computer science. It describes the shape of an object in terms of the boundary lines that can be drawn to enclose it. The idea is to find a set of points, called vertices, which form the convex hull such that any point inside the area enclosed by these points is also part of the convex hull.

Convex hulls have numerous applications in ML, as they can detect patterns and clusters in data sets. For example, if you want to identify specific areas with more concentrated clusters of data points, you could use a convex hull technique to draw boundaries around those areas, highlighting where those clusters are located. This type of analysis can be helpful in fraud detection since it helps identify clusters or outlying behavior that could indicate fraudulent activity. This technique can also improve accuracy when classifying new data sets since it allows us to quickly and easily group similar points into categories without having to examine each point individually.

Gradient: The gradient of a function *f*:ℝ^(*n*)→ℝ is defined as

(4.8)

$\\nabla f\\left( x \\right): = \\left\\lbrack {\\frac{\\partial f\\left( x \\right)}{\\partial x\_{1}},\\frac{\\partial f\\left( x \\right)}{\\partial x\_{2}},\\cdots,\\frac{\\partial f\\left( x \\right)}{\\partial x\_{n}}} \\right\\rbrack^{T}$

In other words, for a function *f*:ℝ^(*n*)→ℝ.

A gradient vector is a mathematical tool that helps to calculate the direction and magnitude of change for certain variables. In ML, gradient vectors are used in optimization algorithms such as gradient descent. Gradient descent is an iterative approach to find the optimum value for specific parameters within a given function by calculating the derivative concerning those parameters. It allows us to find values of parameters that optimize our cost function and minimize errors in our ML models.

In practice, this means that when training complex models such ANNs, backpropagation can be used to calculate the derivative of each layer concerning each parameter (weights and bias) and use it in combination with gradient vectors to reduce errors during the training process. This encourages an efficient search process since we do not have to manually test thousands or millions of combinations before finding an optimal set of weights and bias values for our ANNs.

Properties of a gradient vector

•Orthogonal to the function contours

•Points in the direction of greatest increase of a function

•Negative gradient points in the direction of greatest decrease

•Dot product of a vector *v**v*

Example 10: *f*(*x*,*y*) = 4*x*² + 2*y*² − 5 xy. Find the gradient at (2,3).

$\\nabla f\\left( {x,y} \\right) = \\begin{bmatrix} {8x - 5y} \\\\ {- 5x + 4y} \\\\ \\end{bmatrix}$

Evaluating the gradient at (2, 3),

$\\nabla f\\left( {x,y} \\right) = \\begin{bmatrix} 1 \\\\ 2 \\\\ \\end{bmatrix}$

Stationary Point: A point $\\overline{x} \\in {\\mathbb{R}}^{n}$ is called a stationary point.

Example 11: *f*(*x*,*y*) = *x*² + *y*²

∇*f*(*x*,*y*)=\[2*x*,2*y*\]^(*T*)\=0⇒(*x*,*y*)=(0,0)

That is, the origin is the stationary point.

Optimizing involves finding the optimal weights and hyperparameters that will provide the most accurate performance on unseen data. One way to achieve this is by using gradient descent, where we take small steps toward an optimum point, known as a stationary point or local minimum. In gradient descent, we start at an initial guess and iteratively move towards lower error rates until no further improvements can be made concerning that particular parameter set, known as converging at a stationary point.

The stationary points either have zero gradients because they are local minima (the lowest point in its vicinity) or equal gradients in all directions since they lie on flat surfaces (plateau regions). The primary purpose of optimizing ML models is to find the parameters which produce minimal errors when evaluated on unseen data; thus, identifying these stationary points help us optimize our models and produce more accurate results than before.

Hessian Matrix: For a function *f*:ℝ^(*n*)→ℝ.

ℋ(*x*) = ∇\[∇*f*(*x*)\]^(*T*) = ∇²*f*(*x*)

(4.9)

$\\mathcal{H}\\left( x \\right) = \\begin{bmatrix} \\frac{\\partial^{2}f\\left( x \\right)}{\\partial x\_{1}^{2}} & \\cdots & \\frac{\\partial^{2}f\\left( x \\right)}{\\partial x\_{1}x\_{n}} \\\\ \\vdots & \\ddots & \\vdots \\\\ \\frac{\\partial^{2}f\\left( x \\right)}{\\partial x\_{n}x\_{1}} & \\cdots & \\frac{\\partial^{2}f\\left( x \\right)}{\\partial x\_{n}^{2}} \\\\ \\end{bmatrix}$

Example 12: *f*(*x*,*y*) = 4*x*² + 2*y*² − 5 xy. Find the Hessian matrix.

$\\nabla\\left\\lbrack {\\nabla f\\left( {x,y} \\right)} \\right\\rbrack = \\nabla\\left\\lbrack \\begin{bmatrix} {8x - 5y} \\\\ {- 5x + 4y} \\\\ \\end{bmatrix} \\right\\rbrack = \\begin{bmatrix} 8 & {- 5} \\\\ {- 5} & 4 \\\\ \\end{bmatrix}$

The Hessian matrix is a matrix of a given function’s second-order partial derivatives (derivatives of the derivatives). It is instrumental in ML to determine if a local maximum or minimum exists at a certain point by determining whether the underlying function is convex or concave. Moreover, it can help identify which parameters are essential for predicting output and how to improve them.

For example, we wish to determine the parameters leading us to the maximum global result for some ML problem. We can use the Hessian matrix to take partial derivatives of each parameter concerning the objective function and then compute its eigenvalues. If all the eigenvalues are positive, it implies that its corresponding parameter plays a vital role in predicting outputs as it contributes positively towards achieving better results; if any eigenvalue is negative, its corresponding parameter does not have much influence over predicting output and should be adjusted accordingly to achieve better results.

[4.3Optimization Problems](#07_Contents.xhtml#sub-54)

Optimization is defined informally as selecting the best choice about specific criteria from a set of alternatives or available choices. An optimization problem, in general, is defined as either a minimization or a maximization of a well-defined function of variables, subject to some constraints. Optimization problems are widely used in ML to help find a set of parameters that provide the best possible result. This is achieved by defining an objective function, which measures the performance of a given model, and then optimizing this function so that it is maximized or minimized.

For example, when dealing with supervised learning tasks such as classification or regression, an optimization problem is often used to determine the optimal parameters of the model that lead to maximum accuracy on unseen data. This can be done by minimizing some error metric such as mean squared error or log loss, and then finding parameters that minimize this metric.

Similarly, unsupervised learning algorithms also use optimization techniques such as clustering algorithms to identify data patterns without any associated labels. Optimization problems are also helpful for hyperparameter tuning when training a neural network model. They allow us to search through different combinations of hyperparameters (such as the number of layers and the number of neurons per layer) while maximizing our validation metrics (such as accuracy), thereby allowing us to achieve better performance from our models.

Optimization can be broadly classified into three categories: (a) linear and non-linear, (b) constrained and unconstrained, and (c) discrete, continuous, and probabilistic.

Linear optimization involves finding optimal solutions to problems, such as minimizing a cost function or maximizing a profit, to find the most efficient solution possible. It is often used when creating supervised ML models since it helps find best-fit solutions to linear problems. It can also be used in unsupervised models, where it can identify clusters or trends in data by optimizing parameters involved in clustering algorithms or principal component analysis.

Non\-linear optimization looks for an optimal solution without requiring an exact mathematical formula. It helps with more general tasks, such as training neural networks and other deep learning architectures, where traditional linear methods cannot provide accurate results due to their limitations in dealing with non-linear mapping functions. Non-linear optimization algorithms work by looking at how different inputs affect outputs and then selecting those inputs which produce the best results given specific criteria, allowing for more accurate predictions from complex data sets.

Constrained and unconstrained optimization techniques enable us to create more accurate models by setting up certain boundaries or constraints that need to be met while optimizing an algorithm’s performance. Unconstrained optimization refers to finding an optimal solution without imposing any restrictions or constraints on the parameters. It is used in many types of ML applications where all the parameters are unknown, such as supervised learning algorithms like decision tree and SVM, as well as deep learning techniques like backpropagation. This technique involves trying out different values for each parameter until the most optimal solution is achieved.

On the other hand, constrained optimization refers to finding an optimal value while imposing restrictions or constraints on the possible values that can be used for each parameter. This technique is often used in regression and classification problems where some general information (such as feature range) can be applied to narrow down possible solutions. Furthermore, constraints can also be imposed on objective functions (such as linearity or non-linearity constraint) to find better solutions with fewer iterations/steps compared to unconstrained optimization techniques; this reduces computational cost significantly while still achieving high accuracy.

Discrete, continuous, and probabilistic optimization helps us make decisions based on random probability distributions rather than predetermined values, such as step sizes in gradient descent methods. With discrete optimizations, we can make decisions based on discrete values representing categories in a data set rather than continuous values between two points; this enables us to understand better how each variable impacts the overall outcome being optimized for better accuracy for ML algorithms like decision trees or clustering methods like K\-means.

Continuous optimization looks at continuous variables, where derivatives are taken into account when optimizing parameters; this helps identify global minima, which further boosts our model’s performance even further through careful tuning from derivatives taken from mathematical equations used in calculus-related operations like gradient descent methods used heavily in deep learning applications such as convolutional neural networks (CNNs).

Lastly, probabilistic optimization attempts to make best guesses by approximating functions using probability distributions rather than set values; this helps us combine multiple pieces without having exact answers but still getting close enough results due to its ability to simulate different distributions allowing it to tackle uncertainty found within data sets more accurately. This makes it perfect for dealing with unstructured data sets produced from natural language processing (NLP) tasks like sentiment analysis applications.

4.3.1Notations and Basic Terminology

(4.10)

Minimize *f*(*x*) subject to *f*[*i*](*x*) ≤ 0, *i* = 1⋯*m*, *h*[*j*](*x*) = 0, *j* = 1⋯*p*

Equation (4.10) represents the basic notation of an optimization problem. The objective of the problem is to determine *x*.

•*x* ∈ ℝ^(*n*) is called the optimization variable.

•The function *f*:ℝ^(*n*)→ℝ is known as the objective function or cost function.

•The inequalities *f*[*i*](*x*) ≤ 0 are called inequality constraint functions.

Inequality constraints can be applied to a problem to solve it. They determine the values of the solution’s variables, thus providing the boundaries for a solution. In ML, inequality constraints can be used to solve problems such as optimization and feature selection. They can lead to more accurate predictions and better results when applied correctly.

Inequality constraints are also helpful in improving the performance of supervised learning algorithms like classification and regression trees (CART). In CART models, an inequality constraint is used with cost-sensitive splitting rules, encouraging economically beneficial decisions rather than statistically optimal ones. Overall, using appropriate inequality constraints during model training ensures better generalizability of ML algorithms while avoiding potential performance issues caused by overly complex models.

•The equalities h[j] (x)= 0 are called the equality constraints and the corresponding functions *h*[*j*]:ℝ^(*n*)→ℝ are called equality constraint functions.

Equality constraints refer to any restriction that requires two values to be equal. In ML, equality constraints are helpful when optimizing complex models. By adding an equality constraint, the algorithm can use mathematical equations and/or other forms of logic to better convert data into information that can be used for predictive analysis or model optimization. This allows the algorithm to work more efficiently and accurately by accounting for all possible solutions within a given set of parameters.

•The set of points for which the objective function and all constraints are well defined is called the domain of the optimization problem. The domain of the optimization problem defined in Equation (4.10) is

(4.11)

$D = \\left( {\\underset{i = 1}{\\overset{m}{\\cap}}f\_{i}} \\right)\\, \\cap \\left( {\\underset{j = 1}{\\overset{p}{\\cap}}\\, h\_{j}} \\right)~$

The domain of optimization problems also helps machines identify patterns among large quantities of data more efficiently than humans can. For example, when dealing with unstructured data such as text documents or images, an optimization problem could determine which features are most important for predicting a specific outcome or classifying an item correctly from its contents. This type of approach is commonly used in deep learning applications where researchers rely on DNNs to extract meaningful information from vast amounts of data quickly and accurately without requiring too much manual work.

Optimization algorithms are essential in helping machines learn faster and make accurate predictions based on given inputs while reducing manual labor costs associated with traditional analysis approaches requiring significant human involvement at each step.

•A point x ϵ D is called feasible point if it satisfies all the constraints defined in Equation (4.10).

•The problem defined in Equation (4.10) is said to be a feasible problem if there exists at least one feasible point. Otherwise it is called as infeasible problem.

•The set of all feasible points is called the feasible set.

Feasible sets and problems are an essential part of ML. They help us understand the data and how it relates to each other. Feasible sets collect variables that can be used to solve a given problem. These variables can include categorization, clustering, classification, and regression, which help ML algorithms optimize results. Feasible problems, on the other hand, are mathematical equations or models used to obtain optimal solutions for a particular problem set. For example, when dealing with linear regression problems, we use the least-squares approach to find the best-fit line to predict future values based on past data points.

Similarly, when dealing with classification problems, we use a logistic-regression approach. In both cases, the model is optimized using cost or loss functions, which help us get optimal solutions for our problems.

•The optimal value of the problem defined in Equation (4.10) is defined as

(4.12)

*o**p**t*^(\*)\=inf{*f*(*x*)|*f*[*i*](*x*)≤0,*i*\=1⋯*m*, *h*[*i*](*x*)=0, *i*\=1⋯*p*},

where inf represents the infimum value or minimum value

•For an infeasible problem, opt ^(\*) = ∞

•If there are feasible points x[k] such that *f*(*x*[*k*])→−∞*a**s**k*→∞, then such a problem is said to be unbounded.

•A point x ^(\*) is said to be an optimal point if it is a feasible point and solves the problem defined in Equation (4.10) such that f (x^(\*))= opt ^(\*).

•If a point x is feasible and f(x) ≤ opt ^(\*) + ϵ, then x is called ϵ –optimal.

•If an optimal point exists, then the problem is solvable.

•An optimization problem can also be a maximization problem, by considering the negation of the objective function in the minimization problem.

4.3.2Representation of Optimization Problems in Standard Form

The standard form of optimization is a mathematical method used to optimize an objective function by minimizing or maximizing the value of the function. This involves finding an equation’s maximum or minimum values or inequality, subject to certain constraints. The standard form requires that all variables are non-negative and on the left side of all inequalities, while any values that constrain the solution must be on the right side.

For example, an inequality such as x + 2 ≤4 in its standard form can be written as x ≤ 2. In this case, 2 is a constraint because it must be subtracted from x to fit into the required format. All equality constraints must also be equal to zero for them to fit into this form. For instance, if we have p = q + 3, then in its standard form, this would become p – q = 3, and q would no longer appear on either side since it has been replaced by 0 (the right-hand side). This method lets us quickly identify which variables need adjustment to achieve our desired outcome and simplifies problem-solving.

Minimize *f*(*x*)

subject to low[*i*] ≤ *x*[*i*] ≤ high[*i*], *i* = 1⋯*n*, *x*[*i*] ∈ ℝ^(*n*)

This problem can be converted to the standard form as

Minimize *f*(*x*)

subject to low[*i*] − *x*[*i*] ≤ 0, *i* = 1⋯*n*

*x*[*i*] − high[*i*] ≤ 0, *i* = 1⋯*n*

4.3.3Local Optima and Global Optima

A feasible point is said to be locally optimal if there are no other feasible points in its neighborhood with a lower objective value. A feasible point is said to be globally optimal if there are no other feasible points in its neighborhood with a lower objective value.

Formally they are defined as follows: A point x is called locally optimal if it is feasible and there exists some R\> 0 such that all feasible points z with x – z[2] ≤ R satisfy f(x) ≤ f(z).

Note: x – z[2] represents the Euclidean norm.

A point x is called globally optimal if it is feasible and for all feasible points z, f (x) ≤ f (z).

Local optima and global optima are concepts used in ML to determine the optimal solution to a problem. Local optima is the best solution within a particular region, while global optima is the best solution that could be achieved anywhere. Local optima can be seen as narrow valleys or hills in a landscape of possible solutions. Getting stuck in one of these local optima means that any changes made to improve one aspect of the solution will worsen other aspects, resulting in a worse outcome than staying at that optimum local state. The relative flatness and closeness of neighboring solutions mean that finding an even better solution than this local maximum requires big jumps across various parameters instead.

On the other hand, global optima are like being on top of a mountain peak from which every direction looks downwards – it is much easier to identify improvement areas and take steps towards them without risking getting stuck in another suboptimal state again. Furthermore, any changes will likely result in an improved overall outcome since all neighboring solutions look less attractive than this summit point.

ML algorithms use different techniques, such as gradient descent or simulated annealing, to search for local and global optima when solving problems involving multiple input variables (which can often yield thousands or even millions of possible combinations if left unchecked). This helps ensure they find both satisfactory and ‘best’ results by exploring all possible configurations before giving up on their search process – maximizing accuracy and effectiveness for tasks such as an image or speech recognition where solutions must be near perfect for successful completion.

For a convex optimization problem, all locally optimal points are globally optimal.

[4.4Convex Optimization](#07_Contents.xhtml#sub-55)

An optimization problem is convex if its objective function is a convex function, inequality constraints are convex and equality constraints are affine.

(4.13)

Minimize *f*(*x*) subject to *f*[*i*](*x*) ≤ 0, *h*[*j*](*x*) = 0, *i* = 1⋯*m*, *j* = 1⋯*p*,

where f[i] (x) ≤ 0 are convex sets and h[j] (x)= 0 are affine functions.

The three main requirements for a convex optimization problem are:

•Objective function should be convex

•Inequality constraints should be convex

•Equality constraints are affine functions only

The feasible set of a convex optimization problem is convex since its domain is defined as

(4.14)

$D = \\text{domain}\\left( f \\right)\\, \\cap^{}\\left( {\\underset{i = 1}{\\overset{m}{\\cap}}f\_{i}} \\right) \\cap^{}\\left( {\\underset{j = 1}{\\overset{p}{\\cap}}h\_{j}} \\right)$

The inequality constraints defined in Equation (4.13) should always be less than or equal to zero because the zero-sublevel set of f[i] is a convex set and hence the feasible region. If the constraints are greater than or equal to zero, it is no longer a convex set. The optimal value determined would no longer be a global optimum.

Convex optimization is preferred over general optimization due to the fundamental property that any locally optimal point is globally optimal.

Formally, if x is feasible and x ϵ D and satisfies all constraints and minimizes f in a local neighborhood, then

(4.15)

*f*(*x*) ≤ *f*(*y*)∀ feasibly, *x* − *y*[2] ≤ *ρ*

Linear programming (LP), quadratic programming (QP) and semi-definite programming (SDP) are special cases of convex optimization problems.

[4.5Unconstrained Optimization](#07_Contents.xhtml#sub-56)

Minimization/Maximization problems defined over *f*:ℝ^(*n*)→ℝ without any constraints on the input are called unconstrained problems. Optimizing such unconstrained problems is called unconstrained optimization.

Depending on specific criteria and variables, unconstrained optimization is used to find the optimal solution to a problem or task. By using unconstrained optimization, it becomes easier to train models in ML and make them more accurate. In ML, the goal is to minimize a cost function or error rate. This is where unconstrained optimization comes into play; it helps us find the best possible parameters for our model so that our cost function can be minimized as much as possible (or at least be as close to minimal as possible).

Unconstrained optimization algorithms such as gradient descent are used since they efficiently find local and global minima of functions with many variables. Using unconstrained optimization techniques, we can find an optimal set of parameters to give us a minimum error rate throughout our training process. This enables us to create better models which are more accurate and precise when presented with unknown data points.

If all the eigenvalues of the Hessian matrix **ℋ** are positive, the matrix is said to be positive definite.

If all the eigenvalues of the Hessian matrix **ℋ** are less than zero, the matrix is said to be negative definite.

If some eigenvalues of the Hessian matrix **ℋ** are positive and some may be negative or zero, the matrix is said to be indefinite.

4.5.1Solving an Unconstrained Optimization Problem when the Input is a Scalar

Newton’s Method is a widely used optimization technique used to find the minimum of an unconstrained optimization problem in ML. It is an iterative method that can be used to solve non-linear equations and is applied to any function, regardless of its nature (linear, non-linear, convex, or non-convex).

In an unconstrained optimization problem in ML, it helps to understand derivatives and the concept of gradient descent. When dealing with an unconstrained problem, we usually aim to find the point at which the cost function has its lowest value. This point corresponds with the global minimum for that particular objective function. Gradient descent allows us to move towards this global minimum by taking small steps down our objective function until it reaches its local minima; that is, where our partial derivative equals 0. It tends to work well when we have small data sets; however, as data sets become larger and more complex, gradient descent can take quite some time before converging upon its best solution (as each step taken on the search space could be pretty significant). This is where Newton’s Method comes into play.

Instead of attempting many small steps like gradient descent, Newton’s Method takes one significant step per iteration towards finding a local minimum by using information from first- and second-order derivatives (or gradients) at each iteration in our search space. This also helps ensure we do not get stuck at any points on our search space due to flat areas or saddle points within the objective function – something that would cause problems with traditional methods such as gradient ascent/descent when trying to optimize for unconstrained problems in ML. Instead, Newton’s Method can quickly identify potential optima points within its search space by using first- and second-order derivatives. This allows us to find better solutions faster than other techniques, such as gradient ascent/descent!

Assume that the function *f*:ℝ→ℝ. Starting from an initial estimate x1, the next point can be approximated. In general,

(4.16)

$x\_{k + 1} = x\_{k} - \\frac{f\\left( x\_{k} \\right)}{f'\\left( x\_{k} \\right)}$

The process is repeated till convergence occurs.

| 5 || 1.414216 || 0 || 2.828427 |

The process gets converged and the approximate solution is $1.414216 \\approx \\left. \\sqrt{}2 \\right.$

Newton’s method gives a good approximation to a function, but there are some drawbacks:

  i.If *f*^′(*x*[*k*]) = 0, the method fails.

 ii.In some cases, the approximation may repeat the values.

iii.It is sensitive to the initial choice.

 iv.In some cases, x[n] may not be defined.

4.5.2Gradient Descent Method (Solving an Unconstrained Optimization Problem when the Input is a Vector)

Gradient descent (GD) is a first-order optimization algorithm used to determine the local minimum/maximum of a given multivariate function. GD is a fundamental algorithm used in ML to update the parameters of a model based on an error/loss function. The algorithm works by calculating the gradient of the loss function concerning each parameter and then updating each parameter in such a way that it will reduce the value of the loss function. This process is repeated until we reach a point where further updates no longer improve the model’s performance.

GD is usually used for supervised learning tasks, such as linear and logistic regression or neural networks, where you have labeled data that you can use to calculate errors/losses. By optimizing these parameters, we can make predictions more accurately and efficiently than if we had just used trial-and-error methods.

The requirements for GD are the function should be differentiable and convex. If a function is differentiable, it has a derivative for each point in its domain. For a univariate function to be convex, the line segment connecting any two points must lie on or above the curve. Another method to check whether a univariate function is convex or not is by calculating the second-order derivative and checking if it is greater than zero; that is, *f*^″(*x*) > 0.

Example 18: *f*(*x*) = *x*² + *x* − 5

*f*^′(*x*) = 2*x* + 1; *f*^″(*x*) = 2

Since the second-order derivative is greater than zero, the given function is strictly convex.

Example 19: *f*(*x*) = *x*⁴ − 2*x*³ + 2

*f*^′(*x*) = 4*x*³ − 6*x*² = *x*²(4*x*−6)

*f*^″(*x*) = 12*x*² − 12*x* = 12*x*(*x*−1)

If *f*′(*x*) = 0,.The slope at these points is zero and hence they are possible candidates for the function’s extrema (minimum or maximum).

If *f*^′′(*x*) = 0,.

The function is convex for x < 0 and x > 1. For values between 0 and 1, the function is concave since the second-order derivative is less than zero.

At the point *x* = 0, the function has minimum value. Since the function is convex at certain points, the function is called quasi-convex.

For a multivariate function, the gradient is a vector of partial derivatives in each main direction.

Example 20: *f*(*x*,*y*) = 2*x*² + *y*²

$\\frac{\\partial f\\left( {x,y} \\right)}{\\partial x} = 4x\\frac{\\partial f\\left( {x,y} \\right)}{\\partial y} = 2y$

$\\nabla f\\left( {x,y} \\right) = \\begin{bmatrix} {4x} \\\\ {2y} \\\\ \\end{bmatrix}$

Gradient at point (1, 2) is

$\\nabla f\\left( {1,2} \\right) = \\begin{bmatrix} 4 \\\\ 4 \\\\ \\end{bmatrix}$

The gradient vector indicates that the slope is identical in both the x\- and y\-axes.

Working mechanism: We start with an arbitrary point and look for the next point to move to. The decision will be based on direction and step size. The direction will help us to move in a particular direction so that the function converges. The step size determines how quickly the function gets converged. The process is repeated until the function converges to a stationary point.

Start with an arbitrary point *x*⁰

(4.17)

⇒*x*^(*k* + 1)\=*x*^(*k*)−*λ*∇*f*(*x*^(*k*))

Since the objective is minimization of the given unconstrained function, a sensible approach is to choose the step size in such a way that it will minimize the value of the next point. A higher value of step size may not converge or diverge (shoot the point out of the region). A lower value of step size will proceed towards convergence slowly. A moderate value will move towards convergence.

Gradient Descent Algorithm

Step 1: Set k = 0.

Step 2: Choose the initial point *x*⁰.

Step 3: Calculate the gradient at this point.

Step 4: Choose the next point in the negative or opposite direction of the gradient using Equation (4.17).

Step 5: Repeat steps 3 and 4 until the stopping criteria is met.

The stopping criteria can be either fixing the number of iterations or ∇*f*(*x*^(*k*)) ≥ *ε*.

[4.6Constrained Optimization](#07_Contents.xhtml#sub-57)

An ML problem is an optimization problem where we seek the best possible outcome given certain conditions. Constrained optimization helps find this optimal solution by introducing constraints on how far away from the optimal point we can go. For example, a common constraint in neural networks is that weights cannot be too small or too large, which helps avoid overfitting and underfitting when training models. Constrained optimization can also help avoid bias during training by enforcing fairness constraints such as non-discrimination based on age or gender. This prevents models from making unfair or biased decisions against certain groups of people and ensures fairness in automated decision-making processes.

Constrained optimization techniques also allow us to solve complex problems by considering multiple objectives simultaneously, helping us quickly identify trade-offs between different goals and objectives when building our model architectures. Finally, constrained optimization helps with the interpretability of results, which is especially important with ML algorithms that produce complex outputs, such as deep learning models. By adding simple constraints like ‘keep features related’ or ‘maximize model accuracy within a reasonable time,’ we can improve our understanding of how individual parts contribute to overall performance without sacrificing the stability or accuracy of our model predictions.

A constrained optimization problem is of the form

(4.18)

min *f*(*x*)

The Lagrangian associated with this problem is

(4.19)

$\\min\\left( {x,\\lambda,\\upsilon} \\right) = f\\left( x \\right) + \\sum\\limits\_{i = 1}^{m}\\lambda\_{i}g\_{i}\\left( x \\right) + \\sum\\limits\_{j = 1}^{p}\\upsilon\_{j}h\_{j}\\left( x \\right)$

The *λ*[*i*]^′ and *υ*[*j*]^′ are called Lagrangian multipliers. The Lagrangian produces a family of lower bounds to the cost function at every feasible point.

Lagrangian multipliers are often used in ML to solve optimization problems. They are used to optimize the parameters of a system by employing constraints that limit and help shape the outcome of a function. For example, ML algorithms often employ regularization, which involves introducing penalty terms into an objective function to reduce overfitting and improve generalization. This penalty term can be expressed as a Lagrangian multiplier, where one can specify the regularization one desires for each parameter or feature set within the model. This technique can help keep models from overfitting while helping them perform better on unseen data.

Another example is when using neural networks for classification tasks; Lagrangian multipliers are commonly used to attempt to optimize decision boundaries between classes by adding constraints on specific parameters to try and increase accuracy or reduce misclassification errors. Introducing constraints through these penalty terms during optimization helps an algorithm find better decision boundaries between different classes.

Example 22: Minimize *x* + *y*.

The constraint is an external factor.

The Lagrangian associated with this problem is

*L*(*x*,*y*,*υ*) = *x* + *y* + *υ*(*x*²+*y*²−1)

Calculate the gradient of this function to determine the stationary point.

$\\nabla L\\left( {x,y,\\upsilon} \\right) = \\begin{pmatrix} {1 + 2\\upsilon x} \\\\ {1 + 2\\upsilon y} \\\\ {x^{2} + y^{2} - 1} \\\\ \\end{pmatrix}$

∇*L*(*x*,*y*,*υ*) = 0

                                                       ⇒1+2*υ**x*\=0;1+2*υ**y*\=0;*x*²+*y*²−1=0

Solving these, we get $x = y = \\frac{- 1}{2\\upsilon}\\,\\text{and}\\,\\upsilon = \\pm \\frac{1}{\\left. \\sqrt{}2 \\right.}$

The stationary points are $\\left( {\\frac{1}{\\sqrt{2}},\\frac{1}{\\sqrt{2}}} \\right)\\text{and}\\left( {\\frac{- 1}{\\sqrt{2}},\\frac{- 1}{\\sqrt{2}}} \\right)$

Example 23: Maximize *f*(*x*,*y*) = *x**y*. Though it is a constrained optimization problem, the problem looks simple. For such simple problems, we can use the direct substitution method.

Direct substitution allows us to rewrite the constraints in a single variable.

Rewriting the given constraint, we get *y* = 100 − *x*.

Now the problem is transformed as *f*(*x*,100−*x*) = *x*(100−*x*) = 100*x* − *x*²

By differentiating f, we get *f*^′(*x*) = 100 − 2*x*.

By equating *f*^′(*x*) = 0,

We determine the second-order derivative *f*^″(*x*) =  − 2 < 0

Hence the function will be maximized at (50, 50).

The same problem can also be solved using Lagrangian multipliers.

*L*(*x*,*y*,*λ*) = *f*(*x*,*y*) + *λ*(*x*+*y*−100) = *x**y* + *λ*(*x*+*y*−100)

$L^{\\prime} = \\begin{pmatrix} {y + \\lambda} \\\\ {x + \\lambda} \\\\ {x + y - 100} \\\\ \\end{pmatrix}$

*L*^′\=0⇒*x*\=*y*\=−*λ*,

                                   *x*+*y*\=100⇒−2*λ*\=100⇒*λ*\=−50⇒*x*\=*y*\=50

[4.7Dual Optimization Problems](#07_Contents.xhtml#sub-58)

Dual optimization is an ML technique that simultaneously optimizes two objectives. This can be useful when there are competing goals in the same optimization problem. For example, building a recommendation system for online shoppers might require optimizing for accuracy and speed of results or balancing between minimizing false positives and false negatives in fraud detection algorithms. In dual optimization techniques, one objective is seen as ‘primary’ and the other as ‘secondary’. The primary objective is optimized first, followed by the secondary objective, which tries to improve the values found by optimizing the primary objective. To achieve this, each step of an optimal solution must satisfy both objectives. At any given time, either one may be slightly sacrificed (while still being above a certain threshold) so that they are both satisfied with mutually compatible solutions over time.

The optimal solution found using dual optimization will only sometimes be perfectly balanced between both objectives, but it should generally still provide satisfactory results. By using dual optimization instead of traditional single-objective methods, engineers can ensure that their systems are more robust and can take into account many different types of requirements simultaneously without sacrificing too much on any individual metric.

Duality Theorem: Every maximization problem (primal) defined in standard form in linear programming (LP) will have an LP minimization problem called dual. The primal and dual problems are linked. Every feasible solution of one problem gives a bound on the optimal value of the other. This is called duality theorem. Duality theorem is a powerful tool used in ML to make better decisions. It states that if two optimization problems are related, the solution to one problem will be related to the solution of the other.

In supervised learning, duality theorem is often used to solve LP problems such as regression or classification tasks. Suppose we have a set of data points with certain features (independent variables) and specific labels (dependent variables). We can use LP techniques to determine which features are more important for predicting the labels correctly. This allows us to identify which features have higher predictive power and improve our models accordingly. In unsupervised learning tasks such as clustering or anomaly detection, duality theorem can help us determine how two data sets might be related even though they may not contain identical labels or classes. This allows us to find patterns in data that would otherwise go unnoticed.

In reinforcement learning tasks such as game-playing algorithms, duality theorem helps us create strategies for minimizing loss by comparing scenarios based on their expected rewards for different actions an agent takes (such as a player). By calculating expected rewards from different states within a game-playing environment using LP techniques derived from this theorem, we can optimize strategies for different situations more efficiently than without its use. Finally, it has been found that neural networks also benefit from incorporating this theorem into their design process during optimization attempts, as it helps reduce overfitting and improves the accuracy of outputs when predicting unseen data points.

Primal and Dual Problems: Let the problem defined in Equation (4.20) be considered as primal.

$\\text{Maximize}\\sum\\limits\_{j = 1}^{n}c\_{j}x\_{j}$                             

$\\text{subject}\\,\\text{to}\\,\\sum\\limits\_{j = 1}^{n}a\_{ij}x\_{j} \\leq b\_{i}\\forall i = 1\\cdots m$

(4.20)

*x*[*j*] ≥ 0                                                

The dual of the primal is defined as

$\\text{subject}\\,\\text{to}\\,\\sum\\limits\_{j = 1}^{m}( - a\_{ij})y\_{i} \\leq - c\_{j}\\forall j = 1\\cdots n$

(4.21)

*y*[*i*] ≥ 0                                        

Weak duality theorem states that any feasible solution to the dual problem is greater than any feasible solution to the primal problem. In other words, the optimal solution of a problem cannot be worse than the optimal solution of its dual problem. This means that even if an exact solution to a problem is hard to find, one can still get a good upper bound on the best possible value by solving its dual version instead. In ML, this theorem can solve optimization problems related to supervised and unsupervised learning algorithms. For example, minimizing the objective function (or cost function) in linear regression models requires finding the right combination of model parameters to minimize prediction error. Solving this problem’s dual version may yield a different solution. However, it provides us with a lower bound on our minimum possible prediction error, which allows us to determine whether or not our current model parameters are sufficient for obtaining good predictions or if more fine-tuning is needed.

Similarly, in clustering applications such as K\-means and Gaussian mixture models (GMM), weak duality theorem can be used to find approximate solutions when closed-form expressions for computing optimal cluster assignments are unavailable or too computationally costly. In GMM, for instance, it is usually impossible to obtain exact solutions since each data point must have its probability distribution associated with it; however, by using weak duality theorem, we can construct improved lower bounds on parameters for each data point without resorting to computationally expensive methods like Monte Carlo simulations/sampling-based algorithms. Finally, this theorem has been applied successfully in Markov decision processes (MDPs). In MDPs, we need to solve complicated optimization problems involving multiple variables and constraints; here, too, weak duality helps us obtain better estimates of optimal values by solving simpler versions of these problems, which results in better approximations than simply relying on heuristic search techniques like hill climbing.

Strong duality theorem states that if the primal problem has an optimal solution (*x*[1]^(\*),*x*[2]^(\*),⋯,*x*[*n*]^(\*)) such that

(4.22)

$\\sum\\limits\_{j = 1}^{n}c\_{j}x\_{j}^{\*} = \\sum\\limits\_{i = 1}^{m}b\_{i}y\_{i}^{\*}$

Strong duality theorem is used in ML to provide mathematical proof for optimizing particular algorithms. The theorem states that for any given optimization problem, there exists a solution that maximizes the objective function and simultaneously meets the problem’s constraints. In other words, if an algorithm has been designed to efficiently find a solution or set of solutions that meets specific criteria or objectives, then this solution can be proven optimal through solid duality. Strong duality is essential in specific ML algorithms such as SVMs. In these cases, it guarantees that any proposed solution will meet its specified objectives while providing insight into how this optimal solution was found and how to improve upon it. For example, SVM algorithms use strong duality to ensure they can accurately classify data points by finding an optimal hyperplane that maximizes its margin distance from each class boundary point.

Consider a constrained optimization problem

Minimize *f*(*x*)                              

subject to *g*[*i*](*x*) ≤ 0, ∀*i* = 1⋯*m*

(4.23)

*h*[*j*](*x*) = 0∀*j* = 1⋯*p*          

This problem is also called a primal optimization problem.

The primal optimization problem is a mathematical problem that involves finding the optimal solution for a set of parameters. This problem can be used to optimize specific ML algorithms and processes. Primal optimization problems are beneficial in deep learning, where they are used to help create and improve neural networks. For example, many deep learning algorithms utilize primal optimization problems to identify the optimal combination of weights and biases within a network. This helps ensure the network can accurately recognize patterns, identify objects in images or videos, or perform other tasks with maximum accuracy. Primal optimization can also determine the best parameters for accurate predictions when using regression models or supervised ML approaches.

Primal optimization problems can also help reduce overfitting by helping researchers find an optimal model size and number of layers in a neural network. By using this technique, researchers can find an ideal balance between having too few layers leading to underfitting and too many layers leading to overfitting. Overall, primal optimization effectively allows researchers and engineers to optimize ML algorithms with minimal effort. It allows them to quickly identify an optimal solution from various possibilities without needing extensive trial-and-error testing methods that take up more time and resources than necessary.

[4.8Dynamic Programming](#07_Contents.xhtml#sub-59)

Dynamic programming solves problems by combining solutions to sub-problems. A dynamic programming approach solves sub-problems or sub-sub-problems only once and store the results in a table-like structure. This approach is mostly used for solving optimization problems.

Principle of Optimality: A problem is said to satisfy the principle of optimality if the sub-solutions of an optimal solution of the problem are optimal solutions by itself for their sub-problems. The principle of optimality is widely used in ML for finding the best model structure through an iterative process. For example, it can be used to find the optimal set of parameters for a given model, determine a neural network’s optimal size and complexity, or define the best hyperparameters for a given problem. In essence, this approach involves solving sub-problems within each iteration and then combining their solutions to arrive at a better solution than any individual sub-problem’s solution. This method has successfully tackled challenging problems such as feature selection, semi-supervised learning, reinforcement learning optimization, and deep learning optimization.

A Markov decision process (MDP) consists of states, actions, rewards, and descriptions of the effect of each action in each state. Reinforcement learning aims to learn an optimal policy and MDP provides the environment. Dynamic programming is employed in such cases to determine the optimal solutions.

[4.9Sublinear Algorithms](#07_Contents.xhtml#sub-60)

Sublinear algorithms are those that solve a given problem by reading a minute scale of the input and process the input in a sublinear time before the solution is given as output. These algorithms may give exact solutions or provide approximate solutions through randomization.

Sublinear algorithms are becoming increasingly popular in ML. These algorithms can be used for large data sets that are too big to process with traditional methods. The main idea of using sublinear algorithms is to reduce the number of calculations needed to get accurate results from a large data set. This helps improve performance, reduce time spent on processing, and minimize the resources required for the task at hand. In ML, sublinear algorithms can be used for various tasks such as feature selection, clustering, classification, and regression.

Example 27: Determine an odd number in a given array A\[1: n\] consisting of a permutation of {1∙∙∙n} for n\> 1 and which outputs an index *i* such that A\[i\] is an odd number.

A deterministic approach outputs an exact solution in O(n) time. A randomized algorithm may produce an output in O(1) time. The idea is simple: randomly pick an element and check whether it is odd or not. Repeat until you find an odd number.

Streaming algorithms are those that solve a given problem by reading the input as it comes (streaming input) and give an exact solution or approximate solution with the help of randomization. These algorithms will not store the input sequence at all; they run ‘on the fly’. They process the streaming input using only a sublinear amount of memory.

Like the concept of randomized algorithms and approximate algorithms, sublinear algorithms aim for some solution when there is no solution available in polynomial time.

[4.10Graphs](#07_Contents.xhtml#sub-61)

A graph is a non-linear data structure consisting of a non-empty set of vertices and a set of edges. It is represented as G = (V , E) An example of a graph is shown in [Fig. 4.7](#12_Chapter4.xhtml#fig4-7). with four vertices and seven edges.

*V* = {*v*[1],*v*[2],*v*[3],*v*[4]}

A graph is represented by an adjacency matrix or an adjacency list. For the graph shown in [Fig. 4.7](#12_Chapter4.xhtml#fig4-7), the adjacency matrix ([Table 4.1](#12_Chapter4.xhtml#tab4-1)) is defined with dimensions |*V*| × |*V*|.
