The entries in the adjacency matrix indicate the number of edges between the corresponding vertices. Between vertices v[2] and v[3], there are two edges; hence the number 2 in the adjacency matrix.

Undirected Graph: The edges in an undirected graph are unordered, that is, an edge between two vertices represented by (u, v) or (v, u) is the same.

Undirected graphs are useful in ML because they allow for the representation of data relationships. In particular, they can be used to identify patterns between different variables and help decide which ones should be used in the model. For example, an undirected graph could be used to understand how two variables interact; if one variable has a direct influence on another variable, these two variables will have a direct connection in the graph. This type of analysis can be helpful when building models as it can help determine which factors are most important for a given outcome.

Undirected graphs can also help analyze complex data sets by clustering similar data points together or identifying outliers that require further investigation or removal from the data set. Using network structures makes it possible to infer hidden connections between observations and uncover insightful information about the data set. This makes undirected graphs essential for exploratory analysis and feature selection during model building.

Directed Graph: The edges in a directed graph are ordered or represented by a directed pair. A directed graph is an essential tool for ML, as it can represent relationships between data points and explore different paths from one point to another. The ability to traverse a graph structure allows algorithms to identify patterns in data and draw valuable conclusions from them. In addition, the directed graph can be used for tasks such as clustering and classification. For example, a directed graph can be used in supervised learning tasks such as regression analysis, where one must predict the value of a dependent variable given some independent variables. By using the relationships represented by edges in the graph structure, algorithms can learn how changing certain features of an object or entity might affect its output value. This makes it easier to understand which features are essential when predicting values and deciding how best to use that information.

In unsupervised learning tasks such as clustering analysis or NLP, directed graphs help identify general patterns among pieces of data that are otherwise unrelated or difficult to classify manually. This helps machines learn how different pieces of information may correlate, allowing them to make more accurate predictions about unknown data points based on what they already know.

Here, the edge between the vertices u and v are represented as (u, v) in which the tail of the edge is at u and the head is at v. Hence (u, v) and (v, u) are different.

An edge from a vertex to itself is called a self-loop. Self-loops can be used to model situations where a node is somehow related to itself. For example, if one wanted to model the friendship between two people, one could have an edge with both ends pointing at the same vertex. If there is more than one edge between a pair of vertices, the edges are called multiple edges. Multiple edges are used in ML to capture and quantify the strength of relationships between different entities. For example, in a social network, multiple edges can be used to model how closely two people are connected or the likelihood that they will interact with each other. In a recommendation system, multiple edges can be used to score the affinity between items related by their category or context. This information can be used by algorithms such as collaborative filtering or matrix factorization to make recommendations. Multiple edges also enable algorithms such as neural graph networks, which help encode complex relationships among entities within a graph structure and use those complex interactions to make predictions more accurately than traditional methods.

For a graph with n vertices, the maximum number of distinct edges is $\\frac{n\\left( {n - 1} \\right)}{2}$.

Complete Graph: An undirected graph with exactly n(n \- 1)/2 edges is called a complete graph. In ML, complete graphs help identify patterns in data that are difficult to detect. For example, we want to identify which variables are related to each other. In this case, it is much easier to use a complete graph than to examine individual pairs of variables separately. A complete graph gives us an overview of the entire data set and makes it easier to see how different variables interact. Complete graphs also help machines make decisions based on large data sets or high-dimensional problems where multiple factors may be at play at any given time. By analyzing patterns within a complete graph, ML algorithms can more easily determine which factors contribute most towards specific outcomes or decisions and make predictions based on those findings. Finally, complete graphs offer an effective way of visualizing data so that humans can better understand its structure and meaning and identify outliers or anomalies more quickly than without this tool.

Subgraph: For a graph G = (V, E), there exists a graph *G*′ such that *V*(*G*^′) ⊆ *V*(*G*) and *E*(*G*^′) ⊆ *E*(*G*).

![](Images/f4-8.jpg)

[Figure 4.8](#12_Chapter4.xhtml#fig-4-8)  A subgraph of the graph given in [Fig. 4.7](#12_Chapter4.xhtml#fig4-7)

Subgraphs are helpful in ML because they allow the machine to identify patterns and relationships in the data. Subgraphs are subsets of graphs that contain all or part of an original graph’s nodes and edges ([Fig. 4.8](#12_Chapter4.xhtml#fig4-8)). By breaking down the main graph into smaller components, subgraphs allow machines to find patterns in complex data sets easily. For example, suppose we were trying to predict credit card fraud using a data set of customer transactions. Here, we could create subgraphs by grouping customer transactions according to the date, merchant type, or location. This would allow us to understand customer spending patterns better and detect anomalies that may indicate fraudulent activity.

Subgraphs also enable machines to learn from previously learned models while still being able to recognize new relationships. By creating multiple subgraphs from similar but distinct data sets, machines can compare results from previous models with current ones and make better predictions about future data points more quickly and accurately than ever. In addition, subgraph algorithms can be used for dimensionality reduction, which helps reduce noise in large data sets so that the machine can focus on essential features instead of being overwhelmed by irrelevant information. This is especially helpful when working with unstructured data sets where it is difficult for computers to identify meaningful patterns from many available data points due to their sheer volume or complexity.

Path: A path from a vertex v1 to v3 is a sequence of vertices where any two adjacent vertices are connected by an edge.

Cycle: A cycle is a path where the initial vertex and the final vertex are the same. In other words, the sequence’s starting and ending points are the same. The path can go through many vertices before returning to its beginning, never visiting any vertex twice (except for the start and end). This means that it forms a closed loop. Cycles are essential in graph theory because they can measure properties like connectivity or the distance between two points in a connected graph. They also solve specific problems like finding minimal spanning trees or identifying strongly connected components in directed graphs.

Connected Graph: An undirected graph is said to be connected if and only if there exists a path between every pair of distinct vertices. An undirected graph is connected if there is a path from any vertex to another vertex. This means that for any two distinct vertices in the graph, there is a way to get from one to the other without re-visiting previously visited nodes. In other words, every node in an undirected graph can be reached from every other node by some sequence of edges or steps. If there is no path between two distinct vertices, the undirected graph is not considered connected.

Degree of a Vertex: The number of edges incident on a vertex in an undirected graph is called the degree of the vertex. A vertex (also known as a node) is a point on a graph, and the degree of that vertex represents how many other nodes it is connected to. This number can be used to measure the strength of connections between nodes and understand how they relate. In ML, the degree of a vertex can help determine which connections are the most important in an algorithm and better understand the data being analyzed. For example, suppose one node has a high degree compared to others in the same network. This could indicate that this node is more important than others for making correct predictions or classifications with the algorithm.

This concept can also be used when building models such as neural networks or decision trees where understanding which features are the most important (and therefore should be given more weight) helps improve performance. In these cases, higher degrees may indicate features that are more predictive or meaningful than those with lower degrees, indicating they should not receive much attention from the model as they lack relevance for predictions/decisions made by it.

For a directed graph, the in-degree of a vertex v is the number of edges for which v is the head. The out-degree of a vertex v is the number of edges for which v is the tail.

[4.11Transforms](#07_Contents.xhtml#sub-62)

The Fourier transform of a continuous function *f*(*t*) is defined as

$F\\left( \\mu \\right) = \\int\\limits\_{- \\infty}^{+ \\infty}f\\left( t \\right)e^{- j2\\pi\\mu t}dt$,

where t and µ are continuous variables.

The inverse Fourier transform is defined as

$f\\left( t \\right) = \\int\\limits\_{- \\infty}^{+ \\infty}f\\left( t \\right)e^{j2\\pi\\mu t}d\\mu$

These two equations represent a Fourier transform pair.

Euler’s formula, *e*^( − *j*2*π**μ**t*) = cos (2*π**μ**t*) − *j*sin (2*π**μ**t*)

Fourier transform is a mathematical technique to decompose any given function into a series of sine and cosine functions. It is an essential tool in ML because it allows us to analyze data more effectively and efficiently by changing it from the time domain into the frequency domain. In ML, Fourier transform can decompose complex signals (such as images) into simpler components that are easier for a computer to interpret and understand. By breaking down an image or sound clip into its essential elements, we can better decide what should be included in our model or program when using ML algorithms. For example, suppose we have a picture of someone’s face. Fourier transform can help break this picture down into separate parts, such as eyes, nose, and lips, allowing us to give these different parts their weights when constructing our model or program for recognition purposes.

Fourier transform also helps reduce noise in data sets so that only relevant features remain, which can then be taken forward for further processing with various ML algorithms like SVMs and neural networks (NNs). This way, noise is eliminated while preserving meaningful information to improve the accuracy of predictions made with ML models built on such data sets.

Convolution: The convolution of two functions involves superimposing one function over the other about its origin and sliding it past the other. At every displacement location during the sliding, the computation includes the sum of products. It is defined as

$\\left( {f\*h} \\right)\\left( t \\right) = \\int\\limits\_{- \\infty}^{+ \\infty}f\\left( \\tau \\right)h\\left( {t - \\tau} \\right)d\\tau$

Convolution is an ML technique that helps us identify patterns in data by performing mathematical operations on different inputs. It is commonly used in image recognition and classification tasks, where it helps to identify features within an image that can help distinguish one object from another. The basic is to take multiple small windows of data and apply a set of mathematical operations, such as multiplication, addition, or subtraction, across those windows to detect certain patterns or features. This process is repeated until a desired outcome is reached, resulting in a set of values that represent the image’s features. The result can then be used for further analysis or prediction tasks.

In ML applications, convolution can help computers understand which parts of an image are important for classifying objects or predicting outcomes. For example, suppose we want to predict whether there will be rain tomorrow based on an array of weather images from the past week. We could use convolutional filters to identify which parts of each picture are most likely related to rainfall – like dark clouds or heavy rain – so that our algorithm can consider these patterns when making predictions about tomorrow’s weather.

Properties of Convolution

•Convolution is commutative, that is, the order in which signals convolve has no effect on the result.

*x*(*t*) \* *y*(*t*) = *y*(*t*) \* *x*(*t*)

•Convolution is distributive over addition.

*x*(*t*) \* \[*y*(*t*)+*z*(*t*)\] = \[*x*(*t*)\**y*(*t*)\] + \[*x*(*t*)\**z*(*t*)\]

•Convolution is associative.

*x*(*t*) \* \[*y*(*t*)\**z*(*t*)\] = \[*x*(*t*)\**y*(*t*)\] \* *z*(*t*)

•Shift property: Convolution of a signal with time shift results in a shift in the output signal.

If *x*(*t*) \* *y*(*t*) = *z*(*t*),

Discrete Cosine Transform (DCT): Consider a sequence *p*(*n*), 0 ≤ *n* ≤ *N* − 1. The one-dimensional DCT of this sequence is defined as

$q\\left( k \\right) = \\alpha\\left( k \\right)\\sum\\limits\_{n = 0}^{N - 1}p\\left( n \\right)\\cos\\left\\lbrack \\frac{\\pi\\left( {2n + 1} \\right)k}{2N} \\right\\rbrack,0 \\leq k \\leq N - 1$

$\\alpha\\left( 0 \\right) = \\frac{1}{\\left. \\sqrt{}N \\right.}$                                                                              

$\\alpha\\left( k \\right) = \\sqrt{\\frac{2}{N}1 \\leq k \\leq N - 1}$                                                   

The inverse transform is given by

$p\\left( n \\right) = \\sum\\limits\_{k = 0}^{N - 1}\\alpha\\left( k \\right)q\\left( k \\right)\\cos\\left\\lbrack \\frac{\\pi\\left( {2n + 1} \\right)k}{2N} \\right\\rbrack,0 \\leq n \\leq N - 1$

Forward transform and inverse transform together form the DCT pair.

The N × N discrete cosine transform matrix is given by

$c\\left( {k,n} \\right) = \\left\\{ \\begin{matrix} \\frac{1}{\\left. \\sqrt{}N \\right.} & {k = 0,0 \\leq n \\leq N - 1} \\\\ {\\sqrt{\\frac{2}{N}}\\cos\\left\\lbrack \\frac{\\pi\\left( {2n + 1} \\right)k}{2N} \\right\\rbrack} & {1 \\leq k \\leq N - 1,0 \\leq n \\leq N - 1} \\\\ \\end{matrix} \\right.$

DCT is a commonly used ML technique that reduces the amount of data in an image or audio signal by removing less important information from it. This allows for more efficient storage and transmission of the data. In addition, DCT helps retain most of the essential features and reduces noise in the signal. In computer vision, DCT detects image features such as edges, shapes, and textures. It can be applied to grayscale and color images, allowing for faster processing since it focuses on only a few significant frequencies instead of all of those within an image. In addition, this technique can achieve more explicit object recognition with fewer parameters than with other methods like Fourier transforms or wavelets.

It can also be used to compress large data sets before they are transmitted over networks or stored on disk drives because reducing data size reduces transfer time and storage costs significantly. In addition to computer vision applications, DCT is popularly utilized in speech processing tasks like speech recognition systems and text-to-speech synthesizers due to its ability to extract salient characteristics from sound waves that are otherwise undetectable by human ears, such as pitch periodicity patterns and formant structure, among others. Furthermore, the extracted features help machines convert speech signals into meaningful words and sentences with better accuracy rates than other methods, such as Fourier transforms or wavelet analysis techniques. As a result, it is extremely popular among automatic speech recognition systems that use models trained using ML algorithms like DNNs, SVMs, and hidden Markov models (HMMs).

Discrete cosine transform (DCT) and discrete Fourier transform (DFT) are integral to signal processing. Yet, they serve different purposes and exhibit distinct characteristics, particularly in the context of optimization algorithms. DCT, utilizing only real numbers, is closely related to the Fourier series coefficients of a symmetrically extended sequence, which makes it highly suitable for applications that benefit from data compression, such as image and audio encoding. This is due to the DCT’s ability to concentrate signal energy into a few coefficients, a property known as spectral compaction. On the other hand, DFT, employing complex numbers, is related to the Fourier series coefficients of periodically extended sequences and is widely used for spectral analysis across various fields.

Properties of DCT

•DCT is real and orthogonal.

•DCT is not the real part of DFT.

•DCT has excellent energy compaction for highly correlated data.

•DCT is a fast transform.

Discrete Sine Transform (DST): The sine transform pair for one-dimensional sequences is given as

$q\\left( k \\right) = \\sqrt{\\frac{2}{N + 1}}\\sum\\limits\_{n = 0}^{N - 1}p\\left( n \\right)\\sin\\frac{\\pi\\left( {k + 1} \\right)\\left( {n + 1} \\right)}{N + 1}0 \\leq k \\leq N - 1$

$p\\left( n \\right) = \\sqrt{\\frac{2}{N + 1}}\\sum\\limits\_{k = 0}^{N - 1}q\\left( k \\right)\\sin\\frac{\\pi\\left( {k + 1} \\right)\\left( {n + 1} \\right)}{N + 1}0 \\leq n \\leq N - 1$

The N × N DST matrix is given by

$\\sqrt{\\frac{2}{N + 1}}\\sin\\frac{\\pi\\left( {k + 1} \\right)\\left( {n + 1} \\right)}{N + 1}0 \\leq k,n \\leq N - 1$

DST is a powerful mathematical tool used in ML and other areas of data science. It converts a signal or image into its frequency components, allowing for more efficient processing and analysis. In ML, DST is applied to data sets that are too large or complex to be processed quickly by traditional methods. Decomposing the data set into its frequency components allows for faster computation of patterns and correlations. This makes identifying clusters within the data possible, leading to better predictions or decisions from machine learning models. DST has also been applied successfully in image processing applications such as facial recognition and object detection algorithms.

Properties of DST

•Sine transform is real, symmetric and orthogonal.

•Sine transform is not the imaginary part of DFT.

•Sine transform is a fast transform.

[4.12Information Theory](#07_Contents.xhtml#sub-63)

Information theory is a branch of mathematics that deals with quantifying and manipulating information. It is primarily used to study communication systems and data compression. In recent years, information theory has also been applied to ML, where it can provide insights into learning algorithms and their performance. Claude Shannon first developed Information Theory in 1948 in his seminal paper “A Mathematical Theory of Communication.” Shannon defined the fundamental concepts needed for a mathematical theory of information: entropy, mutual information, and channel capacity. These concepts were then used to study communication systems such as phone networks, radio broadcasting, and optical fiber cables.

In ML, applications of information theory are used to measure the complexity or uncertainty of a data set or task that an algorithm needs to learn from or solve, respectively; the more complex a task is thought to be, the higher its entropy value will be according to information theory metrics. In addition, ML researchers have been able to use these same metrics to evaluate performance on various problems as well as compare different learning algorithms based on their respective performances on those tasks at hand for both speed (training time) and accuracy (success rate).

Mutual information has been helpful for feature selection within data sets, meaning that rather than having all the features included within model input, engineers will select only relevant features, thus reducing noise in data while still preserving important relationships between variables.

The definitions of various terms related to information theory are given below:

Random variable: A real-valued function defined over a sample space of a random experiment is called a random variable. It can be either discrete or continuous. Random variables are a valuable tool in ML as they can quantify the uncertainty associated with predictions or results. For example, a random variable (like probability) can assign probabilities to different outcomes of a prediction algorithm. This allows the ML system to assign higher probabilities to more likely outcomes and lower probabilities to less likely ones. It also makes it easier for humans to interpret and make decisions based on the results of an algorithm. Random variables can also be used for decision-making in reinforcement learning algorithms. By applying a specific reward value or penalty value, the model can learn which action produces the highest expected return based on its understanding of random variables. This helps give better control over decisions by weighing pros and cons using values assigned by random variables rather than relying solely on intuition or pure trial-and-error methods. In addition, random variables provide insight into how different data sets interact when analyzing complex systems such as neural networks. They provide information about the correlations between input data points and their respective outputs from the ML models being trained with them. This further allows us to identify areas of improvement where we could tweak parameters to increase accuracy or efficiency when creating our models, which help in making better-informed decisions when developing ML algorithm.

•Discrete random variable: A random variable that takes a finite set of distinct values is called a discrete random variable. It is distinct in that it can only take whole numbers or specific values from a finite list, as opposed to continuous random variables, which can take any value within an interval. This means that the probability of a discrete random variable taking any value within its range must sum up to 1. For example, suppose you have an experiment where you roll two dice and count the total number of dots (dots being the possible values). The number of dots could be any whole number between 2 and 12, giving 11 possible outcomes (2–12). The probability for each outcome will vary depending on how many combinations are available for each number. For example, there are six different ways to obtain 7 by rolling two dice: (1 + 6), (2 + 5), (3 + 4), (4 + 3), (5 + 2), and (6 + 1). Therefore, the probability of rolling 7 equals 6/36, which is equal to 1/6. All in all, discrete random variables are useful for situations where we want to calculate probabilities about certain events with pre-defined outcomes, such as rolling dice or flipping coins.

•Continuous random variable: A random variable that takes infinite values defined over an interval is called a continuous random variable. It can take any value from an infinite set of numbers within a given interval. It is different from a discrete random variable, which has only limited possible values. Examples of continuous random variables include the temperature in degrees Celsius, the depth of water in oceans, and the diameter of a tree trunk. Continuous random variables are often used to describe probabilities related to physical phenomena such as time, space, or velocity. In addition, they are useful for modeling data that has smooth and gradual changes, such as stock prices or population growth. When dealing with continuous random variables, we typically use probability density functions (PDFs) instead of probability mass functions (PMFs). A PDF assigns probabilities to intervals rather than individual points on the number line and helps us determine the chance that a randomly chosen value falls within a certain range. To calculate probabilities related to continuous distributions, we can use integrals instead of sums since they are obtained by integrating over all possible values instead of simply summing up all possibilities, like discrete distributions do. Summation rules no longer apply when dealing with probability density functions since there is no fixed number of outcomes for them; this makes calculating probabilities much more difficult for this type of distribution compared to discrete ones where we just have to add up all the possibilities associated with each outcome in order to obtain our desired result.

Probability distribution (PD): The possibility of each outcome of a random experiment or event can be measured by a probability distribution.

A random event E with a probability P(E) contains $I\\left( E \\right) = \\log\\frac{1}{P\\left( E \\right)} = - \\log P\\left( E \\right)$ units of information.

If P(E) = 1 then P(E) = 0, which indicates that no information is attributed to it, that is, there is no uncertainty associated with the event. PD is a critical concept in ML used to capture uncertainty and randomness. It allow us to estimate the likelihood of events happening or not happening and measure the strength of relationships between variables. PD can be instrumental in the decision-making processes, helping to determine which model architecture or hyperparameters will produce the best results. For example, when building models such as classification algorithms or neural networks, probability distributions can be used to select appropriate input features with the most predictive power and minimize overfitting. A PD can also help validate models by testing whether they are sensitive enough to changes in small amounts of data points. The prediction accuracy of a model is also influenced by prior knowledge about its expected performance, which can be obtained from studying probability distributions associated with different values for particular parameters like regularization coefficient lambdas and learning rates. Finally, probability distribution plays an important role when making predictions from models – it helps create estimates for what may happen in the future based on probabilities calculated from past data points rather than absolute values (such as Bayesian inference). This approach allows us to build more reliable prediction systems that are less prone to errors due to outliers or extreme cases where the output differs drastically from our expectations given a particular set of inputs.

Entropy: The entropy of a discrete random variable x with a probability distribution *p*(*x*) is defined as

$H\_{x} = - \\sum\\limits\_{x \\in \\chi}p\\left( x \\right)\\log\_{2}p\\left( x \\right)$

Entropy gives a measure of the uncertainty of a random variable.

In information theory, entropy specifies the minimum number of bits needed to encode the class of an instance. In ML, entropy provides a measure of impurity in a collection of training data. Entropy is used to measure the amount of information contained in data. It can be used as an evaluation metric to assess the performance of a model and is also incorporated into many algorithms used for decision-making and optimization. The primary use of entropy in ML is related to decision trees. Decision trees are a type of algorithm that use hierarchical structures to classify data points. Entropy measures the uncertainty within each decision tree branch, allowing us to decide which branch requires further exploration and which should be discarded. This helps us evaluate how well our model performs against unseen data, making it an essential part of assessing the overall performance of a model.

Another common application of entropy in ML is feature selection or feature importance analysis. By calculating the entropy values for different features, we can better understand how much information they contain and determine which ones have more important contributions when predicting our target variables. When dealing with large data sets with many features, calculating entropies can help us reduce noise by selecting only relevant features that provide helpful information about our target variable. Finally, entropy plays an important role when it comes to optimization problems; this includes neural networks or other complex models built on data sets with multiple features that need some regularization methods (such as L1/L2) applied to them before being trained on unseen data points for better generalization performance and avoiding overfitting issues, thus ensuring better predictions. Entropy can help determine which weights should be assigned higher values to reduce computational complexity while still optimizing performance levels by choosing those weights with higher relevance (more predictive power).

For example, tossing a coin is a random event. The two possible outcomes are heads and tails with equal probability of 0.5. Entropy of this event is calculated as

$H\_{x} = - \\sum\\limits\_{x \\in \\chi}^{}p\\left( x \\right)\\log\_{2}p\\left( x \\right) = - \\sum\\limits\_{i = 1}^{2}0.5\*\\log\_{2}\\left( 0.5 \\right)$

 =  − (0.5\*(−1)+0.5\*(−1)) = 1                                 

Uniform probability of the outcomes of the event yields maximum uncertainty, and hence entropy is maximum.

Information gain: The expected reduction in entropy caused by partitioning the samples according to a particular attribute is called information gain. It is one of the most critical concepts in ML. It helps machines make decisions by evaluating the quality of data and providing insight into the amount of information held within a given set of data. In ML, information gain determines which attributes are most useful or relevant in making accurate predictions. This allows us to identify and focus on features that will impact our results most when making predictions. In essence, information gain measures how better off we are when a particular attribute (or split) is used versus not using it. For example, if splitting a data set based on an attribute would cause two different subsets to be created with distinct distributions for each subset (if there was an informational relationship between that attribute and class membership), this would be considered information gain because it would provide more information than what we had before splitting the data set. This would allow us to better learn from our data and make more accurate predictions down the line. To measure this information gain, metrics like entropy can be used, which calculate how much randomness or disorder there is within a given set of data. This enables us to quantify whether or not there is any real benefit in terms of increased accuracy when using different attributes or splits during the training phase of ML algorithms such as decision tree induction methods. For example, suppose a particular split/attribute provides no real benefit compared to another. In that case, it will have low information gain as opposed to one that does provide a benefit which might result in higher gains.

Let S be the set of training samples having many attributes represented by *A* = {*A*[1],*A*[2],⋯,*A*[*n*]}.

$\\text{Information}\\,\\text{Gain}\\left( {S,A\_{i}} \\right) = \\text{Entropy}\\left( S \\right) - \\sum\\limits\_{v\\, \\in \\,\\text{values}\\,\\text{of}\\, A\_{i}}\\frac{\\left| S\_{v} \\right|}{\\left| S \\right|}\\text{Entropy}\\left( S\_{v} \\right)$

The second term represents the expected entropy after *S*.

[4.13Manifolds](#07_Contents.xhtml#sub-64)

Machine learning deals with data pertaining to higher dimensions. Visualization of data in higher dimensions is difficult to plot. In order to plot the data for better understanding and visualization, the dimensions of the data should be reduced. There are many methods available for dimensionality reduction.

A manifold is a mathematical structure that describes a curved space. It is the generalization of ideas used in Euclidean geometry to describe objects moving in an environment with variable curvature. A manifold can be thought of as an abstract mathematical object that smoothly connects multiple points. To understand this better, think of it like a sheet of paper; if you bend one corner, the whole sheet will become curved, yet all the points on it are still somehow connected. This happens when we model our world using manifolds – even though space may be curving around us, we can still use mathematics to make sense of it by connecting all its points. Manifolds also allow us to describe how different shapes interact with each other and how they change over time and distance. In short, manifolds provide us with a powerful tool for understanding our universe from both a practical and theoretical perspective!

The process of modeling the manifold is called manifold learning. Locally linear embedding (LLE) is a manifold learning technique used for non-linear dimensionality reduction. LLE produces low-dimensional embedding of higher dimensional data by relating training instances to their close neighbors. LLE is a non-linear dimensionality reduction technique used to reduce data dimensions while preserving its original structure and information. This can be beneficial in cases where data has high dimensionality, which makes it challenging to visualize or analyze. The goal of the LLE technique is to find lower dimensional representations of the original data that are locally similar while preserving global structure. Local similarity means that similar points in the data set remain close together after performing dimensionality reduction. This can be achieved by having each point represented by its K\-nearest neighbors, as these points are likely to be locally similar. To preserve the global structure and identify essential features, distances between faraway points cannot be ignored in this process.

To reduce the dimensions of a data set using LLE, first, each data point must find its K\-nearest neighbors and form an n\-dimensional vector with those data points (where n is equal to the number of samples). Next, it will calculate weights for each neighbor so that all n vectors are aligned with one another mostly along their local directions but still maintain distant correlations from one another; this is done by minimizing an objective function called reconstruction error which measures how well every point can be reconstructed from its neighbors using this weight matrix built up from K\-nearest neighbors selection step. Finally, after weights have been found for each sample’s corresponding neighbor, these weighted samples are projected onto a lower dimensional space using singular value decomposition (SVD) or other techniques such as PCA.

SVD is a powerful and versatile method used in many fields of mathematics, computer science, and engineering. SVD is an algorithm used to decompose a matrix into its constituent parts. It is also known as the matrix factorization process. This decomposition breaks down the original matrix into three smaller matrices: two unitary matrices and one diagonal matrix containing the singular values. The SVD algorithm has been used in various applications including image compression, signal processing, facial recognition systems and text mining. In image processing, for example, it can be used to reduce the size of a picture by discarding some of its information that is considered redundant or not useful for further analysis or display purposes. In terms of text mining applications, SVD may be used to analyze documents by capturing their semantic content through term-document matrices (TDMs). By combining words from different documents within these TDMs, we can properly analyze these documents’ content by identifying topics discussed within them and whether or not those topics are well represented across all document samples; this allows us to group similar documents together based on their content or subject matter with greater accuracy than without using any form of clustering/grouping algorithm like KNN/K\-means clustering methodology.

SVD can also be applied in reducing noise from audio signals as well as making data more compressible for storage purposes through reduction in dimensionality; this helps improve both memory efficiency as well as speed up computation times. The result will contain all the global information in the original sizeable dimensional space and also provide us with compressed representation reduced down into lower dimensional space without losing any essential local/global structures while being computationally efficient.

Summary

•A set is a well-defined collection of objects, with finite sets used for classification, clustering, and regression. Empty sets, denoted by ∅, represent missing or irrelevant data points. Infinite sets, containing an infinite number of elements, are used in machine learning for large data sets or continuous data. The Cartesian product of sets is used in data analysis to identify relationships between variables. Relations, subsets of the Cartesian product, express relationships between elements and are used to make predictions using supervised learning algorithms like decision trees, SVM, and neural networks.

•Functions allow machines to make accurate predictions based on changing inputs, especially in complex tasks like stock price prediction or image recognition problems. Convex functions, such as strictly convex functions and convex combinations, minimize the total cost associated with performing tasks. Convex combination methods combine multiple models, reducing complexity and improving accuracy. The convex hull concept describes the shape of an object in terms of boundary lines, with vertices forming the convex hull.

•Gradient vectors are mathematical tools used in machine learning to calculate the direction and magnitude of change for variables. They are used in optimization algorithms like gradient descent to find the optimum value for specific parameters within a given function. The Hessian matrix is a matrix of a given function's second-order partial derivatives, helping to identify local maxima or minima. Optimization can be classified into three categories: linear and non-linear, constrained and unconstrained, and discrete, continuous, and probabilistic.

•Local and globally optimal points are considered locally and globally optimal. Constrained optimization helps find the best solution while accounting for specific constraints. Dual optimization optimizes two objectives simultaneously. The weak duality theorem states that any feasible solution to the dual problem is greater than any feasible solution to the primal problem. The strong duality theorem provides mathematical proof for optimizing algorithms.

•Dynamic programming solves problems by combining solutions to sub-problems. Sublinear algorithms solve problems by reading a minute scale of input and processing it in a sublinear time. Complete graphs help identify difficult-to-detect patterns in data. Subgraphs help identify patterns and relationships in data. Fourier transforms decompose functions into sine and cosine functions, allowing for efficient data analysis. Information Theory, a branch of mathematics, has been applied to machine learning to provide insights into learning algorithms and performance.

Learning Objectives

At the end of this chapter, you will be able to:

•Explain the fundamental concepts of computational learning theory

•Describe the objectives and historical development of computational learning theory

•Explain the significance and main methodologies of computational learning theory, including inductive, deductive, abductive, and reinforcement learning

•Explain the probably approximately correct (PAC) learning model and its relevance

•Analyze the complexity theory of machine learning, covering computational, space, and sample complexities

•Evaluate the time complexity of learning algorithms and the mistake-bound learning model

•Appreciate the principles of generative learning and contrast it with discriminative models

•Assess various evaluation metrics used in computational learning theory

•Anticipate future trends and directions in computational learning theory, including deep learning, explainable AI (XAI), and quantum machine learning

[5.1Introduction](#07_Contents.xhtml#sub-65)

Computational learning theory (CLT) is a branch of artificial intelligence (AI) that focuses on the design and analysis of algorithms that learn from data. It is a relatively new field of research, but it has already had a significant impact on the development of machine learning (ML) and AI. At its core, computational learning theory is concerned with understanding the principles that govern the learning process. It seeks to understand how machines can learn from data, how they can generalize from that data, and how they can use that knowledge to make decisions. It also seeks to understand how machines can learn from experience and how they can adapt to changing environments. CLT theory also focuses on the application of learning algorithms. This involves understanding how learning algorithms can be used in real-world applications, such as in robotics, natural language processing (NLP), and computer vision.

[5.2Objectives of Computational Learning Theory](#07_Contents.xhtml#sub-66)

CLT is closely related to the field of statistics, which also deals with the analysis of data. The main objective (goal) of computational learning theory is to develop algorithms that can learn from data and make predictions about future data.

The field of computational learning theory has been in existence since the 1950s and has seen tremendous growth in recent years. This is due to the increasing availability of large data sets, the development of powerful computational tools, and the emergence of powerful ML algorithms. At its core, computational learning theory is concerned with the development of algorithms that can learn from data. This involves the development of algorithms that can identify patterns in data and use those patterns to make predictions about future data. This is done by using a variety of techniques, such as supervised learning, unsupervised learning, reinforcement learning, and deep learning.

Supervised learning involves the use of labeled data, where the labels are known in advance. Unsupervised learning involves the use of unlabeled data, where the labels are not known. This type of learning is used to identify patterns in data and to cluster data points into groups.

Reinforcement learning is a type of learning where an agent interacts with an environment and receives rewards or punishments based on its actions. This type of learning is used to develop agents that can learn to perform tasks in an environment. Deep learning is a type of learning that uses artificial neural networks (ANNs) to learn from data. This type of learning is used to develop models that can identify patterns in data and make predictions about future data.

Another objective (goal) of CLT is in understanding the boundaries (limits) of what can be learned from data. This includes being aware of the learning algorithms’ sample complexity. The quantity of data points a learning algorithm must encounter to learn a function is known as the sample complexity. The sample complexity indicates the amount of data an algorithm needs to learn a function. These metrics vary based on the characteristics of the learning challenges, such as the size or complexity of the hypothesis space the learner is considering, the degree of accuracy required to approach the target concept, and the probability that the learner will generate a reasonable hypothesis.

[5.3History](#07_Contents.xhtml#sub-67)

The history of CLT can be traced back to the 1950s, when Alan Turing proposed the Turing Test to measure a computer’s ability to think like a human. Turing’s work laid the foundation for the development of AI. In the 1960s, AI researchers began to explore the idea of using computers to learn from data. This led to the development of the first ML algorithms, such as decision trees and neural networks.

The 1970s saw the development of supervised learning algorithms, such as linear regression and logistic regression. These algorithms were able to learn from labeled data and make predictions about the future. In the 1980s, unsupervised learning algorithms, such as clustering and principal component analysis, were developed. These algorithms were able to learn from unlabeled data and make predictions about the future.

In the 1990s, the first deep learning algorithms, such as convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and recurrent neural networks (RNNs), were developed. These algorithms were able to learn from large amounts of data and make predictions about the future. Today, computational learning theory is an active area of research and is used in a variety of applications.

[5.4Importance of Computational Learning Theory](#07_Contents.xhtml#sub-68)

The importance of CLT lies in its ability to help us understand the underlying principles of ML and AI. By understanding these principles, we can develop algorithms that can learn from data and make predictions about future events. This is especially important in AI, where algorithms are used to make decisions and solve problems.

CLT also helps us understand the limitations of ML algorithms, so we can develop better algorithms that can learn from data more efficiently and accurately. This is useful in data mining, where algorithms are used to identify patterns and trends in large data sets.

Finally, using CLT, we can understand how to design algorithms that can learn from data more effectively and efficiently. This is of great value in robotics, where algorithms are used to control robots and make decisions.

Thus, the goal of CLT is to understand the following:

•What kind of tasks are learnable?

•What kind of data is required for learnability?

•What are the time and space requirements of the learning algorithm?

[5.5The Main Methods](#07_Contents.xhtml#sub-69)

At its core, CLT is concerned with understanding the process of learning from data ([Fig. 5.1](#13_Chapter5.xhtml#fig5-1)). This involves understanding the types of data that can be used to learn, the types of algorithms that can be used to learn from data, and the performance of these algorithms on different types of data. In particular, CLT focuses on understanding how algorithms can learn from data in a way that is both accurate and efficient.

![](Images/f5-1.jpg)

[Figure 5.1](#13_Chapter5.xhtml#fig-5-1)  Core of computational learning

There are different types of CLT, each of which focuses on a different aspect of learning from data. As mentioned earlier, supervised algorithms learn from labeled data, unsupervised algorithms from unlabeled data, reinforcement algorithms from rewards and punishments, while evolutionary algorithms learn from evolutionary processes. CLT also focuses on understanding the performance of these algorithms. This involves understanding their accuracy and efficiency, as well as their ability to generalize to new data.

The main methods used in CLT are as follows:

•Inductive learning: This is the most common type of learning used in AI. Here, a computer program is given a set of training data (specific examples of correct inputs and outputs), and it is then tasked with generating a general rule or model that can be used to predict the output for new inputs ([Fig. 5.2](#13_Chapter5.xhtml#fig5-2)).

•Deductive learning: Here, a computer program is given a set of rules or a model (generic) and then tasked with using these to generate correct outputs for new inputs ([Fig. 5.2](#13_Chapter5.xhtml#fig5-2)).

![](Images/f5-2.jpg)

[Figure 5.2](#13_Chapter5.xhtml#fig-5-2)  Inductive and deductive learning

•Abductive learning: Here, a computer program is given a set of training data (incomplete observations) and then tasked with generating a hypothesis (a possible explanation for the data) that is consistent with the data ([Fig. 5.3](#13_Chapter5.xhtml#fig5-3)).

![](Images/f5-3.jpg)

[Figure 5.3](#13_Chapter5.xhtml#fig-5-3)  Abductive learning

•Reinforcement learning: Here, a computer program is given a set of rewards and punishments and then tasked with learning a policy (a set of rules) that will maximize the rewards and minimize the punishments.

We shall now explore each of these in detail.

5.5.1Inductive Learning

Inductive learning is the most common type of ML used in AI. It is a process in which a computer program is given a set of training data comprising examples of correct inputs and outputs. This data is then used to generate a general rule or model that can be used to predict the output for new inputs.

Inductive Learning = Experience + Knowledge + Reasoning

This type of learning uses experience, knowledge, and reasoning to draw conclusions and make predictions. The process of inductive learning is similar to how humans learn from experience. Like humans, machines learn from examples and use that information to predict new situations.

An example of inductive learning is the use of spam filters in email. First, a spam filter is trained on emails that are either spam or not spam. Then, based on the characteristics of those emails, the algorithm creates a model that can be used to classify new emails as either spam or not.

In inductive learning, accuracy depends on the quality of training data. If the training data is biased or insufficient, the model will not precisely predict the output of new inputs. Therefore, it is essential to have a diverse and representative set of training data to ensure the model can make accurate predictions.

The idea that inductive learning is effective is formally stated in the inductive learning hypothesis. This asserts that a hypothesis (a rule or pattern) will fit the data well on brand-new test examples if it fits the data well on a sizable and representative set of training examples. For instance, if the hypothesis ‘all birds can fly’ matches most of the training examples of birds, we can anticipate that it will also match most of the test cases of birds.

However, not all theories are created equal. Some could be too narrow or too broad to explain the data adequately. For instance, the claim that ‘all birds are black’ is overly narrow because it ignores the existence of different bird colors. The assertion that ‘all animals can fly’ is too broad because it encompasses species other than birds. A compelling hypothesis should be just right. This is called the bias–variance trade-off.

Algorithms for inductive learning seek to choose the best hypothesis that accurately describes the data and generalizes it to new data. To do this, they must look through a wide range of potential hypotheses and assess them using a set of standards. One standard might be how accurately the hypothesis matches the training set of data. The hypothesis’ complexity or degree of simplicity could be additional criteria. Occam’s razor, which states that the optimal hypothesis is the one that best fits the facts, is a popular method for balancing these requirements.

Inductive learning is helpful in ML because it helps us to learn from data and make predictions or decisions based on what we have learnt. It can be used, for instance, to categorize photographs of animals based on their characteristics or to suggest products to clients based on their interests. We can gain new knowledge or insights from facts we may not have noticed before with inductive learning.

5.5.2Deductive Learning

This is a type of ML where a computer program is provided with a set of predefined rules or a model that it uses to generate accurate outputs for new inputs. In this approach, the computer must make logical deductions based on the rules or model provided to infer new information and predict outcomes.

Deductive Learning = Knowledge + Reasoning

Deductive learning is a form of reasoning in which a conclusion is drawn from a set of premises or facts. Here, the conclusion is necessarily true if the premises are true. One example of deductive learning is using decision trees in medical diagnosis. A decision tree is created by inputting data from various patients with different symptoms and outcomes. Using this information, the computer generates a decision tree that can be used to predict the prognosis for new patients based on their symptoms. Numerous medical conditions, including heart disease and cancer, have been effectively diagnosed using this method.

Another example is the use of expert systems in finance. Expert systems are computer programs designed to emulate a human expert’s decision-making abilities in a particular field. In finance, expert systems can be used to analyze market trends and predict future prices. By inputting data from various sources, including news articles and financial reports, the system can make informed predictions about the direction of the market.

5.5.3Abductive Learning

This involves generating hypotheses consistent with a set of training data. This approach to learning has become increasingly popular in recent years, with many researchers and developers exploring its potential applications.

It is represented as P(H|E) = P(E|H) × P(H) / P(E). This states that the probability of a hypothesis (H) given evidence (E) is equal to the probability of the evidence given the hypothesis multiplied by the probability of the hypothesis divided by the probability of the evidence. In other words, it is the probability of a hypothesis given the evidence, taking into account the prior probability of the hypothesis.

The basic idea is that the computer program is given a set of training data and then tasked with generating a hypothesis that explains the data. Furthermore, the hypothesis must be consistent with the data, meaning that it must be able to accurately predict new data based on the patterns in the training data.

Abductive learning enables greater flexibility in the learning process, one of its primary advantages. Unlike other types of ML, abductive learning does not require a predefined set of features or variables. Instead, the program can generate its hypotheses based on the patterns it observes in the data.

For example, a company wants to predict which employees will most likely leave in the next year. They could use abductive learning to analyze their employees’ job satisfaction, salary, and other factors and generate hypotheses about which factors are most likely to lead to employee turnover. This information could then be used to develop strategies to retain employees and reduce turnover.

Another example is in medical diagnosis. Doctors can use abductive learning algorithms to analyze patient data and generate hypotheses about the most likely diagnoses based on the symptoms and other clinical factors. This can help physicians make more precise diagnoses and effective treatment plans.

5.5.4Reinforcement Learning

A reinforcement learning program is instructed to make decisions based on rewards and punishments. The program must discover a policy or principles that maximize rewards and minimize punishments. This type of learning is frequently employed in robotics, gaming, and other applications in which the computer must make decisions based on incomplete or ambiguous data.

The Bellman equation is used for reinforcement learning. It describes the relationship between the expected reward of a given action and the expected future rewards of all possible actions. It states that the expected reward of a given action equals the immediate reward plus the discounted expected reward of the best action that can be taken in the future. It is named after Richard Bellman, who formulated it in 1957.

Mathematically, it can be expressed as: V\*(s) = max(Q(s,a)) + E\[V\*(s′) | s,a\]. In this equation, V\*(s) is the optimal value of the state s, Q(s, a) is the expected value of taking action a in state s, and E\[V\*(s′) | s, a\] is the expected value of the resulting state, and a is the action in state s.

One example of reinforcement learning is training a robot to navigate a maze. The robot is given rewards for reaching the end of the maze and punishments for hitting walls or getting stuck. Through trial and error, the robot learns which actions lead to rewards and which to punishments, and it adjusts its behavior accordingly.

Another example is in training a computer program to play a game like chess. The program is given rewards for winning the game and punishments for losing. Through repeated games and analysis of successful strategies, the program learns which moves will most likely lead to victory and which should be avoided.

Reinforcement learning can be a powerful tool for creating intelligent systems to make decisions based on incomplete or uncertain information. However, it is essential to design the rewards and punishments carefully to ensure that the system learns the desired behavior.

[5.6Probably Approximately Correct Learning](#07_Contents.xhtml#sub-70)

Learning is a process that involves acquiring knowledge and skills through experience, study, or instruction. One type of learning that has gained increasing attention in recent years is probably approximately correct (PAC). This method is beneficial when the data is noisy or incomplete, as it allows for the creation of models that can accurately predict outcomes even with imperfect input.

The PAC equation is a mathematical formula describing the learning process from a given set of data. It states that given a set of data points, a learning algorithm can approximate a target function with a certain probability and accuracy. The equation is defined as:

P(f(x) ≈ y) ≥ 1 \- ε,

where P is the probability, f(x) is the target function, y is the output of the learning algorithm, and ε is the error rate.

An example of PAC learning is in speech recognition. When a person speaks, their voice can be affected by various factors, including background noise, accents, and speech impediments. To accurately recognize speech, a model must account for these variations. Using a PAC learning approach, researchers can create models that can identify patterns in speech, even when the audio data is not perfect.

Another example is in computer vision. Here, the input data can be images or videos, which may contain a variety of distortions or errors. For instance, a picture of a cat may be taken from an unusual angle, be blurry, or have other objects in the background. To accurately identify the cat in the image, a PAC learning model can be trained to recognize specific characteristics of cats, even when these characteristics are not always present in the input data.

A hypothesis *f*:*X*→*Y* is said to be consistent with training samples (*x*[1],*y*[1]), ⋯, (*x*[*n*],*y*[*n*])iff(*x*[*i*]) = *y*[*i*]∀*i*.

Given any set of labeled examples S, an algorithm *A* consistent with S if it exists and outputs ‘no consistent concept’ otherwise. The goal of the PAC model is to define hypothesis h such that h has a small error over D.

Given a sample set *S* = {(*x*[1],*y*[1]),⋯(*x*[*m*],*y*[*m*])}, the empirical error of a concept h with respect to S is defined as

$err\_{S}\\left( h \\right) = \\frac{1}{m}\\sum\\limits\_{i = 1}^{m}I\\left\\lbrack {h\\left( x\_{i} \\right) \\neq y\_{i}} \\right\\rbrack$

The idea of the PAC model is to assume that the training samples are from a single fixed distribution space. The goal is to use the sample set S to learn a concept h that has small true error on D.

PAC learning aims at efficient learning. To achieve this, we need to prove that an efficient learning algorithm determines a hypothesis that is approximately identical to the target concept. In this process, we define two parameters ε and δ and proceed to prove that with a probability of at least (1 - δ), a system can learn a concept with an error of at most ε

An algorithm learns in the PAC model if it probably (with confidence (1 - δ) outputs a hypothesis which is approximately correct (has a risk of at most ε).

Complexity for finite consistent hypothesis space

$m \\geq \\frac{1}{\\varepsilon}\\left\\lbrack {\\ln\\left( H \\right) + \\ln\\left( \\frac{1}{\\delta} \\right)} \\right\\rbrack$

Here, labeled examples are sufficient, so that with a probability of (1 - δ), all h ϵ H with

*e**r**r**o**r*[*D*](*h*) ≥  ∈ have *e**r**r**o**r*[*S*](*h*) > 0

$error\_{D} \\leq \\frac{1}{m}\\left\\lbrack {\\ln\\left( H \\right) + \\ln\\left( \\frac{1}{\\delta} \\right)} \\right\\rbrack$
