Unsupervised learning is a machine learning (ML) technique in which a machine is given unstructured data with no labels and asked to find patterns, similarities, and relationships between the data points. The output of this process is a model that can be used to make predictions or draw insights from the data. Unlike supervised learning, there is no human intervention. Instead, the algorithm must uncover hidden structures and relationships within the given data set.

Unsupervised learning algorithms are often used for clustering data sets into groups based on specific characteristics or dimensions or for anomaly detection, where outliers in the data set are identified. Unsupervised learning can also be used in natural language processing (NLP) tasks such as identifying topics within a document.

[7.2What and Why of Unsupervised Learning](#07_Contents.xhtml#sub-86)

Unsupervised learning is a type of ML where the computer program tries to find patterns and relationships in data without being given specific examples or labels to learn from. It is like trying to solve a puzzle without being given any hints. Instead, the program uses algorithms to explore the data and find patterns on its own.

For example, an unsupervised learning algorithm takes the input data set containing images of bulls and cows and performs analysis ([Fig. 7.1](#15_Chapter7.xhtml#fig7-1)). The algorithm observes the features of each image, such as shape, size, color, and texture. It then uses clustering techniques to group similar images into clusters. By doing this, it can recognize patterns in the data without knowing which categories of images belong to each cluster.

![](Images/f7-1.jpg)

[Figure 7.1](#15_Chapter7.xhtml#fig-7-1)  Unsupervised learning example

This technique can identify types of bulls or cows even if there is no clear distinction between them in the input data set. For example, suppose two cows have very similar shapes but differ slightly in color or texture. Unsupervised learning algorithms can still identify them as two distinct clusters despite their similarities.

Unsupervised learning is also helpful in separating a single object from its surroundings in an image by creating multiple clusters from that single object and its environment – this is known as segmentation. This technique can help computer vision applications accurately distinguish objects within an image, which is impossible with supervised learning approaches alone. Some examples of segmentation using unsupervised learning are image and document segmentation. In image segmentation, an image is separated into different regions or objects based on color, texture, edges, or other visual characteristics. Document segmentation is typically used to separate a document into its constituent parts, such as paragraphs, headings, and subheadings ([Fig. 7.2](#15_Chapter7.xhtml#fig7-2)).

![](Images/f7-2.jpg)

[Figure 7.2](#15_Chapter7.xhtml#fig-7-2)  Documentation segmentation example

Overall, unsupervised learning algorithms are valuable tools that provide insights into data sets that, due to their complexity, would otherwise require manual analysis. This makes them an excellent tool for data scientists looking to gain insights quickly and effectively from large data sets.

It can also help detect anomalies and outliers in data sets or predict future behaviors by recognizing patterns from past events. In addition, unsupervised learning models can be used for marketing purposes by grouping customers with similar interests together so marketers can better target them with relevant offers and promotions.

Unsupervised learning allows us to uncover insights about our data without it needing to be labeled or categorized; this makes it helpful in dealing with real-world situations where not all ­information is already known beforehand.

[7.3Types of Unsupervised Learning](#07_Contents.xhtml#sub-87)

In ML, unsupervised learning allows computers to identify patterns in data without training data or human instruction. Clustering, anomaly detection, dimension reduction, and association rule learning are the four primary subcategories of this form of learning ([Fig. 7.3](#15_Chapter7.xhtml#fig7-3)).

![](Images/f7-3.jpg)

[Figure 7.3](#15_Chapter7.xhtml#fig-7-3)  Types of unsupervised learning

Each of these types is now discussed in detail.

7.3.1Clustering

Clustering algorithms are an essential type of unsupervised ML used to identify patterns in data and group similar data points together. Clustering is used to find structure in unlabeled data, such as trends and groupings, to understand the data set better. The main goal is to create clusters or groups of data points that are like each other and dissimilar from points in other clusters.

There are two main types of clustering algorithms ([Fig. 7.4](#15_Chapter7.xhtml#fig7-4)): hard (assigning a point to one cluster based on similarity) and soft (assigning a point to multiple clusters, allowing for overlap).

![](Images/f7-4.jpg)

[Figure 7.4](#15_Chapter7.xhtml#fig-7-4)  Types of clustering

Hard clustering is when points are assigned to one cluster based on their similarities with other points in the cluster. For instance, if you have a set of fruits like apples, oranges, and bananas, you could use hard clustering to group the fruits according to whether they are sweet or sour. The apple would be grouped under sweet, while the orange would be part of the sour cluster ([Fig. 7.5](#15_Chapter7.xhtml#fig7-5)).

![](Images/f7-5.jpg)

[Figure 7.5](#15_Chapter7.xhtml#fig-7-5)  Hard clustering example

Soft clustering is when points are assigned to multiple clusters simultaneously and overlapping between clusters is allowed. For example, we have a set of animals, including cats, dogs, horses, cows, and goats; we could use soft clustering for this data set by creating a pet cluster (cats, goats and dogs) as well as a farm animal cluster (horses, goats and cows) which overlap since goats belong to both groups ([Fig. 7.6](#15_Chapter7.xhtml#fig7-6)).

![](Images/f7-6.jpg)

[Figure 7.6](#15_Chapter7.xhtml#fig-7-6)  Soft clustering example

Hard and soft methods can help group similar items to make patterns between them more apparent. Clustered data can then be studied in detail, allowing us to understand trends or discover new knowledge within our data sets. Clustering algorithms can be applied across various fields, including image segmentation, customer classification for marketing research, statistical analysis for discovering data trends, and classifying diseases in medical science.

There are different types of clustering methods ([Fig. 7.7](#15_Chapter7.xhtml#fig7-7)), each with its own advantages and disadvantages:

•Partitioning Clustering: This method divides the data into non-hierarchical groups, such as K\-means, K\-medoids, etc. Each data point belongs to exactly one cluster, and the number of clusters is specified in advance. This method is suitable for spherical and well-separated clusters, but it may not work well for complex shapes or noisy data.

•Hierarchical Clustering: This method creates a tree-like structure of clusters, such as agglomerative or divisive clustering. Each data point can belong to more than one cluster, depending on the level of the hierarchy. The number of clusters can be determined by cutting the tree at the desired level. This method can capture complex shapes and outliers, but it may be computationally expensive and sensitive to the choice of distance metric.

•Density-based Clustering: This method identifies clusters as dense regions of data points, separated by low-density regions, such as DBSCAN. Each data point belongs to at most one cluster, and some data points may not belong to any cluster (noise). The number of clusters is not specified in advance, and it depends on the density parameters. This method can handle arbitrary shapes and outliers, but it may not work well for varying densities or high-dimensional data.

•Distribution Model-based Clustering: This method assumes that the data points are generated by a mixture of probability distributions, such as Gaussian mixture models. Each data point belongs to one or more clusters with certain probabilities, and the number of clusters is specified in advance or determined by model selection criteria. This method can capture the statistical properties of the data, but it may not work well for non-Gaussian or overlapping clusters.

•Fuzzy Clustering: This method assigns a degree of membership to each data point for each cluster, such as fuzzy C-means. Each data point belongs to one or more clusters with different degrees of membership, and the number of clusters is specified in advance. This method can handle overlapping and noisy data, but it may be sensitive to initialization and convergence criteria

![](Images/f7-7.jpg)

[Figure 7.7](#15_Chapter7.xhtml#fig-7-7)  Types of clustering algorithms

7.3.1.1K-means Clustering

This is a popular unsupervised ML technique for data exploration and analysis. It used for grouping or clustering data points into distinct clusters or categories. K\-means aims to divide the data set into meaningful subgroups based on specific characteristics. The algorithm examines each data point and assigns it to one of several groups based on attribute similarities. The name comes from the fact that it requires a specific number of groups (K) before the algorithm can be run. Thus, K specifies the number of predefined clusters that must be generated. After that, the algorithm will divide the data set into K clusters by determining each cluster’s centroid (or center point). This is accomplished through an iterative process in which points are assigned to their closest centroid at each step. Then the centroids are updated based on the average of all points assigned to them in that iteration. Finally, the cluster data points are assigned to the nearest centroid until no point remains unassigned.

Centroids are the geometric centers of shapes or objects. They can be calculated by finding the average of the coordinates of all the points that make up the shape or object. For example, to find the centroid of a triangle, we can use the formula:

(x, y) = ( (x1 + x2 + x3) / 3, (y1 + y2 + y3) / 3)

where (x1, y1), (x2, y2) and (x3, y3) are the vertices of the triangle. This formula works because the centroid divides each median of the triangle into two segments with a ratio of 2:1. A median is a line segment that connects a vertex to the midpoint of the opposite side.

Here is a simple example of how to find the centroid of a triangle. Suppose we have a triangle with vertices A(2, 4), B(6, 8) and C(10, 4). To find the centroid, we plug in the coordinates into the formula:

(x, y) = ( (2 + 6 + 10) / 3, (4 + 8 + 4) / 3)

(x, y) = (18 / 3, 16 / 3)                            

(x, y) = (6, 16/3)                                    

Therefore, the centroid of the triangle is at (6, 16/3). We can verify this by drawing the medians and observing that they intersect at this point.

The K\-means algorithm works by partitioning a data set into K distinct clusters, based on the similarity in data points. It can work with the following types of data:

•Discrete numerical data: These are countable values, like the number of products sold or visits to a website. For example, if you have data on the number of products sold in different regions, K\-means can cluster regions with similar sales figures. This helps identify areas with similar sales patterns.

•Continuous numerical data: These measurable values can take any value within a range, like temperature or height. For instance, with data on the annual income and age of individuals, K\-means can cluster individuals with similar income and age profiles. This practical application is particularly useful for market segmentation, where you want to identify groups of people with similar financial and demographic characteristics.

•Continuous entities: These refer to data points that can be represented on a continuous scale. For example, in image processing, pixel intensities are constant values. K\-means can segment an image into different regions based on pixel intensity, which is helpful in object detection and image compression applications.

However, this algorithm has difficulties with categorical data, outliers, and non-linear data. Furthermore, it would help if you decided how many data clusters you wanted. Finally, K\-means is best applied to smaller data sets because it iterates over all the data points. As a result, if the data set contains many data points, it will take longer to classify them.

We need two inputs for K\-means clustering to work correctly: the desired number of clusters/groups and a set of observations with associated values (features). Initially, we must assign a cluster label to each observation/data point/feature vector at random, typically 0 or 1. However, any integer value depends on how many clusters we want the data set divided into (K). Then, for each group, we need to calculate the centroid, which represents both its mean location along every dimension as well as its overall size/volume when measured against all other groups in the data set.

Once these steps are completed, we can begin looping over the data set multiple times while adjusting the centroids accordingly through an iterative process known as expectation maximization. This works towards minimizing intra-cluster distances while simultaneously maximizing inter-cluster distances by assigning the observations new labels corresponding with whichever group they belong to closest after having gone through every iteration thus far. This provides us with ever more accurate predictions regarding which observations fall within which categories/subgroups across the entire sample space when compared against one another using Euclidean distance metric(s).

After a pre-specified amount of time has passed with no significant changes between iterations, convergence should be reached quickly given enough resources for computation, ensuring genuine classification accuracy.

Assume a company makes sports shoes and wants to divide its customers into two distinct groups: male and female. We would begin by gathering customer information such as age, gender, shopping preferences, and spending patterns, among other things, and then use K\-means clustering-based methodology to determine distinct criteria to determine who should go where.

For example, the majority of those aged between 18 and 25 tend to spend money on shoes, whereas the opposite is true for those aged 30+, thereby creating a clear distinction based solely on age. This suggests that spending habits on shoes differ significantly between two age groups: those aged 18–25 and those aged 30 and above.

•Age-based spending habits: The younger demographic (18–25) tends to spend more money on shoes. This could be due to fashion trends, social influence, and a higher interest in personal appearance. The older demographic (30+) is less likely to spend as much on shoes. They might prioritize other expenses such as family needs, mortgages, or savings.

•Gender-based analysis: Once the data is broken down by gender, the numbers for males and females in each age group align perfectly with the overall trend. This alignment provides a strong basis for decision-making, indicating that both young men and women (18–25) are more likely to spend on shoes, while older men and women (30+) are less likely to do so.

•Assumptions and conclusions: Based on the spending patterns, it can be assumed that the younger demographic (18–25) falls in the category of higher shoe expenditure, while the older demographic (30+) falls in the category of lower shoe expenditure. This distinction empowers marketers and businesses to tailor their products and marketing strategies to target the appropriate age groups effectively.

Steps

Step 1: Data Collection. The first step is to gather data on customers. In this case, we gather customer information such as age, gender, shopping preferences, and spending patterns.

Step 2: Define K. Next, we need to define the number of clusters (K) we want to form. In this example, we want to divide customers into two distinct groups: male and female.

Step 3: Initialize Centroids. The next step is to randomly initialize K centroids. A centroid is a point at the center of a cluster. In our example, we randomly select two centroids: one for males and one for females.

Step 4: Assign Data Points to Clusters. The next step is to assign each data point to its nearest centroid based on the Euclidean distance. In our example, we would calculate the distance of each customer from each centroid and assign them to the nearest centroid based on gender.

Step 5: Update Centroids. After all data points have been assigned to clusters, we update the centroids of each cluster based on the mean value of all the data points in that cluster. This is done to ensure that the centroid is at the center of the cluster.

Step 6: Reassign Data Points. We then reassign each data point to its nearest centroid based on the updated centroid values. This process is repeated until the centroids no longer move, or the maximum number of iterations is reached.

Step 7: Interpret Results. The final step is to interpret the results of the clustering algorithm. In our example, we would interpret the results by analysing the characteristics of the customers in each cluster to determine distinct criteria that determine who should go where, based on gender.

Example 1: Let us consider our example with five data points (records): we assume that the first three data points are males and the last two data points are females. The spending on shoes and age of each data point is given in [Table 7.1](#15_Chapter7.xhtml#tab7-1).

[Table 7.1](#15_Chapter7.xhtml#tab-7-1)Spending pattern

 
| Customer ID || Age || Gender || Spending on shoes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 || 20 || Male || 500 |
| 2 || 25 || Male || 800 |
| 3 || 30 || Male || 400 |
| 4 || 35 || Female || 700 |
| 5 || 50 || Female || 300 |

The centroid of the male cluster is computed as follows:

The mean age of the male cluster is (20 + 25 + 30)/3 = 25

The mean spending on shoes of the male cluster is (500 + 800 + 400)/3 = 567

Therefore, the centroid of the male cluster is (25, 567).

The centroid of the female cluster is computed as follows:

The mean age of the female cluster is (35 + 50)/2 = 42.5

The mean spending on shoes of the female cluster is (700 + 300)/2 = 500

Therefore, the centroid of the female cluster is (42.5, 500).

Repeat steps 4–6 until convergence: We now repeat steps 4–6 until the centroids no longer change. In our example with only five data points, we have already converged, and we have found the two clusters:

The male cluster has customer IDs 1, 2, and 3, with centroid (25, 567)

The female cluster has customer IDs 4 and 5, with centroid (42.5, 500)

Once we have identified the two clusters, we can allocate the customers to the male or female cluster based on their distance from the two centroids. In practice, we would use many more data points and more than two clusters to obtain a more accurate clustering.

Next, the algorithm calculates the means of each cluster, which will serve as the new centroids. In our example, the mean spending and age of the customers in each cluster will be calculated, resulting in new centroids for the male and female groups. We sssign each customer to the nearest centroid based on their feature values. The distances between each customer and the centroids are calculated, and the customers are assigned to the group with the nearest centroid. This process is repeated until the centroids no longer change or a maximum number of iterations is reached.

In the end, we will have two distinct groups, male and female, based on their spending patterns and age. This information can be used by the company to tailor their marketing efforts and product offerings to each group’s preferences and needs.

Example 2: A person wants to divide customers into two distinct clusters based on the type of frequent product purchased. They could input individual item information about products bought previously and find relevant relationships between items people purchased to determine if certain items make the same part cluster, influencing the decision-making process of picking different items for future occasions. Let us assume we have a set of 5 customers and their purchase history for different products. The columns could include Customer ID, Product 1, Product 2, Product 3, etc., with the number of columns depending on the number of products the company sells. We can use K\-means clustering to group customers based on the products they buy the most.

Steps

1.Choose the number of clusters: In this example, we want to divide customers into two clusters based on the type of product they purchase the most.

2.Choose the initial centroids: Randomly select two customers from the data set to be the initial centroids for each cluster.

3.Calculate the distance: Calculate the distance between each customer and each centroid. The most common distance metric used is the Euclidean distance.

4.Assign customers to clusters: Assign each customer to the cluster with the closest centroid.

5.Calculate new centroids: Recalculate the centroid of each cluster as the mean of all the customers assigned to that cluster.

6.Repeat steps 3–5: Repeat steps 3-5 until the centroids no longer change, or a maximum number of iterations is reached.

7.Interpret the results: Once the algorithm has converged, the resulting clusters can be interpreted based on the products that each customer purchases most frequently.

For example, cluster 1 may consist of customers who purchase Product 1 and Product 2 the most frequently, while cluster 2 may consist of customers who purchase Product 3 and Product 4 the most frequently. The company can then use this information to tailor its marketing strategies to each cluster accordingly.

For example, if we have a set of 5 customers and 4 products, our item frequency matrix may look like [Table 7.2](#15_Chapter7.xhtml#tab7-2).

[Table 7.2](#15_Chapter7.xhtml#tab-7-2)Five customers and four products

 
| Customer || Product 1 || Product 2 || Product 3 || Product 4 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 || 3 || 2 || 1 || 4 |
| 2 || 0 || 1 || 4 || 2 |
| 3 || 2 || 3 || 0 || 1 |
| 4 || 1 || 2 || 3 || 2 |
| 5 || 3 || 1 || 2 || 0 |

Compute the distance between each data point and each centroid. In our example, we would compute the distance between each customer and each of the two centroids, which represent the two clusters (frequent buyers of Product A and frequent buyers of Product B).

Assign each data point to the nearest centroid. This step involves grouping the customers who are closest to each centroid, based on the distance computed in the previous step. For example, if a customer bought Product A twice and Product B once, they would be assigned to the cluster of customers who frequently buy Product A.

Recalculate the centroids of each cluster based on the new groupings in step 5. This involves computing the mean of all the data points assigned to each centroid. In our example, we would calculate the average frequency of purchases for each product in each cluster.

Convergence is achieved when the centroids no longer move significantly between iterations. At this point, the algorithm stops, and the clusters are considered finalized. Once the clusters have been determined, the company can use this information to make decisions about product development, marketing, and sales strategies.

Choosing an Appropriate Number of Clusters (K)

Selecting the optimal number of clusters is a critical stage in clustering analysis, as it dictates the division of data and the potential insights that may be extracted from it. Therefore, it is essential to establish criteria or procedures to determine the appropriate number of clusters.

The number of clusters chosen might be influenced by prior information or subject expertise. For instance, while clustering the data of university students, we can utilize the count of departments or faculties as an initial reference. This assumption is based on the idea that students from distinct departments exhibit distinct characteristics or behaviours. When clustering movie data based on two qualities, namely budget (high or low) and casting (star or non-star), it is appropriate to utilize four groups as these attributes have four potential combinations.

Business requirements and resource constraints are additional factors that can influence the selection of the number of clusters. Occasionally, we may have a distinct aim or purpose for clustering the data, such as partitioning, categorization, or suggestion. In such instances, we may have a predetermined quantity of clusters that we aim to attain, guided by the specifications or limitations of the problem. For example, a filmmaker may categorize movies to appeal to various audiences or markets. In doing so, they may have a predetermined number of segments they aim to establish, such as mainstream, niche, art-house, or independent. Suppose a filmmaker has limited resources in terms of budget or time. In that case, they may cluster movies to identify the most lucrative or viable combination of funding and casting.

Nevertheless, there are several instances where we lack any previous information or explicit objectives for grouping the data. For such situations, it is necessary to employ statistical methods or criteria to ascertain the most suitable number of clusters. These are now discussed in detail.

The elbow method determines the most suitable clusters in a clustering algorithm by calculating the sum of squared distances (SSD) between every data point and its designated cluster center. The cluster center represents the mean or typical location inside each cluster, whereas the SSD quantifies the level of compactness or homogeneity within each cluster. Optimally, our objective is to minimize the SSD, indicating that the data points are near their respective cluster centers and distinctly segregated from neighboring clusters. Nevertheless, when the number of clusters is augmented, the SSD will exhibit a more gradual decline as the data is progressively divided into increasingly smaller groups. Eventually, increasing the number of clusters will have diminishing returns on improving the SSD and could potentially lead to the introduction of noise or overfitting.

By employing K\-means clustering with various values of K, we may generate a plot of the SSD for each K value. This may be depicted as shown in [Fig. 7.8](#15_Chapter7.xhtml#fig7-8).

![](Images/f7-8.jpg)

[Figure 7.8](#15_Chapter7.xhtml#fig-7-8)  Elbow method to identify the K value

The silhouette method is used to assess the effectiveness of clustering outcomes. To utilize the silhouette method, it is necessary to compute the silhouette score for each data point. The silhouette score is a metric that quantifies the quality of clustering in a data set.

Let us represent the index of the data point. a(i) denotes the average distance between i and all other points in the same cluster, whereas b(i) represents the minimum average distance between i and all other points in any other cluster. The silhouette score s(i) is a metric that falls within the range of –1 to 1, with –1 indicating poor clustering and 1 indicating well-separated clusters. The formula for s(i) is calculated by subtracting a(i) from b(i) and then dividing the result by the larger value between a(i) and b(i).

A number nearing 1 indicates that the data point strongly resembles its own cluster (high cohesion) and a significant dissimilarity to other clusters (high separation). A data point with a value close to 0 indicates its proximity to the boundary between two clusters, making it potentially assignable to either. A number around –1 indicates that the data point exhibits low cohesiveness within its cluster and low separation from another cluster, indicating a high degree of dissimilarity.

The silhouette score for each cluster is calculated as the mean of the silhouette scores of all the data points within that cluster. The silhouette score for the entire data set is computed as the mean of the silhouette scores for each cluster. The ideal number of clusters is the one that maximizes the silhouette score for the given data set.

Consider a scenario where we possess a data set comprising four distinct attributes, and our objective is to categorize it into either two or three distinct groups. We can use a clustering technique to acquire the clustering results. Subsequently, the silhouette method can be employed to assess the calibre of each clustering outcome. [Table 7.3](#15_Chapter7.xhtml#tab7-3) displays the silhouette ratings for each data point and cluster in various scenarios.

[Table 7.3](#15_Chapter7.xhtml#tab-7-3)Silhouette rating example

 
| Data point || Cluster 1 (K = 2) || Cluster 2 (K = 2) || Cluster 1 (K = 3) || Cluster 2 (K = 3) || Cluster 3 (K = 3) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 || 0.65 || \- || 0.65 || \- || \- |
| 2 || 0.55 || \- || 0.55 || \- || \- |
| 3 || 0.60 || \- || \- || 0.60 || \- |
| 4 || \- || 0.70 || \- || \- || 0.70 |
| 5 || \- || 0.75 || \- || \- || 0.75 |
| 6 || \- || 0.80 || \- || \- || 0.85 |
| Cluster || 0.60 || 0.75 || 0.60 || 0.60 || 0.75 |
| Data set || \*\*0.68\*\* ||  || \*\*0.65\*\* ||  ||  |

It is evident that when K = 2, the score is higher than when K = 3. This indicates that two clusters are more suitable for this data set than three. It is evident that the data points in Cluster 2 exhibit higher silhouette scores compared to those in Cluster 1, suggesting that Cluster 2 is more tightly-knit and distinct than Cluster 1.

The silhouette approach is a useful tool, but it also has certain limits. For example, it may not perform optimally for data sets with clusters that overlap or have non-spherical shapes or for data sets that contain noise or outliers. Thus, it is recommended to employ alternative approaches such as visual examination, subject expertise, or statistical analyses to supplement the silhouette method.

The gap statistic approach is used to ascertain the most suitable clusters in a given data set. The underlying concept is that data should exhibit more structure or patterns rather than random noise. Consequently, the SSD between the data points and their cluster centers should be minimized by clustering the data. The gap statistic approach aims to determine the ideal equilibrium by comparing the SSD of the actual data with randomly produced data with similar features, such as size and form. The assumption is that the randomly produced data lacks any discernible structure or clusters, resulting in minimal variation in its SSD when the number of clusters is altered. The gap statistic approach computes the gap, a metric that quantifies the disparity between the log(SSD) of the observed data and the log(SSD) of the randomly generated data for each cluster count. As the gap increases, the actual data exhibits a greater degree of pattern or clustering than the random data. The ideal number of clusters is the one that maximizes the gap.

Let us consider an example of clustering some two-dimensional data points. We can calculate the SSD for each clustering by summing up the squared distances between each data point and its cluster center. [Table 7.4](#15_Chapter7.xhtml#tab7-4) shows the SSD values for each clustering.

[Table 7.4](#15_Chapter7.xhtml#tab-7-4) SSD values for each clustering

 
| Number of clusters (K) || SSD |
| --- | --- |
| 2 || 9.2 |
| 3 || 6.4 |
| 4 || 4.8 |
| 5 || 3.6 |

The SSD value decreases to the growth (increase) in the number of clusters, as anticipated. Nevertheless, this information does not provide the ideal clustering solution, as we need knowledge regarding the expected SSD resulting from random noise.

To address this, we can produce a set of random data that matches the size and structure of the original data and, after that, compute the SSD for each possible number of clusters. We can iterate this procedure to obtain the mean SSD for each cluster quantity. [Table 7.5](#15_Chapter7.xhtml#tab7-5) illustrates an instance of arbitrary data and its corresponding average SSD values.

[Table 7.5](#15_Chapter7.xhtml#tab-7-5)Average SSD values for random data

 
| Number of clusters (K) || Average SSD |
| --- | --- |
| 2 || 8.9 |
| 3 || 8.7 |
| 4 || 8.6 |
| 5 || 8.5 |

The mean SSD for random data remains very stable regardless of the number of clusters, as anticipated. Consequently, clustering random data has minimal impact in reducing its dispersion.

Now, we can compute the gap statistic for each cluster count by subtracting the logarithm of the SSD of the actual data from the logarithm of the SSD of the random data. [Table 7.6](#15_Chapter7.xhtml#tab7-6) displays the gap values corresponding to each cluster count.

[Table 7.6](#15_Chapter7.xhtml#tab-7-6)Gap values for each cluster count

 
| Number of clusters (K) || Gap |
| --- | --- |
| 2 || \-0.03 |
| 3 || \-0.17 |
| 4 || \-0.23 |
| 5 || \-0.26 |

It is evident that the difference widens as the number of clusters rises, yet it remains negative for all values of K. Consequently, all clustering has an SSD equal to or higher than that of random noise. As a result, none of the clustering possesses a discernible structure or pattern. Based on this scenario, it may be inferred that no definitive number of clusters is most suitable for this particular data set.

The gap statistic approach is a widely used for determining the most suitable number of clusters in a given data set. Nevertheless, this technique has imperfections and some limits and assumptions that must be considered. An essential premise of the gap statistic approach is that the reference distribution, created randomly, shares similar attributes with the real data, including dimensionality and shape. Consequently, the random data must possess an equivalent amount of characteristics and instances as the actual data and should have a uniform distribution within the identical domain. Nevertheless, attaining this objective in practice may be challenging and unreliable, as actual data frequently exhibits intricate structures and patterns that simplistic random models do not adequately represent.

Another obstacle is its reliance on our capacity to generate random data that faithfully emulates noise. Noise refers to the undesired fluctuations or inaccuracies in the data not associated with any cluster. The gap statistic approach assumes that noise is equally distributed and has no correlation with the clusters. However, this assertion may not hold for certain real data sets, as noise may exhibit a discernible structure or pattern that can impact clustering outcomes. If the noise is connected with certain attributes or data, it can generate new clusters or distort the actual ones. This can result in inaccurate gap values and incorrect determination of the ideal number of clusters..

Another constraint of the gap statistic method is establishing a range of potential cluster numbers, which might be challenging to determine. The range should be sufficiently broad to encompass the genuine best value while avoiding excessive computations and erroneous outcomes. If the range is excessively limited, there is a possibility that we will overlook the optimal value and ultimately obtain clustering that is less than ideal. In the case of a wide range, we may face issues like overfitting or underfitting, where we either identify an excessive number of little clusters or a limited number of large clusters that fail to represent the actual data structure accurately.

Another limitation is its failure to account for additional factors that impact the clustering’s quality, such as the clusters’ shape, size, or distance from each other. The analysis solely concentrates on the SSD for quantifying the dispersion inside clusters. Nevertheless, SSD may not be comprehensive or satisfactory in capturing all the intricacies or inclinations of diverse clustering applications or scenarios. It is imperative to exercise prudence and supplement it with other techniques or standards to guarantee resilient and dependable clustering outcomes.

7.3.1.2Hierarchical Clustering

Hierarchical clustering is a robust unsupervised learning algorithm that uses a hierarchical approach to group data points into clusters. It begins by assigning each data point its cluster, then works to merge them in a hierarchical tree structure as it determines the similarities and differences between different data points. As a result, the algorithm can identify patterns and create clusters based on shared characteristics by comparing these characteristics. This type of clustering can be used for various applications, such as customer segmentation or recognizing patterns in large data sets.

One advantage of hierarchical clustering is that it does not require prior knowledge about the data set or any assumptions about its structure, making it suitable for exploratory analysis. It often produces more accurate results than other algorithms since it can capture subtler differences between groups of objects compared to other methods. Users can easily modify clusters based on their specific needs by changing parameters such as similarity criteria or linkage methods.

Let us consider a data set of customers of an online store, where each customer is described by their age, gender, income, and purchase history. The goal is to cluster the customers based on their similarity in terms of these features.

Steps

Step 1: Distance Calculation. The first step is to calculate the distance between each pair of customers. Here, we can use the Euclidean distance as a measure of similarity between customers. We can represent the data set in tabular form where each row represents a customer and the columns represent the features. [Table 7.7](#15_Chapter7.xhtml#tab7-7) shows the details for five customers.

[Table 7.7](#15_Chapter7.xhtml#tab-7-7)Customer details

 
| Customer || Age || Gender || Income || Purchase history |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 || 30 || Male || 50000 || Low |
| 2 || 35 || Female || 60000 || Medium |
| 3 || 25 || Female || 40000 || High |
| 4 || 45 || Male || 80000 || Low |
| 5 || 50 || Female || 90000 || High |

Step 2: Creating a Distance Matrix. Next, we need to define a distance or similarity measure between the customers based on their features. One possible choice is the Euclidean distance, which is the square root of the sum of squared differences between corresponding feature values. For example, the Euclidean distance between customer 1 and customer 2 is:

sqrt((30-35)^2 + (0-1)^2 + (50000-60000)^2 + (0-1)^2) = 10001.41,

where we have encoded the gender and purchase history features as binary variables (0 for male/low, 1 for female/high). Using this distance measure, we can construct a distance matrix ([Table 7.8](#15_Chapter7.xhtml#tab7-8)) that shows the pairwise distances between all customers.

[Table 7.8](#15_Chapter7.xhtml#tab-7-8)Distance matrix

 
| Distance || 1 || 2 || 3 || 4 || 5 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 || 0 || 10001.41 || 10001.41 || 30001.41 || 40001.41 |
| 2 || 10001.41 || 0 || 20001.41 || 20001.41 || 30001.41 |
| 3 || 10001.41 || 20001.41 || 0 || 40001.41 || 50001.41 |
| 4 || 30001.41 || 20001.41 || 40001.41 || 0 || 10001.41 |
| 5 || 40001.41 || 30001.41 || 50001.41 || 10001.41 || 0 |

Step 3: Building the Dendrogram. A dendrogram is a tree-like diagram that shows the hierarchical ­relationship between the customers based on their similarity. We start by considering each customer as a separate cluster and then merge the closest clusters until we end up with a single cluster that contains all the customers.

We perform the clustering algorithm using different methods such as single linkage, complete linkage, average linkage, or Ward’s method. Here, we will use single linkage, which merges the clusters that have the smallest minimum distance between any pair of their members.

The algorithm starts with each customer as a separate cluster:

{1}, {2}, {3}, {4}, {5}

The smallest distance in the matrix is 10001.41, which occurs between customer 1 and customer 3, and between customer 2 and customer 4. We can merge these pairs into two clusters:

{1, 3}, {2, 4}, {5}

The next smallest distance is 20001.41, which occurs between customer 2 and customer 5, and between customer 3 and customer 5. We can merge these pairs into two clusters:

{1, 3, 5}, {2, 4}

The final step is to merge the remaining two clusters into one:

{1, 3, 5, 2, 4}

This is the final clustering result using single linkage hierarchical clustering. The dendrogram for this example is shown in [Fig. 7.9](#15_Chapter7.xhtml#fig7-9).

![](Images/f7-9.jpg)

[Figure 7.9](#15_Chapter7.xhtml#fig-7-9)  Dendrogram example

Hierarchical clustering can be applied to a wide range of data sets and is particularly useful for identifying patterns in large and complex data sets. It can also be used for data visualization and exploratory analysis, as the resulting dendrogram provides a clear visualization of the relationships between the data points.

The two primary types of hierarchical clustering are agglomerative clustering and divisive clustering ([Fig. 7.10](#15_Chapter7.xhtml#fig7-10)).

![](Images/f7-10.jpg)

[Figure 7.10](#15_Chapter7.xhtml#fig-7-10)  Agglomerative and division clustering

Agglomerative clustering is a hierarchical method that begins by treating each data point as an individual cluster. It then progressively combines the most comparable clusters until a certain number of clusters or a predetermined stopping condition is met. Various approaches can be used to quantify the similarity between clusters, including single linkage (minimum distance), complete linkage (maximum distance), average linkage (average distance), and Ward’s method (minimum variance).

Divisive clustering is a hierarchical method that begins by grouping all data points into a single cluster and then proceeds to divide the cluster into smaller clusters iteratively until a specified number of clusters or a predetermined stopping condition is met. Clusters can be divided using many criteria, such as the maximum distance between data points, the minimum density of data points, or the minimal silhouette coefficient.

One instance of hierarchical clustering involves categorizing papers according to their respective subjects. Agglomerative clustering begins by treating each document as its cluster, then combines clusters that share similar words or concepts until a predetermined number of topics or a threshold of similarity is achieved. Divisive clustering begins by grouping all documents into a single cluster and dividing the cluster into smaller subclusters depending on the dissimilarity of words or keywords. This process continues until a predetermined number of topics or a dissimilarity threshold is achieved.

7.3.1.3Fuzzy C-Means Clustering

This is a popular data mining technique that uses fuzzy logic to identify clusters within large, complex data sets. Unlike other clustering algorithms, it does not rely on rigid boundaries to assign labels or define the characteristics of each cluster. Instead, it utilizes probabilistic relationships between data points to assign them to groups based on their likelihood of belonging to each category. This approach allows for more accurate classifications of complex data sets. In addition, it helps uncover subtle patterns that standard methods may otherwise overlook.

The algorithm assigns a membership value or degree of association with each data point in relation to all the other points within the data set. A probability between 0 and 1 is typically used to indicate this value, with higher values denoting a more substantial likelihood of belonging to the cluster and lower values denoting a weaker link. The algorithm evaluates these probabilities to determine which points should be grouped according to their similarities or dissimilarities. Once this has been done, it can use those groupings as categories or labels when classifying new data points into groups accordingly.

Because fuzzy C-means clustering does not require strict rules for assigning classes, it allows for more creative solutions when dealing with complicated data sets that contain outliers and non-conforming values. Furthermore, its ability to identify subtle patterns makes it an invaluable tool for many areas where pattern recognition is essential, such as computer vision applications and financial market analysis. Despite its advantages compared with traditional clustering methods, however, there are still drawbacks associated with this algorithm, such as requiring extensive computational resources, which can limit its usefulness if applied to extensive data sets where time constraints are an issue.

To illustrate this clustering algorithm, let us consider a hypothetical scenario with a data set of customers and their spending habits on various products. The products include shoes, clothing, and accessories. We aim to segment the customers into groups based on their similarity in purchasing behavior, and design customized marketing strategies for each group.

Steps

1.First, we need to specify the number of clusters we want to create and initialize the fuzzy membership matrix. The fuzzy membership matrix contains the degree of membership of each data point to each cluster. We can initialize it randomly or use some heuristic method. For simplicity, let us assume we want to create two clusters, and we initialize the fuzzy membership matrix randomly.

2.Next, we need to calculate the centroids of the two clusters based on the initial fuzzy membership matrix. The centroid of a cluster is the weighted average of all the data points in the cluster, where the weights are the degrees of membership. The centroids represent the center or prototype of each cluster.

3.We need to calculate the distance between each data point and the centroids of the two clusters. We can use any distance measure, such as Euclidean or Manhattan distance. The distance measures how far a data point is from the centroid of a cluster.

4.We need to update the fuzzy membership matrix based on the distance between each data point and the centroids. We use a fuzzy membership function that assigns a higher degree of membership to a data point closer to a cluster’s centroid and a lower degree of membership to a data point farther from a cluster’s centroid. The fuzzy membership function also depends on the fuzziness factor, which controls how much overlap there is between the clusters. A higher fuzziness factor means more overlap, and a lower fuzziness factor means less overlap.

5.Next, we repeat steps two to four until the algorithm converges. The algorithm converges when there is no significant change in the fuzzy membership matrix or the centroids of the clusters.

6.Finally, we need to assign each data point to the cluster with the highest degree of membership. This results in a soft partitioning of the data, where each data point belongs to multiple clusters with different degrees of membership. We can then analyze the characteristics of each cluster and identify common patterns among the customers in each cluster.

To explain how this works, let us consider the data points: {(1, 2), (3, 5), (6, 8), (7, 10)}. Suppose we want to cluster them into two groups: A and B. We start by randomly assigning membership values to each data point for each cluster ([Table 7.9](#15_Chapter7.xhtml#tab7-9)).

[Table 7.9](#15_Chapter7.xhtml#tab-7-9)Fuzzy C-means data point and membership

 
| Data point || Membership in A || Membership in B |
| --- | --- | --- |
| (1,2) || 0.7 || 0.3 |
| (3,5) || 0.6 || 0.4 |
| (6,8) || 0.2 || 0.8 |
| (7,10) || 0.1 || 0.9 |

The membership values indicate how strongly each data point belongs to each cluster. They must sum up to one for each data point. Next, we calculate the centroids of each cluster based on the weighted average of the data points and their membership values. For example, the centroid of cluster A is:

(0.7 \* 1 + 0.6 \* 3 + 0.2 \* 6 + 0.1 \* 7) / (0.7 + 0.6 + 0.2 + 0.1) = 2.9

(0.7 \* 2 + 0.6 \* 5 + 0.2 \* 8 + 0.1 \* 10) / (0.7 + 0.6 + 0.2 + 0.1) = 4

Similarly, the centroid of cluster B is:

(0.3 \* 1 + 0.4 \* 3 + 0.8 \* 6 + 0.9 \* 7) / (0.3 + 0.4 + 0.8 + 0.9) = 5.9

(0.3 \* 2 + 0.4 \* 5 + 0.8 \* 8 + 0.9 \* 10) / (0.3 + 0.4 + 0.8 + 0.9) = 8

Then, we update the membership values of each data point based on their distance to the centroids of each cluster using a formula that involves a parameter called the fuzziness coefficient, which controls how fuzzy the clusters are. A higher fuzziness coefficient means more overlap between clusters, while a lower one means more separation.

The membership value of a data point for a cluster is inversely proportional to the distance to the centroid of that cluster, raised to a power m that controls the fuzziness of the clustering. A higher value of m means more fuzziness, and a lower value means more crispness. A common choice for m is 2.

For example, the distance from (1, 2) to the centroid of cluster A is:

sqrt((1 – 2.9)^2 + (2 – 4.5)^2) = sqrt(5) = ~2.24

The distance from (1, 2) to the centroid of cluster B is:

sqrt((1 – 6.4)^2 + (2 – 8.9)^2) = sqrt(58) = ~7.62

The membership value of (1, 2) for cluster A is:

(1 / sqrt(5))^(2 / (m – 1)) / ((1 / sqrt(5))^(2 / (m – 1)) + (1 / sqrt(58))^(2 / (m – 1))) = ((sqrt(58))^m / ((sqrt(58))^m + (sqrt(5))^m))

If we choose m = 2, this becomes:

(sqrt(58)^2 / ((sqrt(58))^2 + (sqrt(5))^2)) = ((58 / (58 + 5))) = ~0.92

The membership value of (1, 2) for cluster B is:

(1 / sqrt(58))^(2 / (m \- 1)) / ((1 / sqrt(5))^(2 / (m \- 1)) + (1 / sqrt(58))^(2 / (m \- 1)))

\= ((sqrt(5))^m / ((sqrt(58))^m + (sqrt(5))^m))

If we choose m = 2, this becomes:

(sqrt(5)^2 / ((sqrt(58))^2 + (sqrt(5))^2))

\= ((5 / (58 + 5))) = ~0.08                      

We repeat this process of calculating centroids and updating membership values until the membership values converge or reach a predefined threshold. The result is a fuzzy partition of the data points into two clusters, where each data point has a degree of belonging to each cluster.

7.3.1.4DBSCAN

Density-based spatial clustering of noise-induced applications is a well-known algorithm for density-based clustering. It is better than K\-means for identifying clusters as it cross-examines its data points’ density in more extensive spatial databases. The algorithm divides the low-density areas into high-density areas.

Imagine you have a data set with the geographical coordinates (latitude and longitude) of all coffee shops in a city. When you apply DBSCAN to this data set, the algorithm will look for areas where coffee shops are densely packed. For instance, in a downtown area, coffee shops are likely to be close to each other due to high foot traffic and demand. DBSCAN will identify these clusters of coffee shops as a single group.

On the other hand, in suburban areas, coffee shops may be more spread out. DBSCAN will recognize these as separate clusters or even as noise if they are too far apart. For example, if there are only a few coffee shops scattered across a large suburban area, they might not form a dense cluster.

Additionally, DBSCAN can identify outliers. These are coffee shops that are located far from any other coffee shops, such as a lone coffee shop in a remote area. The algorithm will mark these as noise or outliers because they do not belong to any cluster.

The clusters can therefore be found in any arbitrary shape. You will need a minimum number of points within the neighborhood of the starting data point to start the clustering process. Otherwise, those data points would end up as noise. The DBSCAN algorithm also does not require a pre-set number of clusters. This algorithm selects an arbitrary point and then identifies other points near the arbitrary one.

Later, the data points recognized with the help of an arbitrary one are recognized as a cluster. The one far away from the arbitrary point (noise/outliers) is used in other iterations of identifying the clusters. The fact that this algorithm is robust to outliers, or will not include outlier data points in any cluster, gives it a significant advantage over K\-means and MeanShift. K\-means clusters every instance in the data sets, whereas DBSCAN does not include noise points (outliers) in a legitimate cluster. Non-global clusters are challenging for K\-means, whereas DBSCAN handles them without issue. Unlike DBSCAN, the K\-means algorithm does not presuppose that the data set’s data points come from a Gaussian distribution.

In order to demonstrate the functioning of DBSCAN, we shall examine the subsequent data points presented in [Table 7.10](#15_Chapter7.xhtml#tab7-10).

[Table 7.10](#15_Chapter7.xhtml#tab-7-10)DBSCAN data points

 
| ID || X || Y |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 || 1 || 2 |
| 2 || 2 || 2 |
| 3 || 3 || 2 |
| 4 || 4 || 2 |
| 5 || 5 || 2 |
| 6 || 6 || 2 |
| 7 || 7 || 2 |
| 8 || 8 || 2 |
| 9 || 9 || 2 |
| 10 || 10 || 2 |

The algorithm is defined by two parameters: epsilon (eps) and minimum points (minPts). eps represents the upper limit for the distance between two points to be classified as neighbors, while minPts denotes the minimum number of points needed to establish a cluster. For this illustration, let us assume that the value of eps is 1.5 and the value of minPts is 3.

The procedure commences by selecting a random location, designated as point 1, and identifying all adjacent points within a specified distance of epsilon. Point 2 is the sole adjacent point to point 1 in this scenario. Because the number of neighboring points is below the minimum required number (minPts), point 1 is classified as noise and is not allocated to any cluster.

The program subsequently selects another point at random, such as point 4, and identifies its neighboring points within a distance of eps. Points 3, 4, 5, and 6 are adjacent to point 4 in this scenario. Given that the number of neighboring points equals or exceeds the minimum required number of points (minPts), point 4 is designated as a core point and allocated to a newly formed cluster, referred to as cluster A.

The procedure proceeds by enlarging cluster A through the iterative inclusion of all the neighboring points of point 4, and subsequently their respective neighbors, provided that they are within a distance of eps and possess a minimum of minPts neighbors. In this instance, points 3, 5, and 6 are designated core points and included in cluster A. Point 2 is designated as a border point and included in cluster A because it is located within the specified distance (eps) from a core point. However, it does not have the minimum number of neighboring points (minPts).

Subsequently, the program selects another location randomly, denoted as point 8, and proceeds to perform an identical procedure. Points 7, 8, 9, and 10 are adjacent to point 8 in this scenario. Given that the number of neighbors equals or exceeds the minimum number of points (minPts), point 8 is classified as a core point and allocated to a newly formed cluster, referred to as cluster B. The algorithm proceeds by enlarging cluster B by including all the adjacent points of point 8 and their respective adjacent points in a recursive manner. This expansion continues as long as the points are within a distance of eps and possess a minimum of minPts neighbors. In this instance, points 7, 9, and 10 are designated core points and included in cluster B.

The program selects another point randomly, referred to as point 1, and determines that it has already undergone processing and been designated as noise. The algorithm concludes once all the points have been processed.

There are two clusters in the final result: cluster A, which contains the points {2,3,4,5,6}, and cluster B, which contains the points {7,8,9,10}. Point 1 is disregarded as irrelevant data.

Advantages: One of the main benefits of DBSCAN is its ability to detect clusters of various shapes, sizes, and densities without prior knowledge about the data or assumptions about cluster structure. Unlike K\-means and hierarchical clustering, DBSCAN does not require the user to specify the number of clusters beforehand; instead, it automatically detects the number of clusters in the data. It is also robust to noise since it ignores points that are too sparsely distributed or isolated from other points and, therefore, unlikely to be part of any meaningful structure. This makes DBSCAN an ideal choice for analysing complex data sets with noisy features or outliers.

Another advantage is that users do not have to worry about specifying parameters such as distance thresholds which can dramatically affect performance; instead, they can tune two key parameters: ­epsilon (ε) which determines how close two points must be for them to be considered ‘neighbors’; and minPts which specifies what minimum number of neighbors each point must have within a ­certain radius for it to form a cluster. With these parameters appropriately set by an experienced analyst, DBSCAN can easily discover hidden patterns within data sets without relying on prior assumptions about cluster structure or requiring manual user intervention.

Disadvantages: DBSCAN is a practical algorithm for clustering large data sets. However, it can be sensitive to outliers, leading to misclassifications of points and unexpected results. If DBSCAN sets its parameters too low, these outliers might be classified as noise instead of as part of a cluster; if set too high, entire clusters could be missed or improperly grouped due to their similar densities. To avoid this problem, it is essential to consider the outliers present in the data set and adjust the parameters accordingly.

For example, there are many clustered points with low density compared to nearby points. In that case, increasing epsilon and minPts may help ensure that all clustered points are adequately identified. Similarly, if there is more than one group/cluster present with similar densities caused by overlapping clusters or varying densities within one group/cluster itself, then setting epsilon higher than usual will help ensure that all clusters are properly assigned, even though some objects might still fall outside their respective boundaries due to being an outlier.

Finally, when working with large data sets containing multiple overlapped and varied clusters, it is recommended not only to adjust parameter values but also to check for possible outliers beforehand since this will improve accuracy and reduce unnecessary computations when running DBSCAN.

7.3.1.5The Gaussian Mixture Model

The Gaussian mixture model (GMM) combines probability distributions to model data, with each component representing a different kind of pattern in the data. It is a probabilistic model which assigns each observation to one or more clusters based on the likelihood that it belongs to each cluster. The fundamental assumption behind GMMs is that all data points can be explained by a mixture of Gaussian distributions, or ‘clusters.’ Each clusters associated mean and covariance matrix defines its shape and spread within the multidimensional feature space. The number of clusters does not have to be specified beforehand, as the algorithm will determine this during the training phase.

Steps

1.The first step of GMM involves estimating which components best explain the input data by maximizing the likelihood function given by a set of observed data points. This involves estimating parameters such as mean and covariance for each component.

2.In the second step, observations are assigned to clusters according to their likelihoods; that is, how probable it is that they belong to a particular component/cluster, given their values on specific features (such as height, weight, etc.). For example, if two observations have very similar characteristics (they both have similar heights and weights), they would likely be assigned to the same component/cluster since they would likely have originated from one common source (as opposed to two different sources). This allows us to find groups within our data set without needing labels, even when they may overlap (if two clusters have overlapping means). Observations with higher likelihoods for multiple clusters may become part of both groups simultaneously.

Once these steps have been completed, we can use this information for further analysis or even make predictions about future behavior.

One way to understand GMM is to use the expectation maximization (EM) algorithm, which iteratively updates the parameters until convergence. The EM algorithm consists of two steps: the E-step and the M-step. In the E-step, the algorithm computes the posterior probability of each data point belonging to each component, based on the current parameters. In the M-step, the algorithm updates the parameters by maximizing the log-likelihood function, which is a weighted sum of the log-likelihoods of each component.

For example, suppose we have a data set of heights and weights of 10 people, as shown in Table 7.11.

Table 7.11GMM data points

 
| Height || Weight |
| --- | --- |
| 170 || 65 |
| 180 || 75 |
| 190 || 85 |
| 160 || 55 |
| 165 || 60 |
| 175 || 70 |
| 185 || 80 |
| 195 || 90 |
| 155 || 50 |
| 150 || 45 |

We can use GMM to cluster this data into two groups, assuming that each group follows a bivariate Gaussian distribution, and then estimate the parameters of these distributions from the data. The parameters we need to estimate are:

•The mean vector for each group, which is a two-dimensional vector that contains the average height and weight of the group.

•The covariance matrix for each group, which is a two-by-two matrix that captures the variability and correlation of height and weight within the group.

•The mixing coefficient for each group, which is a scalar that indicates the proportion of the data that belongs to the group.

We can initialize the parameters randomly, such as:

–Mean of group 1: (160, 60)

–Mean of group 2: (180, 80)

–Covariance of group 1: \[\[100, 0\], \[0, 100\]\]

–Covariance of group 2: \[\[100, 0\], \[0, 100\]\]

–Weight of group 1: 0.5

–Weight of group 2: 0.5

Estimation of these parameters can be done using the EM algorithm:

1.Expectation step: In this step, we compute the probability of each data point belonging to each group, given the current estimates of the parameters. This probability is also known as the responsibility or posterior probability. For example, if we have two groups with means (170,65) and (180,75), and equal covariances and mixing coefficients, then the probability of the first data point (170,65) belonging to the first group is higher than the second group, because it is closer to its mean. The formula for computing this probability is based on Bayes’ theorem and the multivariate Gaussian density function.

2.Maximization step: In this step, we update the estimates of the parameters based on the probabilities computed in the expectation step. We use these probabilities as weights to compute the weighted average and covariance of each group. We also normalize these probabilities to obtain the new mixing coefficients. The formulas for updating the parameters are derived from maximizing the log-likelihood function of the data.

Then we can apply the EM algorithm to update the parameters until convergence. After a few iterations, we may obtain the following results:

–Mean of group 1: (152.5, 47.5)

–Mean of group 2: (182.5, 77.5)

–Covariance of group 1: \[\[62.5, -12.5\], \[-12.5, 62.5\]\]

–Covariance of group 2: \[\[62.5, -12.5\], \[-12.5, 62.5\]\]

–Weight of group 1: 0.4

–Weight of group 2: 0.6

We repeat these two steps until convergence, which means that the parameters do not change significantly between iterations. The final estimates of the parameters define the GMM that best fits the data.

Based on these parameters, we can assign each data point to the most likely group, as shown in [Table 7.12](#15_Chapter7.xhtml#tab7-12).

[Table 7.12](#15_Chapter7.xhtml#tab-7-12)GMM data points with final classification

 
| Height || Weight || Group |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 170 || 65 || 2 |
| 180 || 75 || 2 |
| 190 || 85 || 2 |
| 160 || 55 || 2 |
| 165 || 60 || 2 |
| 175 || 70 || 2 |
| 185 || 80 || 2 |
| 195 || 90 || 2 |
| 155 || 50 || 1 |
| 150 || 45 || 1 |

This is one possible clustering result using GMM. The advantage of GMM is that it can capture the shape and orientation of the clusters, unlike other methods such as K\-means that assume spherical clusters. The disadvantage of GMM is that it requires more parameters and computations than other methods, and it may suffer from overfitting if the number of components is too large or the data is sparse.

7.3.1.6MeanShift Clustering

It is a clustering algorithm that iteratively shifts the centroids of the data points toward the higher-density areas. It does not require labeled data, nor does it involve any predetermined targets or outputs. Unlike the K\-means algorithm, the MeanShift algorithm does not require us to specify the number of clusters. Suppose you need clarification on the patterns in the data, the algorithm automatically determines the number of clusters. Dense data point areas use a sliding-window centroid-based algorithm to locate the center group/class points. All center point candidates are considered to be the mean value of the sliding window points. Such windows are then sorted post-processing to remove duplicates and give the final group center points.

Image segmentation tasks are where MeanShift clustering is most frequently used. Kernel density estimation is the foundation of the MeanShift algorithm. This algorithm iteratively assigns each data point to the closest cluster centroid, which is initialized arbitrarily. Then, each point is iteratively moved in the space based on where the most points are, that is, the mode. This method overcomes the selection of groups and cluster centers as the mean values are discovered automatically. The clusters also exhibit data sense due to convergence to the areas having maximum data points intuitively. Here, the window size is crucial as it determines the scale of the clustering and directly affects the number of clusters detected. A smaller window size can lead to many small clusters, while a larger window size may merge distinct clusters into a single one. Thus, if the window size is too small, it may result in overfitting. If the window size is too large, it may lead to underfitting. The radius of the window size is thus a critical factor that can lead to non-trivial and sometimes disadvantageous clustering results.

A randomly selected circular sliding window is defined as point C with kernel radius r. The hill-climbing MeanShift algorithm shifts the kernel through successive iterations to higher-density regions and repeats the process until convergence is obtained. Finally, in the post-processing stage, the candidate windows are filtered. A final set of centroids and the assigned groups of data points are produced as a result of this process ([Table 7.13](#15_Chapter7.xhtml#tab7-13)).

[Table 7.13](#15_Chapter7.xhtml#tab-7-13)MeanShift clustering data points

 
| Height || Weight |
| --- | --- |
| 170 || 65 |
| 180 || 75 |
| 190 || 85 |
| 160 || 55 |
| 165 || 60 |
| 175 || 70 |
| 185 || 80 |
| 195 || 90 |
| 155 || 50 |
| 150 || 45 |

Steps

1.Initialize each data point as a cluster centroid.

2.For each data point, calculate the mean of all points within a certain radius (the bandwidth) centered at the data point. For example, if we use a bandwidth of 10 cm for height and 5 kg for weight, then the mean of the points within this radius for the first data point (170 cm, 65 kg) is (172.5 cm, 67.5 kg).

3.Shift each data point to the mean calculated in the previous step. For example, the first data point will move from (170 cm, 65 kg) to (172.5 cm, 67.5 kg).

4.Repeat steps 2 and 3 until convergence or a maximum number of iterations is reached. Convergence means that the data points do not move significantly after shifting.

5.Identify the cluster centroids as the points that have not moved after convergence. These are the modes of the density function and represent the clusters in the data.

Using this algorithm, we can obtain two clusters from the given data: one cluster with four points around (195 cm, 90 kg) and another cluster with six points around (165 cm, 60 kg).

Advantages: MeanShift clustering is an efficient and flexible tool for analyzing data. It can quickly identify clusters of any size or shape in complex data sets without the need for prior knowledge about the data. MeanShift is also robust against noise and outliers, making it suitable for real-world applications where the data may contain errors or inconsistencies that adversely affect other clustering algorithms. This makes it an ideal choice for exploratory analysis when trying to understand how variables are related to a data set. MeanShift clustering is also widely used in ML applications such as object tracking and image segmentation due to its flexibility and efficiency compared to clustering algorithms like K\-means clustering. With MeanShift, ML models can quickly recognize patterns in large volumes of data, leading to more accurate predictions than would otherwise be possible with traditional methods.

Disadvantages: One of the main disadvantages of MeanShift clustering is its inability to handle high-dimensional data sets effectively. As dimensions increase beyond 10 or 12, the algorithm’s reliance on distance metrics becomes increasingly meaningless. It needs to scale better when dealing with larger data sets. Another disadvantage is the difficulty in selecting appropriate parameters, such as bandwidth and kernel functions, which require significant domain knowledge or trial-and-error experimentation if they must be chosen correctly. This can lead to suboptimal results if done incorrectly, making it essential for users to understand how these parameters affect the clustering process before they begin their analysis. Finally, due to its reliance on local optimization methods such as the hill climbing technique, MeanShift clustering can sometimes converge onto local optima instead of global ones – resulting in inaccurate clusters even when applied correctly.

7.3.1.7Gaussian Mixture Density Estimation

Gaussian mixture density estimation (GMDE) is an important unsupervised learning technique used to find patterns in complex data sets and make predictions without prior knowledge of class labels. It uses probability density functions (PDFs) to model the data, combining multiple PDFs into one overall probability distribution. The PDFs are determined by fitting Gaussian distributions on each cluster since they are best suited to represent the shape of data points in such data sets. The EM algorithm is then used to estimate the parameters for each mixture model component.

This algorithm starts by assuming initial parameter values for each component and then adjusts them through successive iterations so that they best fit the data. Each iteration calculates the probability that a given point belongs to a particular component based on its current parameter values. It modifies them accordingly during maximization steps to have more influence over certain parts of the data set that need better representation. Once this process has been completed and stable parameter estimates obtained, these PDFs can be utilized for further analysis, such as predicting new observations or gaining insights into patterns within data sets.

For example, we want to predict whether someone will buy an item or not based on their past purchasing habits. In this case, we would use GMDE algorithms such as K\-means clustering or EM which would help us identify clusters in our data set using their probability densities and thereby accurately predict which customers may be likely buyers or non-buyers depending on what clusters they belong to. This powerful tool helps businesses better understand their customers by identifying hidden relationships between different variables, ultimately allowing them to make better decisions when it comes time for product development or marketing strategies. GMDE can also be effectively used in medical diagnosis. Doctors can detect diseases early before symptoms appear based on patient history by clustering patients with similar characteristics together according to their associated probabilities.

GMDE works by estimating the parameters of multiple Gaussian distributions, which are mathematical functions that look like bell curves, to best fit the observed data and determine its underlying structure. This process is called maximum likelihood estimation (MLE). It involves adjusting each component’s parameters until they reach their highest possible likelihood, given their respective clusters of observations. This technique can help us make more accurate predictions about new observations based on past ones without additional training or information about the underlying phenomenon being studied.

For example, consider the situation where you want to forecast whether it will rain tomorrow based on the weather today. You could use MLE with GMDE to estimate the probability distribution between how much rainfall there typically is on days with similar temperatures and wind speeds as today. Once you have determined this probability distribution, you can make more informed decisions regarding how likely tomorrow’s rainfall amount will fall within specific ranges given current conditions.

Once completed, these components can be used to classify unseen observations into corresponding clusters based on their likelihood value concerning each component’s PDFs; higher values indicate a higher likelihood of association with a particular cluster. In comparison, lower values will point toward less likely associations with other clusters nearby in feature space. GMDE can also generate predictions about unseen data points or perform clustering tasks such as outlier detection and anomaly identification when combined with other ML algorithms like K\-means and hierarchical clustering.

7.3.1.8Markov Random Field

Markove random field (MRF) is a powerful mathematical tool used to model complex relationships between different variables. They are instrumental in tasks such as computer vision, NLP, medical diagnosis, and many more. The basic idea is that each variable is associated with its local environment rather than its global state. For example, in an image model, each pixel will depend on the pixels around it; or in a text model, each word will depend on its neighboring words rather than the entire document. MRFs allow us to capture long-range correlations in data and thus make better predictions than traditional methods.

Besides being used for complex tasks like forecasting the weather or predicting stock prices, MRFs can also be used for more specific learning activities like solving puzzles or playing games. For instance, when solving a jigsaw puzzle, we can use an MRF-based approach which assigns probabilities to different pieces depending on how well they fit together and how likely they are to form part of the solution. Similarly, when playing a board game like chess or checkers, we can use an MRF structure that assigns weights to certain moves based on their likelihood of being beneficial for winning the game in particular situations.

7.3.2Anomaly Detection

Anomaly detection is when a program looks for data points that are different from the rest. For ­example, if you have data on how much money people spend at a store, the program might look for data points much higher or lower than the average. This can be useful for identifying fraud or unusual behavior.

Anomaly detection works by gathering information from existing data points, using them as references, and then looking for new data points that deviate from this reference set. Depending on how much an individual point deviates from what is considered normal, the system can flag it as either a potential problem or not worth looking into further. The technique requires no prior knowledge of any distribution – meaning there is no need to specify which types of values should be flagged – making it ideal for detecting unexpected events across different domains and data sets.

Examples include catching fraudulent financial activities in banking records or identifying ­malfunctioning machines in industrial settings. Anomaly detection has numerous advantages over conventional methods, such as supervised learning, when it comes to dealing with missing values and large amounts of noisy data where traditional methods often fail due to their reliance on labeled training sets with complete information about each observation (which may not always be available).

![](Images/f7-11.jpg)

[Figure 7.11](#15_Chapter7.xhtml#fig-7-11)  Types of anomaly detection algorithms

The types of anomaly detection algorithms ([Fig. 7.11](#15_Chapter7.xhtml#fig7-11)) are isolation forest algorithm, local outlier factor (LOF) and one-class support vector machine (OC SVM). These are now discussed in detail.

7.3.2.1Isolation Forest Algorithm

As its name suggests, isolation forest is an ensemble approach that shares similarities with random forest. In other words, it takes the average of the predictions by numerous decision trees when awarding the final anomaly score to a given data point. Isolation forest differs from conventional anomaly detection algorithms by immediately attempting to isolate abnormal data points rather than defining what is considered ‘normal’ and then identifying everything else as anomalous.

Assume that we have the data points shown in [Fig. 7.12](#15_Chapter7.xhtml#fig7-12).

![](Images/f7-12.jpg)

[Figure 7.12](#15_Chapter7.xhtml#fig-7-12)  Isolation forest algorithm: Data points

The isolation forest technique randomly chooses a dimension (specifically, the dimension linked to the x\-axis) and randomly divides the data along that dimension ([Fig. 7.13](#15_Chapter7.xhtml#fig7-13)).

![](Images/f7-13.jpg)

[Figure 7.13](#15_Chapter7.xhtml#fig-7-13)  Isolation forest algorithm: Dimension linked to the x\-axis

The two resulting subspaces establish distinct subtrees. In this instance, the cut occurs to divide a singular point from the rest of the data set. The initial binary tree is composed of two nodes at the first level. One node represents the subtree of points located to the left of the initial cut, while the other node represents the single point on the right ([Fig. 7.14](#15_Chapter7.xhtml#fig7-14)).

![](Images/f7-14.jpg)

[Figure 7.14](#15_Chapter7.xhtml#fig-7-14)  Isolation forest algorithm: Roots with isolation points

It is crucial to acknowledge that the remaining trees in the ensemble will choose distinct starting splits. In the given example, the initial split fails to separate the outlier from the rest of the data ([Fig. 7.15](#15_Chapter7.xhtml#fig7-15)).

![](Images/f7-15.jpg)

[Figure 7.15](#15_Chapter7.xhtml#fig-7-15)  Isolation forest algorithm: Further splits

The resulting tree consists of two nodes ([Fig. 7.16](#15_Chapter7.xhtml#fig7-16)): one represents the points located to the left of the line, while the other represents the points located to the right of the line.

![](Images/f7-16.jpg)
