[Figure 7.16](#15_Chapter7.xhtml#fig-7-16)  Isolation forest algorithm: With two nodes

The method is iterated until each leaf node of the tree corresponds to an individual data point from the data set. In our given example, the second iteration successfully identifies and separates the outlier from the rest of the data ([Fig. 7.17](#15_Chapter7.xhtml#fig7-17)).

![](Images/f7-17.jpg)

[Figure 7.17](#15_Chapter7.xhtml#fig-7-17)  Isolation forest algorithm: Separating outliers from the rest

Upon completion of this stage, the tree would appear as depicted in [Fig. 7.18](#15_Chapter7.xhtml#fig7-18).

![](Images/f7-18.jpg)

[Figure 7.18](#15_Chapter7.xhtml#fig-7-18)  Isolation forest algorithm: With three nodes

It is important to note that a split can occur in the other dimension ([Fig. 7.19](#15_Chapter7.xhtml#fig7-19)), as is the situation with this third decision tree.

![](Images/f7-19.jpg)

[Figure 7.19](#15_Chapter7.xhtml#fig-7-19)  Isolation forest algorithm: Split in multiple dimensions

Typically, an unusual data point will be found in a smaller bounding box at a shallower tree depth compared to other points. During the process of inference with a trained isolation forest model, the ultimate anomaly score is calculated as the mean of the scores generated by each individual decision tree. In the above case, average number of splits before isolation = 3 (2+3+4/3)

Categorical Variables: The isolation forest technique can utilize categorical variables by depicting them as rectangles, with the size of each rectangle being proportional to the frequency of occurrence. This allows for the identification of anomalous values that are less commonly encountered ([Fig. 7.20](#15_Chapter7.xhtml#fig7-20)).

![](Images/f7-20.jpg)

[Figure 7.20](#15_Chapter7.xhtml#fig-7-20)  Isolation forest algorithm: Categorical variables, step 1

We define the set of potential values as the range between the median of the first value and the median of the last value ([Fig. 7.21](#15_Chapter7.xhtml#fig7-21)). We randomly choose a point within the domain and then identify the nearest edge of a specified rectangle. This is used for our split.

![](Images/f7-21.jpg)

[Figure 7.21](#15_Chapter7.xhtml#fig-7-21)  Isolation forest algorithm: Categorical variables, step 2

To maintain equity, the remaining trees within the forest will adopt an alternative sequencing ([Fig. 7.22](#15_Chapter7.xhtml#fig7-22)).

![](Images/f7-22.jpg)

[Figure 7.22](#15_Chapter7.xhtml#fig-7-22)  Isolation forest algorithm: Categorical variables, step 3

The algorithm works as follows:

1.It randomly selects a subset of the data and builds a binary tree by splitting the data based on a randomly chosen feature and a randomly chosen threshold value within the range of that feature.

2.It repeats this process until each data point is isolated in a leaf node or the maximum tree depth is reached.

3.It calculates the path length from the root node to the leaf node for each data point, which is the number of splits required to isolate it.

4.It averages the path length over a forest of such trees and normalizes it to get the anomaly score for each data point. The anomaly score ranges from 0 to 1, where higher values indicate more anomalous data points.

A simple step-by-step example of isolation forest is given below:

1.Suppose we have a data set with two features, x and y, and we want to detect outliers in this data set. We randomly select a subset of the data, say 10 points, and assign them to a binary tree.

2.We randomly select a feature, say x, and a threshold value, say 3.5, within the range of x. We split the data into two groups based on whether their x values are less than or greater than 3.5.

3.We repeat this process for each group, randomly selecting a feature and a threshold value. For example, for the group with x < 3.5, we may select y as the feature and 2 as the threshold value, and split the group into two subgroups based on whether their y values are less than or greater than 2.

4.We continue this process until each data point is isolated in a leaf node or the maximum tree depth is reached. For example, if the maximum tree depth is 3, we stop splitting after three levels of branching.

5.We calculate the path length for each data point by counting the number of splits required to isolate it. For example, if a data point is isolated at the first level, its path length is 1; if it is isolated at the second level, its path length is 2; and so on.

6.We average the path length over a forest of such trees and normalize it to get the anomaly score for each data point. For example, if we build 100 trees and average their path lengths, we may get an anomaly score of 0.8 for a data point that has an average path length of 1.2, indicating that it is very likely to be an outlier.

An isolation tree can be considered a data structure where each leaf represents an outlier (or ­anomaly). For example, suppose a point appears to be located away from its surrounding points. It is considered anomalous and forms its leaf on the isolation tree. Moreover, all standard points, surrounded by other regular points, form their branches on this decision tree structure, thus making it easier to identify anomalies within our data set without any prior labels or training data available beforehand.

The isolation forest algorithm has several advantages over traditional methods, such as clustering, because of its ability to detect even un-obvious outliers without having any prior knowledge about them beforehand and also because of its robustness against outliers caused by noise or measurement errors within our data set, typically found in real-world applications such as fraud detection. Therefore, these reasons, combined with its efficiency compared to other algorithms, make it quite popular among ML practitioners today.

7.3.2.2Local Outlier Factor

The local outlier factor (LOF) algorithm uses density-based clustering to identify outliers in an ­unsupervised manner by looking at how close a particular data point is to its neighbors in an n\-dimensional space, where n represents the number of features present in the data set. The higher value indicates that it is more likely to be an outlier than its neighbors and vice versa; if lower values are given, these points are more likely to be normal points as they have closer neighbors around them.

The LOF algorithm is a powerful tool for anomaly detection. It is a non-parametric method of identifying outliers in data that can help analysts detect points significantly different from their neighboring points. The local outlier factor measures the degree to which an individual point stands out from its immediate area.

The LOF algorithm first calculates each point’s local density using K\-nearest neighbors estimation. This means that for any given point, LOF will look at the K closest observations and calculate the average density value, known as reachability distance (RD). Then, it will take this RD value to compute a score known as the ‘local outlier factor’ or LOF for each point in the data set and compare these values to all other points to determine which are outliers and which are not. It helps identify which observations could be considered anomalies when compared with their neighbors or whole data sets.

To illustrate how the LOF algorithm works, let us consider a sample data set with two features, x and y, and five observations, A, B, C, D and E. The data set is shown in [Table 7.14](#15_Chapter7.xhtml#tab7-14).

[Table 7.14](#15_Chapter7.xhtml#tab-7-14)LOF base data

 
| Observation || X || Y |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A || 1 || 2 |
| B || 2 || 3 |
| C || 3 || 4 |
| D || 10 || 11 |
| E || 11 || 12 |

The first step of the LOF algorithm is to calculate the local density of each point using K\-nearest neighbors estimation. For simplicity, let us assume that K = 2, meaning that we will look at the two closest observations to each point. [Table 7.15](#15_Chapter7.xhtml#tab7-15) shows the distances between each point and its two nearest neighbors, as well as the average distance, which is the RD of each point.

[Table 7.15](#15_Chapter7.xhtml#tab-7-15)LOF nearest neighbor distances

 
| Observation || Nearest neighbours || Distances || Rd |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| A || B,C || 1.41, 2.83 || 2.12 |
| B || A,C || 1.41, 1.41 || 1.41 |
| C || B,D || 1.41, 9.90 || 5.66 |
| D || C,E || 9.90, 1.41 || 5.66 |
| E || D,C || 1.41, 11.31 || 6.36 |

The second step of the LOF algorithm is to calculate the LOF score of each point by comparing its RD value with the RD values of its nearest neighbors. The formula for the LOF score is:

LOF(p) = (Sum of RD values of p’s nearest neighbors / k) / RD(p)

[Table 7.16](#15_Chapter7.xhtml#tab7-16) shows the LOF scores of each point in the data set.

[Table 7.16](#15_Chapter7.xhtml#tab-7-16)LOF scores of each data point

 
| Observation || LOF score |
| --- | --- |
| A || 0.33 |
| B || 0.50 |
| C || 0.50 |
| D || 1.76 |
| E || 1.77 |

The final step is to identify the outliers based on the LOF scores. A point is considered an outlier if its LOF score is significantly higher than one, meaning that it has a much lower density than its neighbors or the whole data set. In this example, points D and E have high LOF scores and are therefore outliers, while points A, B and C have low LOF scores and are therefore normal observations.

In addition to being an effective anomaly detector, LOF is relatively simple: because it uses only one parameter – K\-nearest neighbor – there is no need for complicated tuning or hyperparameter optimization like other ML algorithms require. This makes LOF fast, efficient, and easy to deploy on real-world data sets without much effort or time tinkering with parameters you might encounter when working with more complex algorithms such as SVMs.

7.3.2.3One-Class Support Vector Machine

One-class support vector machine (OC SVM) uses a one-class model to classify data points based on their similarity to other data points in the data set. It uses a non-linear hyperplane that acts as a decision boundary between normal and abnormal observations. The basic concept behind OCSVM is that it creates an n\-dimensional hypersphere or boundary around the training data set and separates any new observations which fall outside this boundary as outliers. This technique creates a hypersphere using kernel functions such as polynomial, linear, sigmoid, or radial basis functions (RBF).

The RBF kernel is most commonly used due to its ability to correctly capture non-linearities within the data set compared with other kernels. We use parameters such as gamma value, cost factor C, which measures penalties for misclassifications, and degree parameter d if using a polynomial kernel to train the model. Gamma value determines how much influence each training example has on the decision boundary, while cost factor C specifies whether higher weight should be given regularization parameters instead of training accuracy when determining optimal decision surface; that is, when C = 0, there will be no penalty for misclassifications while at high values it penalizes more heavily for misclassification errors. Thus, it helps create robust models against overfitting issues like noise present in the data set. A higher gamma value indicates that each example has more influence on constructing a hyperplane. At the same time, a lower one reduces influence but increases generalizability potential by avoiding overfitting. Also, the degree parameter helps us decide how complex our model might get depending on the number of features in our data set.

Once all these parameters are determined, we can proceed with the fitting/training process, where the algorithm finds the optimized solution for the given problem through optimization techniques, such as gradient descent. After obtaining the optimal solution, we need to test our trained model by providing some new unseen data point samples from the same distribution so that the system can figure out whether they belong to the same class.

7.3.3Dimensionality Reduction

Dimensionality reduction is a potent tool for simplifying complex problems while preserving relevant information from an original data set. As the number of variables in a data set increases, so does the complexity of understanding and interpreting those variables.

This technique can reduce the complexity and computational cost of data analysis, improve the accuracy of predictive algorithms, and simplify data visualizations. Principal component analysis (PCA) is one of the most common approaches for dimensionality reduction. PCA works by finding linear combinations between input features such that they explain the most variance between them. By doing this, we can decrease our feature space significantly while only sacrificing a small amount of total variance explained by our model.

Other approaches include linear discriminant analysis (LDA), factor analysis (FA), Sammon’s mapping, and Isomap. Each approach has its strengths and weaknesses, so it pays off to research each before starting any project. For example, if you have six variables from your data set (A, B, C, D, E and F), you could use dimensionality reduction to reduce it to A-B-C-D or A-E-F instead. This would allow us to capture patterns with fewer dimensions than initially assumed without losing valuable insight into our original data set’s structure and value points that might otherwise be missed.

PCA, LDA, and other methods are often categorized as dimensionality reduction techniques, but this is not their primary purpose. Rather, they are methods for finding efficient and meaningful representations of data that capture the most relevant information and discard the noise or redundancy. Dimensionality reduction is a consequence of this process, not a goal in itself.

7.3.3.1Principal Component Analysis

Principal component analysis (PCA) is a method used to reduce a data set’s dimensionality while preserving its most important features. In other words, it can compress large amounts of data into a smaller number of variables with minimal information loss. PCA finds linear combinations (or components) of the original variables that explain the maximum amount of variance in the data. In other words, it finds which combination of variables best captures the most information about all the other variables in your data set. This means that instead of having hundreds or even thousands of separate variables, PCA will reduce them to just a handful without losing much information regarding how they are related and what they represent.

The idea behind PCA is to reduce complex problems into simpler and more manageable ones. It does this by identifying underlying patterns and relationships between different variables and removing those less important for understanding them correctly. In addition, PCA also helps with feature selection; determining which features carry more weight than others can help researchers identify which ones should be focused on when creating models or performing analysis on their data sets.

Steps

Step 1: Collect and Preprocess the Data. This includes organizing the data into an appropriate format, dealing with missing values, removing outliers, and standardizing it. Preprocessing helps ensure that all variables are numerical and can be used in further analysis.

Step 2: Calculate the Correlation between Variables. After preprocessing, each variable needs to be correlated with its corresponding one or more variables before proceeding further with PCA analysis. This correlation between two or more variables can help identify relationships between them, indicating how useful they may be when performing prediction or classification tasks using machine learning algorithms later down the line.

Step 3: Compute the Covariance Matrix: Once the correlation has been calculated, the covariance matrix needs to be computed using suitable mathematical equations available in the literature. The covariance matrix tells us about the degree of variation among different features. It explains how much change a particular feature will bring if there is any change in any other feature. A high covariance value indicates vital dependability among two features, while a low value means less dependability.

Step 4: Perform Eigenvalue Decomposition. This step involves computing eigenvalues from the covariance matrix. Here each column vector corresponds to an eigenvector for feature columns that contain the same elements as those found in the input matrix but arranged differently according to their eigenvalue significance relative to others. This allows us to separate important features from less ­significant ones and reduce dimensions accordingly without losing much information contained within the original data set.

Step 5: Select the Principal Components. Here, we select the best principal components out of all previously computed eigenvectors according to their contribution towards the total variance present within the data set, that is, the highest explained variance ratio should always be chosen first, followed by the second highest, and so on, until the desired number of principal components has been reached. Thus we keep the cumulative explained variance ratio above a certain threshold level, which allows us to maintain the accuracy required for our prediction task while drastically reducing the dimensions involved during the process.

Step 6: Project the Data onto the Selected Principal Components. After deciding upon the best principal components for our model, it is time to project input data into these newly created lower dimensional spaces composed only by selected principal components.

As an example, let us consider a sample data set with four variables: X1, X2, X3, and X4. The data set has 10 observations and is shown in [Table 7.17](#15_Chapter7.xhtml#tab7-17)

7.3.3.2Kernel Principal Component Analysis

Using kernel principal component analysis (KPCA), data can be made less dimensional while reetaining most of its valuable characteristics. KPCA is a non-linear version of PCA used in supervised and unsupervised learning tasks. It uses kernel functions as an alternative to linear transformations to transform data into a lower-dimensional space.

Kernel functions are mathematical operations that transform inputs into non-linear feature spaces for machine learning algorithms. By using kernels, KPCA can capture non-linear relationships from high-dimensional data sets and allows the detection of patterns that would otherwise not be observed with linear methods such as PCA. This makes it ideal for classification, anomaly detection, or image recognition, where simple linear methods cannot adequately model complex relationships between variables.

Steps

1.Choose a kernel function, such as the Gaussian kernel, and compute the kernel matrix K, where K\[i,j\] = k(x\[i\], x\[j\]), for each pair of data points x\[i\] and x\[j\].

2.Center the kernel matrix K by subtracting the mean of each row and column, and dividing by the standard deviation of each row and column. This ensures that the transformed data has zero mean and unit variance.

3.Perform eigenvalue decomposition on the centered kernel matrix K and obtain the eigenvectors and eigenvalues. The eigenvectors are the principal components of the transformed data, and the eigenvalues indicate the amount of variance explained by each component.

4.Select the top k eigenvectors corresponding to the largest k eigenvalues, and project the data onto these eigenvectors. The resulting vectors are the reduced features of the original data.

For example, consider a data set with two features x1 and x2 ([Table 7.23](#15_Chapter7.xhtml#tab7-23)).

| X1 || X2 |
| --- | --- |
| 0 || 0 |
| 1 || 0 |
| 0 || 1 |
| 1 || 1 |

7.3.3.3Linear Discriminant Analysis

Linear discriminant analysis (LDA) is a method used to classify data by finding an optimal linear combination of features. It is a supervised learning technique that separates two or more classes using linear functions. LDA aims to find the best linear discriminant function that will best separate the classes into different categories.

LDA works by first computing the mean and variance for each class to identify which features help distinguish between them. The algorithm then finds the optimal combination of these features to best differentiate between them, which becomes the discriminant function. Finally, the algorithm evaluates how well this function separates each class from one another to determine its accuracy and effectiveness as a classifier.

LDA can be used for dimensionality reduction, feature selection, anomaly detection, and classification problems. It has been proven helpful in applications such as image recognition, face recognition/detection, and speech recognition/synthesis due to its ability to reduce noise while preserving important information within data sets. In addition, it has also been used successfully in medical diagnostics, where it can help diagnose diseases based on symptoms and other attributes provided by patients’ medical records.

Steps

Step 1: Prepare the Data. This means ensuring that data has been appropriately formatted and cleaned before you begin analysis. The data set should include all relevant input variables and the desired outcome variable (such as class labels). In addition, ensure there are no missing values or outliers that could affect the accuracy of the results.

Step 2: Choose an Appropriate Distance Metric. Next, you need to decide on an appropriate distance metric to use when computing distances between points to perform LDA classification. Commonly used methods include Euclidean and Manhattan distance; however, other options are available depending on your application’s needs and objectives.

Step 3: Calculate the Mean Vectors for Each Class. You must calculate the mean vectors for each class of data points in the data set; that is, find the average value across all observations within each group or “class” of data points you want to be classified by LDA classification criteria. The mean vector is then used as a reference point with which distances between other vectors can be calculated using one of the multiple available metrics mentioned above (such as Euclidean or Manhattan).

Step 4: Compute the Between-Class Covariance Matrix. For every pairwise combination of classes within the data set, we need to compute a covariance matrix describing their relative position concerning one another along each feature dimension involved in their comparison; this will allow us better capture any differences among classes with respect not just single values but distributions over multiple variables simultaneously – something essential when performing more advanced forms statistical inference like LDA. We then combine these individual covariance matrices into one larger matrix known as the ‘between-class covariance matrix,’ which captures how much variation exists between two given classes across all features included in our analysis set.

Step 5: Compute the Within-Class Covariance Matrix. Next, you need to calculate the within-class covariances’ describing the variance within individual groups when compared against itself; that is, how much variation exists among members of the same group along the given feature axis. Here again, compute separate matrices for each pairwise combination class before combining them into more significant ‘within-class covariances,’ capturing variances within each distinct grouping studied during this exercise.

Step 6: Compute the Linear Discriminants. Lastly, compute the actual linear discriminants themselves using information gathered from previous steps: utilizing both between- and within-class covariances to determine the best direction axis upon which to project different groups to form optimal separation planes distinguishable individually from one another along complex multidimensional feature spaces. After determining these directions axes, apply the standard hyperplane equation to define boundaries differentiating clusters based upon values observed in past analyses. By applying linear discriminants obtained from model training sets considered during the development phase, any ML solution can achieve robust results, obtaining predictions related to unseen inputs generated outside the original model generation process.
