Overall, LDA provides an efficient way of dealing with high-dimensional data sets where traditional methods have difficulty separating different classes because too many features are present in the data set. Furthermore, accurately identifying relevant features from noisy environments with high-dimensional data sets allows for more accurate classification results than other methods, such as logistic regression or decision tree algorithms, due to their ability to reduce noise while preserving important information within data set points.

7.3.3.4Factor Analysis

Factor analysis (FA) is a statistical technique used to identify an underlying relationship between variables. It is commonly used in research studies to help uncover the latent structures underlying observed data. This technique has been widely applied in various fields, including psychology, economics, and education. At its core, FA involves reducing the number of variables by analyzing each variable about the other variables in a data set. This helps researchers explain how several aspects influence each other and can aid them in understanding which factors are most important when predicting an outcome or phenomenon.

When conducting FA, researchers gather data from participants on different characteristics or items related to their research topic or hypothesis. They then use this data to generate correlations representing how strongly each variable relates to others within the set. As part of this process, they will also calculate factor scores for each participant based on their responses across all items included in the study.

For factor analysis results to be reliable and accurate, researchers must ensure that the data collected is valid and reliable, meaning that it accurately reflects what was measured and does not contain errors due to measurement issues or mistakes during the collection or processing of information. In addition, there must be an adequate sample size as smaller sample sizes can lead to overfitting, where inaccurate patterns are found among unrelated pieces of information due to sparsely distributed data points. Finally, researchers must take special care when interpreting results from FA studies as results may not always reflect authentic underlying relationships but spurious associations based on noise.

There are two types of factor analysis, exploratory and confirmatory.

Exploratory Factor Analysis (EFA): This can condense a vast collection of observed variables into a smaller group of latent factors that can be utilized to explain how the observed variables are related. The goal of EFA is to identify the underlying patterns and relationships among a group of related variables and to uncover hidden or ‘latent’ factors that explain the variation among them.

To achieve this, EFA compares correlation coefficients between pairs of measured items to assess whether they share similar patterns across multiple observations or are merely related by chance. Rather than relying solely on measured variables as predictors, EFA uses matrix algebra techniques and linear models to analyze correlations between measured variables and extract their common underlying factors. These factors represent distinct but related concepts or processes within the studied data set. By uncovering these latent constructs, researchers can better understand how individual variables interact and how they influence overall outcomes, such as customer satisfaction surveys or academic performance metrics. In addition, by accounting for noise caused by measurement error, FA allows researchers to obtain meaningful information from complex data sets quickly and efficiently without sacrificing accuracy or rigor in their models. This makes it an invaluable tool for researchers looking for deeper insights into their data sets and those who need a quick way to reduce the number of predictor variables without sacrificing quality results. It also helps them identify clusters of closely related items that form distinct factors which can be used for further research.

The first step in conducting EFA is identifying the variables relevant to your analysis. Typically, these variables can be numeric or categorical, and they should be related to each other somehow. Next, you need to determine whether any of these correlations are statistically significant – this can be done by running statistical tests such as Pearson correlation or Spearman’s rank correlation tests on your data set.

Once you have identified which correlations are statistically significant, you need to decide which type of FA model you want to use – EFA or CFA. EFA is typically used when there is little prior knowledge about what the factors might look like within your data set; CFA is usually used when there are known factors previously identified during prior research efforts into your data set’s structure and content.

Next, you need to select a factor extraction method for your model – this includes selecting between PCA, MLE, iterative principal components extraction method (IPCEM), and others depending on how many factors you want extracting from your data set and how many iterations with each algorithm will be performed during the process. Once selected, run the chosen factor extraction method on the data set using appropriate statistical software packages such as SPSS or R-software packages like MLR or FactoMineR, depending on which language best suits your needs.

Finally, after running all necessary analyses using factor extraction methods, the evaluation must be conducted using calculated measures such as the Kaiser–Meyer–Olkin (KMO) measure of sampling adequacy and Bartlett’s test of sphericity, cumulative proportion of variance explained, screen plot, etc. After the evaluation study, interpret the findings. This means looking into rotation methods, eigenvalues, eigenvectors, etc., and understanding them through their interpretation. After interpreting results, conclusions should draw based on findings obtained from the exploratory factor analysis study.

EFA is a valuable tool for uncovering hidden relationships between variables within a data set without relying solely on supervised approaches like regression models.

Confirmatory Factor Analysis (CFA): CFA builds upon EFA by testing whether the identified factors are consistent across multiple data sets or samples. This allows researchers to ensure their findings are reliable and not just due to chance or randomness in the tested sample. For example, suppose you want to study how age affects customer satisfaction with your product. In that case, you could use CFA to make sure your results are consistent across multiple surveys with different age groups included. CFA is a statistical technique used to help identify the underlying structure of a set of variables. It tests theoretical models and hypotheses about the relationships between observed variables such as attitudes, behaviours, and attitudes. CFA is often used in psychological research to test theories about personality, cognitive processes, emotions, and other phenomena.

CFA begins by specifying a model or hypothesis about how the various observed variables are related. This model should be based on existing knowledge or theory regarding these variables and their relationships. The researcher then uses statistical techniques to analyze data from various sources (surveys and interviews) to determine whether the proposed model fits the data. If it does, then this means that the hypothesized relations between the observed variables are supported by empirical evidence – that is why it is called ‘confirmatory’ analysis!

The next step involves evaluating how well this proposed model explains the observed variability in your data set (its goodness-of-fit). Typically, researchers make use of several different fit indices such as chi-squared statistic, root mean square error approximation (RMSEA), comparative fit index (CFI), Tucker–Lewis index (TLI), Akaike information criterion (AIC), etc. These fit indices provide an overall measure of how well the hypothesized model fits with the data set, which can give an idea of whether the initial hypothesis needs to be modified.

Finally, after determining if CFA supports the hypothesis, researchers must interpret their results meaningfully and apply them within real-life contexts since CFA offers little insight into causal relations between observed variables or even specific implications for different groups/contexts. In conclusion, CFA can be a powerful tool for researchers looking for evidence behind their assumptions about certain phenomena to guide further research into those topics.

7.3.4Association Rule Mining

An unsupervised learning method called association rule mining can be used to find connections between various elements in a data set. It helps retailers create marketing strategies by uncovering the connections between products that customers often purchase together.

Market basket analysis is a frequently utilized application of association rule mining that businesses employ to gain insights into the purchasing patterns of their clients. It can provide insights into the frequent co-purchasing patterns of products. Which items exhibit complementarity or substitutability? Which products are eligible for cross-selling or upselling? What strategies may enhance the store layout or product positioning to maximize sales?

Consider a scenario where a supermarket aims to examine the transactions made by its consumers during a specific time frame. One distinct rule that may be derived from the data is:

{bread, butter} -> {jam}

This rule implies that customers who purchase bread and butter are highly likely to purchase jam. The rule consists of two components: the antecedent, located on the left-hand side of the arrow, and the consequent, located on the right-hand side. The antecedent denotes the circumstance or reason, while the consequent signifies the result or consequence.

To assess the quality of a rule, it is necessary to quantify its support and confidence. Support refers to the proportion of transactions in the data set that include both the antecedent and the consequent. For instance, if there are 1000 transactions in the data set, and 200 of them include bread, butter, and jam, then the support of the rule is calculated as 200 divided by 1000, resulting in a value of 0.2. Support measures the frequency of a rule in the data set.

Confidence refers to the proportion of transactions that include both the antecedent and the consequent. For instance, if 300 transactions include both bread and butter, and 200 transactions also include jam, then the rule’s confidence may be calculated as 200 divided by 300, resulting in a value of 0.67. Confidence is a measure of the reliability of a rule in predicting the consequent based on the antecedent.

The store can formulate marketing tactics to enhance its revenue by adhering to these guidelines. For example, it can provide discounts or vouchers for jam to consumers who purchase bread and butter or strategically position jam beside bread and butter in the store to stimulate impulsive purchases. In addition, it can detect products that are infrequently purchased together or have poor sales and develop strategies to enhance their visibility or appeal.

Web mining is another application of association rule mining. It systematically extracts valuable information from web data, including web pages, hyperlinks, and server logs. As an illustration, an association rule could be formulated as follows: ‘In the event that a user accesses page A, it is probable that they will also access page B.’

Web mining can be categorized as web content mining, web structure mining, and web usage mining. Web content mining involves examining and interpreting many forms of data found on the internet, such as text, photos, audio, video, and other multimedia information. Web structure mining is concerned with analysing the links and arrangement of websites, including their connectivity and organization. Web use mining examines the actions and engagement of users on the internet, including their browsing history, clickstream data, and feedback.

Web mining has diverse applications and advantages across numerous domains and objectives. It can enhance the quality and relevancy of web search engines by comprehending user queries and preferences. It can improve customization and recommendation systems by offering tailored content and services that align with user profiles and behavior. Web mining can aid in the identification of fraudulent activities and cyberattacks by detecting irregular patterns and abnormalities in web traffic and transactions.

Association rule learning can be divided into three algorithms: Apriori, ECLAT and FP Growth. We will now discuss these three algorithms in detail.

7.3.4.1The Apriori Algorithm

The Apriori algorithm is an ML algorithm that can uncover associations between items in large data sets. It was developed by Rakesh Agrawal and Ramakrishnan Srikant in 1994. The core of the algorithm lies in finding frequent itemsets or items that frequently occur together. This technique is based on the premise that if an itemset occurs frequently in a data set, then any subset of that itemset also occurs frequently. The Apriori algorithm is most commonly used for market basket analysis and recommendation systems.

The algorithm first scans through data to find all single-itemsets (itemsets with one element). These individual itemsets are deemed ‘frequent’ when they meet a minimum user-defined frequency or support threshold, meaning they must appear in at least some predetermined percentage of all transactions for a given data set. This initial stage creates an inventory list from which we can build more powerful and complex itemset combinations, which will also pass our frequency test.

Once frequent single-itemsets have been identified, the next step is to search for pairs (itemsets with two elements) and triples (itemsets with three elements), where each new combination combines one element from our previously identified single-itemset list along with another new element from our entire inventory list generated during the first step.

Steps

1.Perform a database scan and tally the frequency of each item. Gather the items with support value equal to or higher than the minimal support threshold and place them in a set named L1, representing the common 1-itemsets.

2.Create potential 2-itemsets by combining L1 with itself. This involves combining two 1-itemsets with a common prefix of length k – 1, where k is the current size of the itemsets. For instance, the combination of {apple} and {banana} yields {apple, banana}, whereas {apple} and {orange} cannot be combined due to the absence of a shared prefix.

3.Perform another database scan and tally the frequency of each candidate’s 2-itemset. Eliminate the candidates with support lower than the minimal support level and obtain the set L2, consisting of frequent 2-itemsets.

4.Iterate steps 2 and 3 until no more candidates can be generated or more frequent itemsets can be discovered. The set that consists of all Lk sets is equivalent to that of all frequent itemsets.

We utilize the frequent itemsets to discover association rules and enforce a minimal confidence threshold. To obtain the rules, we iterate through each frequent itemset X and construct all non-empty subsets of X. For each subset Y, we create the rule Y -> (X \- Y) if the rule’s confidence meets or exceeds the minimum confidence threshold.

Consider a scenario where a fruit shop offers various fruits, such as apples, bananas, oranges, grapes, and pineapples. In this context, let us examine the transactions that have taken place:

T1: {apple, banana, orange}

T2: {banana, grape}

T3: {apple, banana, grape}

T4: {apple, grape}

T5: {banana, pineapple}

For the Apriori method, we will use a minimum support level of 0.4, which corresponds to 40% of transactions, and a minimum confidence threshold of 0.7, which corresponds to 70% of rules.

First, we thoroughly examine the database and tally the frequency of each item. The occurrence of apple is found in 3 transactions, banana in 4 transactions, orange in 1 transaction, grape in 3 transactions, and pineapple in 1 transaction. The only fruits with support larger than or equal to 0.4 are apples, bananas, and grapes. Therefore, L1 = {{apple}, {banana}, {grape}}.

In step 2, we create potential 2-itemsets by combining L1 with itself. We obtain a collection of sets containing pairs of fruits: {{apple, banana}, {apple, grape}, {banana, grape}}.

In step 3, we perform a second database search to tally the frequency of each candidate’s 2-itemset. The item {apple, banana} appears in 2 transactions, {apple, grape} appears in 3 transactions, and {banana, grape} appears in 2 transactions. Among the options {apple, grape}, only apple and grape have a support value larger than or equal to 0.4. Therefore, the set L2 consists of {{apple, grape}}.

In step 4, generating additional candidates or identifying additional frequent itemsets is no longer possible; hence, we terminate the procedure. The collection of all frequent itemsets can be represented as L = L1 ∪ L2, where L1 and L2 are sets containing the following items: {apple}, {banana}, {grape}, and {apple, grape}.

We employ the L method to discover association rules and enforce a minimal confidence threshold. We iterate through each frequent itemset X in L to obtain the desired outcome. We then build all feasible non-empty subsets of X. For each subset Y, we create the rule Y -> (X - Y) if the rule’s confidence equals or exceeds 0.7. The rules that we obtain are as follows:

{apple} -> {grape} with confidence 3/3 = 1

{grape} -> {apple} with confidence 3/3 = 1.

These principles indicate that customers who purchase apples also purchase grapes with a certainty of 100%, and vice versa.

Calculating this confidence level percentage value requires dividing count(X Y)/ count(X), where X represents target itemset values found directly preceding Y within the applicable subset counts gathered throughout the previous steps. This essentially proves how often related itemsets appear together throughout the entire input data set versus just appearing randomly independent by chance alone – thus removing false positives successfully from the final output results and ultimately resulting in better accuracy.

The Apriori algorithm does not require prior knowledge about data structures, it can process enormous data sets quickly due to its iterative nature, and it produces clear rules that humans can easily understand. On the downside, this method cannot handle numeric data well and tends to generate large numbers of false positives, leading to inaccurate results if they are not carefully filtered out before they reach the results stage.

7.3.4.2The ECLAT Algorithm

ECLAT stands for equivalence class transformation. This algorithm uses a ‘depth-first’ search to find frequent itemsets in a transaction database. It executes faster than the Apriori algorithm. Unlike the Apriori algorithm, which applies to a horizontal data set, the ECLAT algorithm applies only to data sets in the vertical format.

The ECLAT algorithm is a method for finding frequent itemsets in a transactional database. A frequent itemset is a set of items that occurs in more than a specified minimum number of transactions. The ECLAT algorithm uses a vertical data format, where each item is associated with a tidset, which is the set of transaction IDs that contain the item. For example, the tidset (Transaction ID set) of apple is {T1, T3, T4}, the tidset of banana is {T1, T2, T3, T5}, and so on.

Steps

1.It starts with the set of all single items and their tidsets.

2.It sorts the items in descending order of their tidset size.

3.It generates candidate itemsets of size k by joining pairs of item sets of size k – 1 that share the first k – 2 items and have frequent tidsets.

4.It computes the tidset of each candidate itemset by intersecting the tidsets of its parent itemsets.

5.It prunes any candidate itemset whose tidset size is less than the minimum support threshold.

6.It repeats steps 3 to 5 until no more candidates can be generated or all candidates are pruned.

Let us apply this algorithm to the example of associating fruits in a fruit shop with the following transactions and a minimum support of 2.

T1: {apple, banana, orange}

T2: {banana, grape}

T3: {apple, banana, grape}

T4: {apple, grape}

T5: {banana, pineapple}

The algorithm starts with the following single items and their tidsets:

apple: {T1, T3, T4}

banana: {T1, T2, T3, T5}

grape: {T2, T3, T4}

orange: {T1}

pineapple: {T5}

The algorithm sorts the items by their tidset size:

banana: {T1, T2, T3, T5}

apple: {T1, T3, T4}

grape: {T2, T3, T4}

orange: {T1}

pineapple: {T5}

The algorithm generates candidate item sets of size 2 by joining pairs of items that share the first item and have frequent tidsets:

banana apple: {T1, T3}

banana grape: {T2, T3}

apple grape: {T3, T4}

The algorithm computes the tidset of each candidate itemset by intersecting the tidsets of its parent items:

banana apple: {T1} ∩ {T1, T3} = {T1}

banana grape: {T1, T2, T3, T5} ∩ {T2, T3, T4} = {T2, T3}

apple grape: {T1, T3, T4} ∩ {T2, T3, T4} = {T3, T4}

The algorithm prunes any candidate itemset whose tidset size is less than 2:

banana apple: pruned

banana grape: not pruned

apple grape: not pruned

The algorithm repeats the process for itemsets of size 3:

banana grape apple: pruned

grape apple banana: pruned

Since no more candidates can be generated or all candidates are pruned, the algorithm stops and returns the following frequent item sets:

banana

apple

grape

banana grape

apple grape

The most important conclusion is that ECLAT is compatible with the vertical data format. As most data sets are in the horizontal format, we must first convert them to the vertical format before applying this algorithm. Apriori typically performs best when working with a more extensive data set. Thus, small and medium data sets are better suited for the ECLAT method. In the Apriori algorithm, we need to scan the database repeatedly to find frequent itemsets; this limitation is reduced using a vertical ECLAT data set. The database needs to be scanned only once in ECLAT. Due to its use of depth-first search, ECLAT utilizes less memory than Apriori. Therefore, it is faster than Apriori.

7.3.4.3The FP Growth Algorithm

This algorithm is a data mining technique for discovering frequent itemsets in transactional data sets. It is an extension of the Apriori algorithm. The FP Growth algorithm collects the list of items present in each transaction and then finds patterns of items that frequently appear together across many transactions. This algorithm is highly efficient and can process a large amount of data quickly, even compared to other algorithms like Apriori.

It uses a tree structure called FP tree (frequent pattern tree) to store transactions more efficiently than traditional methods such as hash tables or bitmaps. The tree structure allows it to identify frequent itemsets efficiently and quickly as it stores all the information about their frequency in one place rather than looking at individual transactions one by one.

Steps

1.Counting step – where each item’s support count (number of times it appears across all transactions) is calculated.

2.Constructing step – building an FP tree based on the results from step 1.

3.Once the FP tree has been constructed using these steps, the algorithm scans through it for frequent patterns using a pruning strategy where rare items are removed from consideration until only those with sufficient support remain.

4.Finally, patterns found at each level can be combined into larger patterns, making them easier for human understanding or further analysis within a database system such as SQL or NoSQL.

Here are the steps of the algorithm with an example of associating fruits in a fruit shop:

1.Scan the transaction database and count the frequency of each item. Sort the items in descending order of frequency and discard any infrequent items. For example, if the minimum support is 3, then we can discard orange and pineapple from the transactions, and obtain the following sorted list of frequent items: {banana, apple, grape}.

2.Construct the FP tree by inserting each transaction as a path in the tree, following the order of the sorted frequent items. If a path already exists, increment the count of the corresponding node. For example, inserting T1 will create a path of {banana:1 -> apple:1 -> grape:1}. Inserting T2 will create a new branch of {banana:2 -> grape:2}. Inserting T3 will share the prefix {banana:3} with T1 and T2, and then create a new node {apple:2}. Inserting T4 will share the prefix {apple:3} with T1, and then create a new node {grape:3}. Inserting T5 will create a new branch of {banana:4 -> pineapple:1}.

The final FP tree looks like this:

banana:4

| \\

| pineapple:1

| /

apple:3

| \\

grape:3

|

grape:2

3.Mine the FP tree by recursively finding conditional patterns for each item, starting from the bottom of the sorted frequent items list. A conditional pattern is a subpath that leads to an item in the tree, along with its frequency. For example, the conditional patterns for grape are:

–{apple, banana}: 1

–{banana}: 2

–{apple}: 1

4.Construct conditional FP trees for each item by using its conditional patterns as transactions, and applying steps 1 and 2 again. For example, the conditional FP tree for grape is:

banana:3

|

apple:2

5.Extract frequent itemsets from each conditional FP tree by combining its root item with all possible subsets of its branches. For example, the frequent itemsets from the conditional FP tree for grape are:

–{grape}: 4 (support = 4/5 = 0.8)

–{grape, banana}: 3 (support = 3/5 = 0.6)

–{grape, apple}: 2 (support = 2/5 = 0.4)

–{grape, apple, banana}: 1 (support = 1/5 = 0.2)

6.Repeat steps 3 to 5 for each item in the sorted frequent items list until all frequent itemsets are found.

The FP Growth algorithm is a powerful tool that can analyse large data sets and quickly uncover significant patterns. Its scalability and versatility make it an ideal choice for various applications, such as web mining, market basket analysis, recommendation engines, and text mining tasks like sentiment analysis and author identification. With its ability to be deployed on large volumes of data such as Hadoop clusters, this algorithm helps organizations uncover essential insights from their data in a much shorter time than traditional databases. It is used in the banking, retail, healthcare sectors, and other industries requiring quick insight from large data sets.

[7.4Markov Models](#07_Contents.xhtml#sub-88)

Markov models are mathematical tools used to make predictions based on data from the past. These models are used in various fields, including economics, engineering, and medicine.

The central concept behind Markov models is that the future depends on the present predictably. Therefore, they use ‘state transitions’ – changes from one state to another over time. So, for example, if you were trying to predict how a patient’s health would change over time, you would look at their current condition and what factors had led them there (such as diet or lifestyle choices). You can then use previous data and projections about the future to come up with estimates of what might happen next.

A Markov model is essentially an equation that considers these past states and their possible future outcomes. It calculates the probability of each outcome by looking at how often similar events happened in the past, given certain conditions or parameters. This probability can then predict what will happen next, given that certain conditions and variables remain unchanged (or close enough).

In addition to making predictions, Markov models can be used for decision-making processes such as financial investment opportunities or medical treatments for patients with specific diseases or ailments. The model helps determine which path is more likely to lead toward success according to its calculations of probabilities associated with various paths taken through different states over time.

[7.5Hidden Markov Model](#07_Contents.xhtml#sub-89)

Hidden Markove model (HMM) is a powerful and widely used statistical model that can be applied to many tasks, such as speech recognition, machine translation, and bioinformatics. HMM models the probability of an event happening given previous events in a sequence. It assigns probabilities to hidden states that are not directly observed.

At its core, HMM is a probabilistic graphical model composed of two components: states and transitions. States are the underlying unknown events that cannot be observed directly. Transitions represent the chance of changing from one state to another in a series. Based on previous events, these states’ transitions decide what will happen next.

HMM can be used for many applications, such as recognizing handwritten text or speech recognition, because it allows us to consider multiple possible explanations for an observation at any point in time and consider all previous observations when making predictions about future ones. This makes HMMs powerful when dealing with data sequences with variable lengths or incomplete information that other models may struggle with due to their more rigid structure and assumptions about data distributions within them.

HMMs have also been successfully used for machine translation because they can quickly learn complex language patterns from small data sets. This is due to their ability to generalize well across different contexts and languages by considering context-dependent information when making predictions about word orderings within sentences or phrases across multiple languages without having seen them before during the training process. In addition, they are often used in bioinformatics research as tools for analyzing DNA sequences looking at genes’ transcriptional regulation networks.

7.5.1Learning the HMM Parameters

Learning the HMM parameters is essential when dealing with sequential data. This is because HMMs can help us uncover hidden patterns between different elements in a sequence that may remain undiscovered.

To begin, one must first determine the number of states and transitions needed for the model. For example, if we are trying to model gene expression, we would need multiple states representing different levels of gene expression, such as ‘active,’ ‘inactive,’ and ‘transitioning.’ Each state could also have numerous transitions, which determine how it might change from one state to another over time. Once these components have been identified, one must estimate the probability distributions for each state or transition between states by collecting data on what sequences are observed under different conditions and building a model based on these observations. This often involves guessing what these probabilities might look like based on prior experience or intuition before refining them through various methods such as the EM algorithm. The EM algorithm works by adjusting estimated values according to expected values until they converge on optimal solutions which best fit our data set. Once all parameters have been adequately estimated using an appropriate method like the EM algorithm, this information can then be used for making predictions that require accurate probability distributions being learned accurately beforehand.

For instance, this technique has been used to create NLP applications where accurately predicting word usage patterns lead to more effective communication with computers and speech recognition systems where accurate predictions help computers recognize human speech more accurately. In conclusion, learning HMM parameters is an essential part of working with sequential data since it helps us uncover hidden relationships between elements in a sequence which can then be used for prediction tasks that require accurate probability distributions being learned beforehand.

7.5.2Decoding States from Observations

Decoding the states of an ML algorithm can provide valuable insights into its decision-making process and help researchers optimize its performance to maximize accuracy. This is accomplished by observing how different inputs influence the model’s output and then decoding each state to identify areas that could benefit from improvement or changes. To do this, researchers use both visualization tools such as heat maps, which depict each state in terms of its influence on the predictive outcome, as well as probabilistic approaches such as Bayesian networks or Markov models that allow us to trace through all possible paths leading up to any given result. By decoding states from observations, we can better understand why certain decisions were made over others based on their impact on results. For example, suppose that a particular input has significantly affected the output. In this case, we know that it is essential for making accurate predictions and should be given more attention during optimization efforts.

In addition, identifying areas where improvements can be made before making changes or implementing new features allows us to test out what works best without running into unexpected consequences. Visualizations are particularly useful for helping us gain insight into decision-making processes since they allow us to see patterns or clusters emerge from data that would otherwise not be obvious just by looking at it directly. On top of this, probabilistic approaches like Bayesian networks and Markov models serve an essential role in gaining an even deeper understanding since they consider multiple outcomes simultaneously instead of just one result at a time.

[7.6Matrix Factorization and Matrix Completion Models](#07_Contents.xhtml#sub-90)

Matrix factorization and matrix completion models can be used in supervised and unsupervised ML scenarios. In unsupervised learning, matrix factorization is used to discover underlying patterns or clusters in a data set without needing labeled data. For example, it can identify topics within a collection of documents or similar group items in a recommendation system. In supervised learning, matrix completion can fill in missing values in a data set, such as predicting movie ratings based on user ratings. In this case, the model is trained using existing data with known outputs and is then used to predict missing values in new data. In conclusion, it depends on whether the application and use case of matrix factorization and matrix completion models are used in a supervised or unsupervised learning context.

Matrix factorization and matrix completion are two techniques used in data analysis and ML that can be used to solve complex problems. Matrix factorization is used to decompose a matrix into its constituent parts. In contrast, matrix completion is used to infer missing values in matrices.

Matrix factorization breaks down the original matrix into simpler components such as principal components, latent features, or singular values. By applying this method, one can reduce the dimensionality of the original matrix (also known as feature selection), making it easier to analyze by reducing noise and increasing interpretability. For example, suppose you have an input data set with 10 different variables. You could use factor analysis to reduce this data set to 5 variables that are more relevant to your model-building process. This can also help improve predictive performance because it reduces model complexity.

Matrix completion uses statistical methods such as low-rank approximation or nuclear norm minimization. Low-rank approximation reconstructs the complete data from the available observations by minimizing the rank of the reconstructed solution using convex optimization techniques such as gradient descent or regularized least squares. The idea behind low-rank approximation is to approximate the data with fewer independent components (or variables). This reduces the amount of memory and computational power required for computations, simplifying the analysis and making it faster. In low-rank approximation, a subset of features from the data set is chosen that contains most of the information about it. This subset can be determined using algorithms such as PCA or singular value decomposition (SVD). These methods find an orthogonal basis that captures most of the variance in the data set and then use this basis to reduce its dimensionality by representing each as linear combinations of other features in this orthogonal basis. These reduced representations are much easier to store and process than their whole counterparts, allowing for faster computation times without sacrificing too much accuracy or meaningful information about original input features.

Furthermore, low-rank approximation makes algorithm development more manageable because it preserves basic patterns in data sets while reducing noise and irrelevant details, which can overwhelm a model’s performance. For example, consider image detection algorithms like face recognition or object detection using CNN. Low-rank approximations are used prominently both during training as well as inference time due to their computation efficiency benefits over traditional methods like SVM or logistic regression, which require more time for training/inference but provide less accurate results compared to CNNs.

Nuclear norm minimization attempts to recover the underlying low-rank structure of a corrupted data set by minimizing its nuclear norm (sum of singular values). The advantage of this technique over traditional imputation methods (such as mean imputation) is that it can select only those entries that best explain observed patterns in the data while ignoring outliers or irrelevant variables. It utilizes two primary components: nuclear norm regularization and convex optimization. The nuclear norm regularization helps reduce overfitting, while the convex optimization helps find the optimal solution for a given problem. In essence, nuclear norm minimization is an iterative process of looking at a data point and trying to fit it into a predictive model or function. To achieve this, we use mathematical tools such as convex optimization and regularization techniques such as the L1 or L2 norms which help us minimize overfitting. This way, we can build accurate models with fewer parameters than traditional methods like linear regression or K\-means clustering. The essential advantage of this approach lies in its ability to accurately predict results, even with minimal assumptions about the data being used for training models.

In addition, since it minimizes errors rather than maximizes accuracy, it is less prone to ­overfitting than other methods like support vector machines (SVMs). This makes it suitable for dealing with sparse data sets with little information on how input variables are related to output variables.

Both matrix factorization and matrix completion have been widely studied in recent years due their ability help with tasks like discovering hidden features in data sets, recovering corrupted images and videos, predicting user preferences, etc.

[7.7Generative Models](#07_Contents.xhtml#sub-91)

Generative models can be used for both supervised and unsupervised learning tasks. Supervised generative models are trained to utilize labeled data where the output variable is known, such as in classification or regression problems. Examples of supervised generative models include Gaussian naive Bayes and conditional generative adversarial networks (CGAN). On the other hand, unsupervised generative models are trained on unlabeled data, where the output variable is unknown. These generative models are typically used for clustering and dimensionality reduction tasks. Examples of unsupervised generative models include autoencoder, variational autoencoder (VAE), and generative adversarial network (GAN). Whether a model is supervised or unsupervised depends solely on the type of data provided as input to the model and the task at hand.

Generative models generate new data by discovering the underlying structure of existing data. These models are capable of creating realistic-looking data from scratch. They can be used for various tasks, such as generating synthetic images, voice synthesis, natural language processing, text generation, and recommendation systems.

Mixture models are generative models which use statistical techniques to discover clusters in the training set. Given the observed data, they allow you to estimate the probability distribution over a set of variables. Mixture models can make predictions or segmentation decisions on unseen data points using mixture components learned from the training data set. For example, they could be used in image classification tasks where we want to identify different objects or segmentation tasks where we want to differentiate between different areas within an image.

[7.8Latent Factor Models](#07_Contents.xhtml#sub-92)

Latent factor models are based on the idea that there is a secret relationship between different variables or features, known as latent factors. This relationship is usually not visible from the raw data but can be inferred from it. For example, suppose we have a data set containing information about people’s movie preferences. We might assume an underlying latent factor of ‘movie genre interest’ driving these preferences, but this cannot be easily seen in the raw data alone. Latent factor models allow us to uncover this secret relationship by analyzing the correlations between different variables or features in the data set and then inferring which factors could explain them.

The main advantage of latent factor models over traditional methods such as linear regression is that they can account for non-linear relationships between variables and also handle large amounts of data more efficiently than traditional methods do because they only use a small number of ‘latent’ (hidden) factors instead of having to consider every single variable separately. Latent factor models have numerous applications in marketing, finance, image recognition, and natural language processing (NLP).

Since the steps of this mmodel involve complex calculations, most modern implementations rely heavily on vector processing technology such as graphics processing units (GPUs). In addition to speeding up computations significantly compared to traditional CPUs, GPUs can handle larger data sets than what could typically fit into memory on CPUs, which helps facilitate more powerful analyses. This is associate with fewer overhead costs for transferring large amounts of data around during computation cycles resulting in faster convergence times and improved accuracy rates overall.

[7.9Inference Models](#07_Contents.xhtml#sub-93)

Inference in graphical models and belief propagation in ML are closely related concepts as they both refer to gathering information from a given data set. Graphical models, also known as Bayesian networks, are a popular tool for representing relationships between variables. This model provides an efficient way to represent probability distributions over multiple variables by using a graph-like structure that represents the conditional dependencies among them. Inference from these models involves computing the probabilities or values associated with different configurations of the variables. The most common approach is known as belief propagation or message passing.

Belief propagation is based on an iterative algorithm that uses messages passed between nodes in the graph to arrive at a final answer for any given query about the system represented by the graph. It starts with initializing each node with its prior beliefs about its value and then passing messages to other nodes based on their neighbors’ and previous beliefs until all nodes have reached a consensus on their respective values. Propagating these messages throughout all nodes makes it possible to compute answers that accurately reflect the graphical model’s underlying probability distribution, even when considerable uncertainty is involved due to limited data availability or a high degree of randomness present in specific systems (such as weather forecasting).

The algorithm first creates a model, or belief network, consisting of nodes and edges that represent different variables and their possible relationships between them. Each node contains information about how potential specific values are for it, depending on its connections with other nodes in the network. The belief network can be represented in three parts:

•Evidence nodes (which contain observed data)

•Decision nodes (which contain decisions based on evidence)

•Utility nodes (which contain information about how desirable specific outcomes are)

Once these three components are defined, belief propagation begins by passing messages between the nodes to calculate probabilities or expected utility values associated with each node’s state or decision. During each processing cycle, messages will be passed from one node to another based on their connections within the network. This process will continue until all messages have been processed and there is only one possible explanation that has a higher probability than all others (or until there can be no more improvement). The algorithm then stops processing at this point as it has reached its conclusion.

In ML applications, belief propagation can be used for making predictions about future events or states based on observed data points without explicitly forming probabilistic assumptions about them (that is, without access to complete domain knowledge). In addition, while traditional ‘brute force’ approaches may be computationally expensive when confronted with large data sets containing high-dimensional inputs and outputs, belief propagation algorithms scale more efficiently even when faced with such challenges – allowing practitioners to apply inference techniques much faster than before without sacrificing accuracy.

[7.10Non-negative Matrix Factorization](#07_Contents.xhtml#sub-94)

Non-negative matrix factorization (NMF) is a type of factorization technique that involves breaking down a matrix into two component matrices with non-negative elements. The main difference between NMF and other factorization methods, such as SVD, is the restriction on the elements of the factorized components to be non-negative. This restriction has advantages such as improved interpretability since negative values are less meaningful than positive ones in many real-world applications.

The idea behind NMF is that any given complex data set can be composed of simpler parts, or components, underlying its structure, which can then be identified using this technique. To do this, NMF starts by representing the original data set A in terms of two matrices, W and H, whose product approximates A when multiplied: A ≈ WH where W represents ‘weights’ or ‘loadings’ and H represents ‘patterns’ or ‘features.’ Furthermore, both W and H have only non-negative entries, which makes them more interpretable than their counterparts from SVD since negative entries are not meaningful in many cases.

NMF optimizes for both W and H simultaneously by minimizing the distance between A and WH, often measured through squared Frobenius norm ||A–WH||2≤2^2, by iteratively updating each matrix until they converge to a point where they no longer improve results according to some metric such as mean squared error (MSE). Once convergence occurs, we have our optimal solution with optimal weights W∗and patterns H∗that approximate our original data set A ≈W∗H\*. These components can then be used to uncover hidden patterns in data that may not have been previously visible or understood before applying NMF on it.

[7.11Advantages of Unsupervised Learning](#07_Contents.xhtml#sub-95)

Unsupervised ML is a form of AI that can discover patterns in data without any external guidance or labels. This type of AI allows computers to learn independently and uncover hidden relationships in data sets. It works by grouping similar data into clusters and using algorithms to identify patterns within those clusters. By doing this, computers can find correlations between different pieces of data and make predictions about future trends without any help from humans. One advantage of unsupervised ML is its ability to save time and money by automating tasks that would otherwise require considerable human effort. For example, suppose a company has a large data set containing customer information such as age, gender, location, etc. An unsupervised ML algorithm could analyze this data set and uncover hidden trends or correlations between different factors, which might need to be more evident to humans looking at the data set manually. This could enable the company to make better decisions based on these findings, leading to increased profits or improved customer service levels.

Furthermore, it helps reduce computational costs by allowing machines to do work for you that would otherwise be too expensive or time-consuming for a human analyst. Unsupervised ML can also be used for anomaly detection – identifying unusual patterns in data sets that may indicate fraudulent activity or other abnormalities – as well as image recognition applications like facial recognition software, which can identify individuals from images without being told what individual it is looking for first (that is, without having labels). It has also been used for clustering applications where no clear labels are present in the data set, such as market segmentation, where customers are grouped into categories based on their similarities rather than pre-defined characteristics given by humans beforehand (with labels).

[7.12Disadvantages of Unsupervised Learning](#07_Contents.xhtml#sub-96)

Overfitting is prevalent in ML, mainly when the model is excessively intricate or the data is insufficient or distorted. Overfitting arises when the model exhibits high accuracy in fitting the training data; however, it struggles to apply this knowledge to novel or unseen data. This implies that the model can accurately represent the training data’s extraneous information or insignificant aspects rather than the fundamental patterns or frameworks. Let us consider a scenario where we aim to group a set of animal photographs using an algorithm that does not require labeled data. If the algorithm exhibits excessive sensitivity towards the colour or shape of the pixels, it may erroneously group the photos according to these characteristics instead of the actual animal groups. Applying the model to new images with varying colours or forms would yield subpar performance.

An additional drawback of unsupervised ML is the substantial computing expense associated with executing and fine-tuning these algorithms. In contrast to supervised learning, which relies on a well-defined objective function or accuracy metric to drive the learning process, unsupervised learning typically involves exploring many models and parameters without a clearly defined criterion. This process can be highly time-consuming and resource-intensive, particularly when handling extensive and intricate data sets. To perform dimensionality reduction on a high-dimensional data set using unsupervised algorithms like PCA or t-distributed stochastic neighbors embedding (t-SNE), it may be necessary to experiment with different values for the number of components or perplexity. This is done to find the best representation that retains the most information or captures the most significant variation in the data.

Moreover, unsupervised ML frequently yields outcomes challenging for humans to analyse or comprehend. Unsupervised algorithms lack specified labels or categories to give to the data. Instead, they generate their representations or clusters using similarity or distance metrics. These representations or clusters may not align with any relevant or intuitive notions for humans or yield excessive complex hypotheses to confirm or disprove.

Summary

•Unsupervised learning is a type of machine learning where the computer program tries to find patterns and relationships in data without being given specific examples or labels to learn from.

•Clustering algorithms are used to identify patterns in data and group similar data points together. Hierarchical clustering algorithms are used to group similar objects into a hierarchy of clusters. Fuzzy C-Means clustering uses fuzzy logic instead of hard clustering boundaries, making it useful for data sets with overlapping features and classes that cannot be easily separated by traditional methods. DBSCAN (Density-Based Spatial Clustering of Applications with Noise) uses density as the criteria for identifying clusters in spatial databases such as those containing geographic information systems (GIS).

•Gaussian mixture models (GMMs) are probabilistic models that hypothesize each point belongs to one of k Gaussians and assigns weights based on probability values assigning points to multiple clusters simultaneously. MeanShift Clustering algorithm iteratively shifts the centroids of the data points toward the higher-density areas. It does not require labeled data or involve any predetermined targets or outputs.

•Gaussian mixture density estimation finds patterns in complex data sets and makes predictions without prior knowledge of class labels. Markov random fields (MRFs) model complex relationships between different variables.

•Anomaly detection is when the program looks for data points different from the rest. The isolation forest algorithm uses the decision tree to identify anomalies in the data.

•Local outlier factor (LOF) uses density-based clustering to identify outliers in an unsupervised manner by looking at how close a particular data point is to its neighbors in an n\-dimensional space, where n represents the number of features present in the data set.

•One-class support vector machine (OC SVM) tries to identify anomalies by fitting a single model that best separates everyday examples from anomalous ones using the hyperplane separation technique and then classifying any new example into one class or another based on this model constructed during training phase using SVM technique.

•Dimensionality reduction is a potent tool for simplifying complex problems while preserving relevant information from an original data set.

•PCA, or principal component analysis, is a method used to reduce a data set’s dimensionality while preserving its most important features. KPCA is a non-linear version of PCA that uses kernel functions as an alternative to linear transformations to transform data into a lower-dimensional space.

•Linear discriminant analysis (LDA) is a method used to classify data by finding an optimal linear combination of features.

•Factor analysis (FA) is a statistical technique to identify an underlying relationship between variables. The two primary methods of factor analysis are exploratory and confirmatory.

•Association rule mining can be used to find connections between various elements in a data set. The FP Growth algorithm is an efficient method for discovering frequent item sets in a transactional database. The Apriori algorithm can uncover associations between items in large data sets. The ECLAT (equivalence class transformation) algorithm uses depth-first search to find frequent itemsets in a transaction database.

•In supervised learning, the Markov model is trained using labeled data, meaning the data has a target or output variable. The model is then used to make predictions about new, unlabled data. The Markov model is trained using only input data without labeled outputs in unsupervised learning. The hidden Markov model (HMM) is trained using an unlabeled data set in unsupervised learning.

•Unsupervised generative models are trained on unlabeled data, where the output variable is unknown. These generative models are typically used for clustering and dimensionality reduction tasks.

•Latent factor models are generative models that use latent variables (variables not directly observed) to capture patterns in data sets and derive insights from them.

•Inference in graphical models and belief propagation in ML are closely related concepts as they both refer to gathering information from a given data set.

•Belief propagation is an ML algorithm specializing in finding the most probable explanations for a given set of evidence. The belief network can be represented in three parts: evidence nodes (which contain observed data), decision nodes (which contain decisions based on evidence), and utility nodes (which contain information about how desirable specific outcomes are).

Learning Objectives

At the end of this chapter, you will be able to:

•Describe the basics of supervised learning

•Describe the steps involved in supervised learning algorithms

•Explain the K\-nearest neighbor (KNN) algorithm

•Explain the structure and function of decision trees

•Discuss the concept and application of random forests

•Identify different types of linear classifiers

•Explain the advantages of linear classifiers

•Learn how to determine the weights of a linear classifier

•Describe generative models for linear classifiers

•Describe linear discriminant analysis (LDA)

•Explain the naive Bayes classifier

•Explain polynomial regression

•Discuss multinomial logistic regression

•Explain ordinal logistic regression

•Define the perceptron and its activation function

•Identify types of perceptron models (single-layer and multi-layer)

•Discuss the limitations of the perceptron model

•Explain support vector machines (SVM) and their types (linear and non-linear)

•Explain the concept of hyperplanes and support vectors in SVM

•Identify various applications of supervised learning

•Discuss the limitations and challenges of supervised learning

[8.1Introduction](#07_Contents.xhtml#sub-97)

Supervised machine learning (ML) is a branch of artificial intelligence (AI) that uses labeled data to train algorithms that can classify data or predict outcomes. Labeled data means that some input data is already tagged with the correct output, which helps the algorithm learn the relationship between the input and output variables. The goal of supervised learning is to find a mapping function that can generalize well to new data. There are two main types of supervised learning problems: classification and regression.

Classification problems involve assigning data into discrete categories, such as spam or not spam, dog or cat, apple or orange ([Fig. 8.1](#16_Chapter8.xhtml#fig8-1)). For example, a supervised learning algorithm can be used to classify emails based on their content and sender. The algorithm would learn from a training set of emails that have been labeled as spam or not spam by humans. Then, it would apply the learned rules to new emails and assign them to the appropriate category.

![](Images/f8-1.jpg)

[Figure 8.1](#16_Chapter8.xhtml#fig-8-1)  Classification algorithm example

Regression problems involve predicting a continuous value, such as house price or sales revenue. For example, a supervised learning algorithm can be used to predict the price of a house based on its features and location. The algorithm would learn from a training set of houses that have been labeled with their prices by humans. It would then apply the learned function to new houses and estimate their prices.

Supervised learning has many applications in various domains, such as image classification, fraud detection, risk assessment, spam filtering, etc. It can help organizations solve real-world problems at scale and with high accuracy. However, supervised learning requires a lot of labeled data, which can be expensive and time-consuming to obtain. It may suffer from overfitting or underfitting. It may be biased or unfair, if the data or the algorithm reflects some underlying discrimination or prejudice. Therefore, supervised learning requires careful design and evaluation to ensure its validity and reliability.

Steps

1.Collect and label the training data, which should have enough features and examples to represent the problem domain. Features are the attributes or variables that describe the data, such as height, weight, color. Labeling the data means assigning a target value to each example, such as a category, a score, a rating, etc. The target value is what the algorithm aims to predict or classify. The training data should be representative of the problem domain, meaning that it should capture the diversity and complexity of the real-world data.

2.Choose an appropriate algorithm for the problem, based on the type of data, the complexity of the function, and the computational resources available. There are many types of supervised learning algorithms, such as linear regression, logistic regression, decision trees, support vector machine (SVM), and neural networks. Each algorithm has its own advantages and ­disadvantages, and some are more suitable for certain types of data or problems than others. The complexity of the function refers to how flexible or expressive the algorithm is, meaning how well it can capture the non-linear or intricate patterns in the data. The computational resources refer to how much time and memory the algorithm requires to run and learn from the data.

3.Train the algorithm on the training data, by adjusting its parameters to minimize the error or loss function, which measures how well the algorithm fits the data. Parameters are the variables that control how the algorithm works, such as weights, biases, thresholds, etc. The error or loss function is a mathematical formula that quantifies how far the algorithm’s predictions are from the actual target values. The goal of training is to find the optimal values of the parameters that minimize the error or loss function. This can be done by using various optimization techniques, such as gradient descent, stochastic gradient descent, genetic algorithms, etc.

4.Evaluate the performance of the algorithm on a test set, which is a subset of the training data that is not used for training. The test set is used to measure how well the algorithm generalizes to new data. Generalization is the ability of the algorithm to make accurate predictions on unseen or novel data that is not part of the training data. The performance of the algorithm can be evaluated by using various metrics, such as accuracy, precision, recall, F1\-score, mean squared error, etc.

5.Use the algorithm to make predictions on new data or improve it by tuning its parameters or using more data. For example, if the algorithm is trained to classify images of animals into cats or dogs, it can be used to classify a new image of an animal that is not part of the training or test set. Alternatively, if the performance of the algorithm is not satisfactory on the test set or new data, it can be improved by tuning its parameters or using more data. Tuning parameters means changing their values slightly to see if they improve the error or loss function. Using more data means adding more examples or features to the training data to make it more representative and informative.

Some of the most common types of supervised classification algorithms are K\-nearest neighbor (KNN), decision tree, random forest, support vector machine (SVM), linear classifiers, and neural networks.

[8.2K\-Nearest Neighbor](#07_Contents.xhtml#sub-98)

K\-nearest neighbor (KNN) is a supervised ML algorithm that can be used for both classification and regression tasks. The main idea behind KNN is that similar data points tend to have similar labels or outputs. Therefore, given a new data point, KNN can predict its label or output by looking at the labels or outputs of its K closest neighbors in the feature space. The feature space is the n\-dimensional space where each dimension represents a feature or attribute of the data. For example, if we have data about flowers with two features, petal length and petal width, then the feature space is a 2D plane where each point represents a flower.

The goal of KNN is to correctly classify unknown instances by finding similar cases in its training data set that have already been labeled correctly and applying those labels to the unknown instances. To do this, we must first define a distance metric for measuring two data points’ proximity, such as Euclidean distance or cosine similarity. Secondly, we must choose an appropriate value for K – this determines how many neighbors will be used when making predictions about an unknown instance. Finally, we must decide which type of weighting scheme should be used when combining votes from each neighbor – uniform weighting assigns equal importance to all neighbors. In contrast, inverse weighting assigns greater importance to closer neighbors than those far away.

KNN can also be used for regression tasks; instead of assigning class labels based on majority voting amongst neighborhoods, it calculates the mean value or average amongst them (inverse weights may still apply).

KNN is one of the most straightforward yet powerful ML algorithms that allow us to classify unseen data using similarity measures between different observations while avoiding costly parameter estimation procedures like explicit modeling techniques needed in other algorithms such as general linear models. Also, since no prior assumptions are made regarding underlying distribution, it is suitable even when a limited amount of training examples exist, making it a robust model capable of producing reliable results across different scenarios. In addition, portals like Netflix, Amazon, YouTube, and others use them in their recommendation engines.

To find the K closest neighbors of a new data point, KNN uses a distance metric such as Euclidean, Manhattan, or Hamming. Each of these distances is defined in the equations below:

(8.1)

$\\text{Euclidean}\\,\\text{Distance:}\\sqrt{\\sum\\limits\_{i = 1}^{k}\\left( {x\_{i} - y} \\right)^{2}},$

(8.2)

$\\text{Manhattan}\\,\\text{Distance}:\\sum\\limits\_{i = 1}^{k}\\left| {x\_{i} - y} \\right|$,

where x[i] represents the training data point and y represents the test data point.

The distance metric measures how far apart two data points are in the feature space. The smaller the distance, the more similar the data points.

![](Images/f8-2.jpg)

[Figure 8.2](#16_Chapter8.xhtml#fig-8-2)  KNN example

Consider [Fig. 8.2](#16_Chapter8.xhtml#fig8-2). The two classes of training points are plotted as circles and triangles. The test instance is shown as a square. The objective is to classify the square as a triangle or circle. First, identify the distance between the square and all other points (circles and triangles). Display the same in a table with serial number, training point shape (circle, triangle), and distance as columns. Sort the table in the ascending order of distance. If K = 3, choose the first 3 rows (for example, circle, circle, circle). Thus, we classify that the square as belonging to the circle class. If K = 7, choose the first 7 rows (4 circles, 3 triangles). Here also, we classify the square as belonging to the circle class.

Class P data ([Table 8.1](#16_Chapter8.xhtml#tab8-1)) is shown as black circles and class N data as grey circles. The unknown class for the last input is shown with a cross sign ([Fig. 8.3](#16_Chapter8.xhtml#fig8-3)).

[Table 8.1](#16_Chapter8.xhtml#tab-8-1)Classes P and N represented as x and y

 
| x || y || Class |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 58 || 8 || P |
| 58 || 9 || P |
| 58 || 13 || P |
| 60 || 9 || P |
| 60 || 10 || P |
| 63 || 10 || P |
| 63 || 11 || P |
| 60 || 14 || N |
| 63 || 14 || N |
| 65 || 11 || N |
| 65 || 12 || N |
