| 68 || 12 || N |
| 61 || 11 || ? |

![](Images/f8-3.jpg)

[Figure 8.3](#16_Chapter8.xhtml#fig-8-3)  Classes P and N represented as a graph

To determine the class for the query input (61,11), we need to determine the distance between each point to the query input and sort the distances in non-descending order ([Table 8.2](#16_Chapter8.xhtml#tab8-2)).

[Table 8.2](#16_Chapter8.xhtml#tab-8-2)Euclidean distance between x and y and (60,11)

 
| x || y || Class || Euclidean distance between (x, y) and (60, 11) || Ranking distance |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 58 || 8 || P || 3.6 || 8 |
| 58 || 9 || P || 2.82 || 3 |
| 58 || 13 || P || 2.82 || 3 |
| 60 || 9 || P || 2 || 2 |
| 60 || 10 || P || 1 || 1 |
| 63 || 10 || P || 3.16 || 7 |
| 63 || 11 || P || 3 || 5 |
| 60 || 14 || N || 3 || 5 |
| 63 || 14 || N || 4.24 || 9 |
| 65 || 11 || N || 5 || 10 |
| 65 || 12 || N || 5.09 || 11 |
| 65 || 15 || N || 6.40 || 12 |
| 68 || 12 || N || 8.06 || 13 |

Based on the distances, if we chose K = 5, all the three least distances belong to class P and hence we decide the class for (60, 11) as P.

If we chose K = 5, among the five least distances, four distances belong to class P and one distance belongs to class N. Hence we decide the class for (60,11) as P based on the majority.

Once the K closest neighbors are found, KNN performs a majority vote to determine the label or output of the new data point. This means that KNN assigns the most common label or output among the k neighbors to the new data point. For example, if we have a classification problem with three classes, A, B, and C, and we set K = 5, then KNN will look at the labels of the 5 nearest neighbors of the new data point and count how many times each label appears. If there are 3 neighbors with label A, 1 neighbor with label B, and 1 neighbor with label C, then KNN will predict that the new data point belongs to class A.

KNN is a simple and intuitive algorithm that can handle multi-class problems, meaning that it can deal with more than two classes. It can also handle non-linear boundaries between classes, meaning that it can capture complex patterns in the data. However, KNN has some drawbacks as well. One of them is that it can be computationally expensive for large data sets, because it must calculate the distance between every pair of data points and sort them to find the k nearest neighbors. Another drawback is that it can be sensitive to noise and outliers in the data because they can affect the majority vote. Moreover, KNN can be affected by the choice of K and the distance metric, which can influence the accuracy and performance of the algorithm.

In this example, we will use KNN to choose a restaurant based on the ratings, price and cuisine of five data sets. The data sets are shown in [Table 8.3](#16_Chapter8.xhtml#tab8-3).

[Table 8.3](#16_Chapter8.xhtml#tab-8-3)Restaurant rating example

 
| Restaurant || Rating || Price || Cuisine |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| A || 4.5 || $$$ || Italian |
| B || 3.0 || $$ || Chinese |
| C || 4.0 || $$ || Mexican |
| D || 3.5 || $ || Indian |
| E || 4.0 || $$$ || French |

Suppose we want to choose a restaurant that has a high rating, a moderate price and a cuisine that we like. We can use KNN to find the restaurants that are the most similar to our preferences. We first need to define a distance metric that measures how close two restaurants are based on their features. One possible metric is the Euclidean distance, which is calculated as:

$d = \\sqrt{{(r\_{1} - r\_{2})}^{2} + {(p\_{1} - p\_{2})}^{2} + {(c\_{1} - c\_{2})}^{2}}$

where r, p and c are the rating, price, and cuisine of each restaurant, respectively. The cuisine feature can be encoded as a numerical value, such as 1 for Italian, 2 for Chinese, and so on. Using this metric, we can calculate the distance between our preferences and each restaurant ([Table 8.4](#16_Chapter8.xhtml#tab8-4)).

[Table 8.4](#16_Chapter8.xhtml#tab-8-4)  Restaurant rating example, distance calculation

 
| Restaurant || Distance |
| --- | --- |
| A || 1.41 |
| B || 2.24 |
| C || 1.0 |
| D || 2.0 |
| E || 2.24 |

We then choose the K nearest neighbors, which are the restaurants with the smallest distances. In this case, K = 3, so we select A, C and D as the candidates.

The final step is to assign a label to our preferences based on the majority vote of the neighbors. Since two out of three neighbors have a rating of 4.0, we can label our preferences as having a rating of 4.0. Similarly, since two out of three neighbors have a price of ![](Images/dd.png), we can label our preferences as having a price of ![](Images/dd.png). Finally, since there is no clear majority for the cuisine, we can choose the one that we like the most or use another criterion to break the tie. Therefore, based on KNN, we can choose restaurant C as the best option for our preferences.

[8.3Decision Trees](#07_Contents.xhtml#sub-99)

Decision tree is a popular and widely used ML algorithm that can perform both classification and regression tasks. They are based on the idea of dividing the data into smaller and more homogeneous subsets based on some criteria, such as the value of a feature or the outcome of a test. The result is a tree-like structure where each node represents a subset of the data, each branch represents a decision rule, and each leaf represents a final prediction.

The decision tree starts at the top of the tree (the root node) and goes down by following specific rules. The root node of a decision tree contains specific attributes, which are then split into branches or paths at each level, leading to different nodes containing further attributes until one path leads to a particular outcome or decision. Building this flowchart model starts with selecting an attribute from the large data set, then dividing it into multiple tiers by splitting it according to some conditions, and finally arriving at a conclusion after numerous intermediate stages/nodes.

For example, suppose we want to predict whether it will rain tomorrow in Chennai (India), based on various inputs such as temperature, humidity, wind speed, etc. To do this, we can use a decision tree that starts with the most important input, which is temperature. Temperature is a good starting point because research has shown that it has a strong influence on weather patterns.

The decision tree will have a root node that represents temperature, and then it will split into two branches: one for low temperature and one for high temperature. Each branch will then have another node that represents another input, such as humidity. Humidity is also important because it affects how much moisture is present in the air, which can lead to rain. The decision tree will then split again into more branches based on the values of humidity: low, medium, or high.

Each branch will continue to split into more nodes and branches until we reach a leaf node, which is the final prediction. A leaf node will tell us whether it will rain tomorrow or not, based on the combination of inputs that led to it.

For example, if the temperature is low and the humidity is high, the leaf node might say ‘Yes, it will rain tomorrow’. If the temperature is high and the humidity is low, the leaf node might say ‘No, it will not rain tomorrow’. To draw a flow chart for the above scenario, we can use the following steps:

1.Start with a start symbol (a circle or an oval) and write “Start” inside it.

2.Draw an arrow from the start symbol to a decision symbol (a diamond) and write “Temperature?” inside it. This symbol represents the question of whether the temperature is low or high.

3.Draw two arrows from the decision symbol, one pointing to the left and one pointing to the right. Label the left arrow as “Low” and the right arrow as “High”. These arrows represent the possible outcomes of the question.

4.Draw another decision symbol at the end of each arrow and write “Humidity?” inside them. These symbols represent the question of whether the humidity is low or high.

5.Draw two arrows from each decision symbol, one pointing down and one pointing up. Label the down arrows as “Low” and the up arrows as “High”. These arrows represent the possible outcomes of the question.

6.Draw a leaf node (a rectangle) at the end of each arrow and write the corresponding prediction inside them. For example, if the temperature is low and the humidity is high, write “Yes, it will rain tomorrow”. If the temperature is high and the humidity is low, write “No, it will not rain tomorrow”.

7.Draw an arrow from each leaf node to an end symbol (a circle or an oval) and write “End” inside it.

The flow chart should look something like [Fig. 8.4](#16_Chapter8.xhtml#fig8-4).

![](Images/f8-4.jpg)

[Figure 8.4](#16_Chapter8.xhtml#fig-8-4)  Structure of a decision tree

Decision trees are known for efficiently handling both categorical and numerical data. Furthermore, unlike other ML algorithms like linear regression, they do not require any initialization feature scaling before the model is created. They also provide better accuracy compared with other techniques due to non-linearity that is built into the models. Furthermore, data manipulation regarding missing values is optional while working with the decision tree technique since they can build up classifiers even if some values are missing from the data set.

Another excellent application is in medical diagnosis systems where they prove very helpful and accurate while diagnosing patients’ diseases by analyzing massive data sets containing symptoms and treatment information.

Decision trees may encounter issues such as overfitting or underfitting. Overfitting occurs when the model is excessively intricate and accurately fits the available data but fails to generalize to unseen data effectively. Underfitting is when the model is overly simplistic, fails to capture the data adequately, and exhibits subpar performance when applied to new data. To mitigate these issues, specific methodologies can be employed on decision trees, including pruning, regularization, or ensemble methods.

Pruning is the elimination or reduction of specific nodes or branches in a tree that does not significantly add to the prediction or increase error. For instance, if a node possesses just a limited number of samples or minimal information gain, it might be pruned to streamline the model and mitigate the likelihood of overfitting. Pruning can be performed either during the tree’s construction (pre-pruning) or after the tree has structure (post-pruning).

Regularization imposes limits or penalties on the tree’s growth, such as restricting the depth, the number of nodes, or the minimum samples needed at each node. These limitations can impede the tree’s growth, preventing it from becoming excessively large or deep and mitigating the risk of overfitting. Regularization can enhance the computational efficiency and interpretability of the model as well.

Ensemble approaches integrate numerous decision trees, such as random forests or boosting, to construct a more resilient and precise model. Random forests are an ensemble technique that makes many decision trees using various subsets of features and data. The predictions of these trees are then averaged to decrease variation and enhance accuracy. Boosting is an ensemble strategy that progressively generates many decision trees. Each tree aims to rectify the mistakes produced by the preceding trees and then combines their predictions with varying weights to diminish bias and ­enhance accuracy.

Thus, decision tree algorithms can be applied when the problem and data suits the following requirements:

•When the instances are represented by attribute–value pairs

•When the target function has discrete output values

•When the training data contains errors

•When the training data has missing values

8.3.1The Iterative Dichotomiser 3 (ID3) Algorithm

The basic decision tree learning algorithm is the iterative dichotomiser (ID) algorithm. The third version is quite popular and hence it is called ID3.

ID3 learns decision trees by constructing it in top-down fashion. As the name suggests, the algorithm is an iterative method. Dichotomiser means dividing – the algorithm divides the attributes into two or more groups depending on how the decision tree will be constructed. To determine which attribute should be considered as the root node, a statistical evaluation of all the attributes is performed.

Steps

1.Calculate the entropy of the whole data set.

2.Calculate the information gain for each attribute. The attribute with maximum information gain is the root node.

3.If all examples are of the same class, then return the single node with the corresponding class label.

4.Otherwise split the data set into subsets using the attribute A which has maximum information gain.

5.Repeat the process till all the attributes are exhausted or further expansion of the tree is not possible (when the nodes are leaf nodes).

The metrics used in the ID3 algorithm for selection of attributes as nodes in the decision tree are information gain and entropy.

Information gain or gain calculates the reduction in entropy. The node with highest information gain will be chosen. It is calculated as follows:

(8.3)

$\\text{Gain}\\left( {S,A} \\right) = \\text{Entropy}\\left( S \\right) - \\sum\\limits\_{v\\, \\in \\,\\text{values}{(A)}}\\frac{\\left| S\_{v} \\right|}{\\left| S \\right|}\\text{Entropy}\\left( S\_{v} \\right),$

where S represents the entire data set, A represents the attribute, and S[v] represents the number of instances for which the attribute A has the value S[v].

In ML, entropy is a measure of the randomness or disorder within a data set. It quantifies the amount of uncertainty or impurity in the data, helping to determine how well a model can make predictions. It is calculated as follows:

(8.4)

$\\text{Entropy}\\left( S \\right) = - \\sum\\limits\_{i = 1}^{c}p\_{i}\\log\_{2}p\_{i}$,

where S represents the entire data set, c represents the number of classes, and p[i] represents the probability of class i.

For example, consider the play\_tennis data given in Chapter 6. It has a total of 14 attributes, with 9 positive instances and 5 negative instances.

$\\text{Entropy}\\left( S \\right) = - \\left( {\\frac{9}{14}\\log\_{2}\\frac{9}{14} + \\frac{5}{14}\\log\_{2}\\frac{5}{14}} \\right)$          

                                    =  − (0.643 \* (−0.6371) + 0.357 \* (−1.486)

                      =  − (−0.410+(−0.530)) = 0.940

Next we calculate the information gain for each attribute ([Table 8.5](#16_Chapter8.xhtml#tab8-5)).

Searching the Hypothesis Space in Decision Tree Learning: The hypothesis space includes all possible decision trees for the given data. The ID3 algorithm searches the hypothesis space from simple to complex, similar to the one in the hill-climbing approach. It starts with an empty decision tree. The root node is selected. Further nodes are created. The hill-climbing approach is employed using information gain and entropy measures.

ID3 searches the complete space of all finite discrete-valued functions. It maintains only one hypothesis. An important concern is that it has no backtrack option. This indicates that it may get struck on local optima. It may converge to local minima.

It employs all the training samples at each step. But in every step, each attribute is evaluated based on already selected attributes. This means that the hypothesis will be subject to refinement at every step and due to this property, it is less sensitive to errors.

Inductive Bias in Decision Tree Learning: For the given data, there may be decision trees consistent with the data. ID3 prefers short trees to large trees. ID3 selects trees where nodes are attributes with high information gain. Attributes that have high information gain are close to the root node and such attributes are preferred over the other attributes.

The basic difference between ID3 and the candidate elimination algorithm is that ID3 searches a complete hypothesis space (searches all possible decision trees) incompletely whereas the candidate elimination algorithm searches an incomplete hypothesis space completely.

8.3.2The C4.5 Algorithm

The C4.5 algorithm is an improvement on the ID3 algorithm, addressing several of its limitations:

•Handling continuous attributes: Unlike ID3, which can only handle nominal attributes, C4.5 can handle continuous attributes by creating threshold-based splits. For example, if you have a data set with a continuous attribute like “age,” C4.5 can determine a threshold (such as age > 30) to split the data.

•Handling missing data: C4.5 can handle missing data by using a probabilistic approach. It assigns the most probable value based on the distribution of known values. For example, assume there is a customer data set with missing values in the “income” attribute. C4.5 assigns the most probable income value based on the distribution of known incomes in the data set.

•Overcoming overfitting: C4.5 uses pruning to reduce overfitting. It removes branches that have little importance, making the model more generalizable. For example, assume there is a weather data set used to predict whether to play tennis. C4.5 removes branches that do not significantly improve the prediction accuracy, such as those based on rare weather conditions.

•Gain ratio: C4.5 uses the gain ratio instead of information gain to overcome the bias towards attributes with many values. The gain ratio normalizes information gain by the intrinsic information of a split. For example, assume there is a data set with attributes like color and size. C4.5 uses the gain ratio to choose the best attribute for splitting, avoiding bias towards attributes with many unique values like color.

(8.5)

$\\text{Split}\\,\\text{Info}\_{A}\\left( S \\right) = - \\sum\\limits\_{i = 1}^{v}\\frac{\\left| D\_{i} \\right|}{\\left| D \\right|} \\times \\log\_{2}\\left( \\frac{\\left| D\_{i} \\right|}{\\left| D \\right|} \\right)$

Split Info represents the potential information generated by splitting the data set S into v partitions that correspond to v outcomes on attribute A.

Another metric used by C4.5 is the gain ratio, which is defined as

(8.6)

$\\text{Gain}\\,\\text{Ratio}\\left( A \\right) = \\frac{\\text{Gain}\\left( A \\right)}{\\text{Split}\\,\\text{Info}\_{A}\\left( S \\right)}$

The same play\_tennis data is taken again but with some continuous values for some attributes. The data set is given in [Table 8.14](#16_Chapter8.xhtml#tab8-14).

[Table 8.14](#16_Chapter8.xhtml#tab-8-14)Predictions about Play\_Tennis

 
| Sky || Temp || Humidity || Wind || Play\_Tennis |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Sunny || 85 || 85 || Weak || No |
| Sunny || 80 || 90 || Strong || No |
| Overcast || 83 || 78 || Weak || Yes |
| Rain || 70 || 96 || Weak || Yes |
| Rain || 68 || 80 || Weak || Yes |
| Rain || 65 || 70 || Strong || No |
| Overcast || 64 || 65 || Strong || Yes |
| Sunny || 72 || 95 || Weak || No |
| Sunny || 69 || 70 || Weak || Yes |
| Rain || 75 || 80 || Weak || Yes |
| Sunny || 75 || 70 || Strong || Yes |
| Overcast || 72 || 90 || Strong || Yes |
| Overcast || 81 || 75 || Weak || Yes |
| Rain || 71 || 80 || Strong || No |

If the values of the attribute are Boolean, then there will be only two branches for the attribute. Instead, if it is categorical then the number of branches for the attribute will be equal to the number of distinct values of it. If the values are continuous, then a threshold (θ) will be chosen to separate the data as (≤ θ) and (> θ) The threshold should be chosen carefully. The threshold set for Humidity is 75.

For the same play\_tennis data, the gain ratio of the attributes Sky, Temp, Humidity and Wind are 1.71, 0.052, 0.191, and 0.05, respectively. The maximum gain ratio is obtained for the attribute Sky and hence it is the root node for the decision tree generated by C4.5 ([Fig. 8.8](#16_Chapter8.xhtml#fig8-8)).

8.3.3The CART Algorithm

CART stands for classification and regression trees. It can be used for classification and regression problems. If the target variable is set as class labels, then classification is carried out with the resultant decision tree. On the other hand, if the target variable is a number or numerical value that predicts or estimates any quantity, then regression is carried out using the decision tree obtained.

CART uses Gini Index as a metric for splitting the data. It is defined as

(8.7)

$\\text{Gini}\\left( S \\right) = 1 - \\sum\\limits\_{i = 1}^{m}p\_{i}^{2},$

where p[i] is the probability that an instance of S belongs to a class label *c*[*i*] and there are m classes in total. Gini(S ) measures the total impurity of the given data set S.

To find the split, we calculate the Gini Index for each attribute. Let an attribute A be split into two sets D1 and D2 based on the two types of values. Then the Gini Index of A is calculated as

(8.8)

$\\text{Gini}\_{A}\\left( S \\right) = \\frac{\\left| {D1} \\right|}{\\left| D \\right|}\\text{Gini}\\left( {D1} \\right) + \\frac{\\left| {D2} \\right|}{\\left| D \\right|}\\text{Gini}\\left( {D2} \\right)$

For a discrete-valued attribute, the attribute for which the Gini Index is minimum is considered as its splitting subset. For continuous data, a similar strategy is chosen as in the case of the C4.5 algorithm.

The reduction in impurity that is incurred on attribute A is

(8.9)

*Δ*Gini(*A*) = Gini(*S*) − Gini[*A*](*S*)

The attribute that maximizes the reduction in impurity is selected as the splitting attribute.

8.3.4Drawbacks of Decision Tree Learning

Decision trees are a popular ML technique for classification problems. However, they also have some limitations that need to be addressed:

•Cannot handle continuous attributes: Decision trees can only split the data based on discrete values of the attributes. This means that if an attribute has a continuous range of values, such as height or weight, the decision tree has to discretize it into bins or intervals. This can result in loss of information and accuracy, as well as increased complexity of the tree.

•Cannot determine how deep the decision tree grows: Decision trees can grow very large and complex if there are many attributes and classes in the data. This can lead to overfitting, which means that the tree performs well on the training data but poorly on new or unseen data. To avoid overfitting, the decision tree needs to be pruned or stopped at some point. However, there is no clear or optimal criterion for determining when to stop growing the tree. Different pruning methods may result in different trade-offs between accuracy and complexity.

•Cannot handle training data with missing attribute values: Decision trees require that every instance in the training data has a value for every attribute. However, in real-world data, there may be instances with missing or unknown values for some attributes. This can pose a challenge for decision tree learning, as it is not clear how to split the data based on such attributes. There are various methods to deal with missing values, such as ignoring them, replacing them with mean or mode values, or using probabilistic models. However, each method has its assumptions and limitations.

•Computational efficiency is high: Decision tree learning is a greedy algorithm that tries to find the best split at each node of the tree. This means that it has to evaluate all possible splits for all possible attributes at each node. This can be computationally expensive, especially if the data has many attributes and instances. Moreover, decision tree learning does not guarantee finding the optimal or global solution, as it may get stuck in a local optimum.

[8.4Random Forests](#07_Contents.xhtml#sub-100)

Random forest is a type of ML algorithm that can perform classification and regression tasks. It is based on the idea of ensemble learning, which means combining multiple weak learners to create a strong learner. A weak learner is a simple model that can make predictions, but with a high error rate. A strong learner is a complex model that can make accurate predictions, but with high computational cost.

The weak learners in random forests are decision trees, which are graphical models that split the data into smaller subsets based on some criteria. For example, if we want to classify a person as having diabetes or not, we can use a decision tree that asks questions like ‘Is the person’s age above 50?’ or ‘Is the person’s blood sugar level above 200?’. Each question leads to a branch in the tree, and each branch ends with a leaf node that represents a class label (diabetes or no diabetes).

Random forest uses many different decision trees. Each decision tree predicts in a random forest, and the outcome is determined by which prediction receives the most votes. This method is used to determine the random forest’s result for classification tasks ([Fig. 8.9](#16_Chapter8.xhtml#fig8-9)).

![](Images/f8-9.jpg)

[Figure 8.9](#16_Chapter8.xhtml#fig-8-9)  Random forest example

To illustrate how random forests work, let us consider some examples:

•Imagine that we are attempting to predict a person’s BMI (body mass index) value from a data set of their heights and weights. Here, we may use a supervised learning technique, such as linear regression. However, we can take things further with random forest by considering different input parameters like age, gender, height, and weight, which may boost our prediction accuracy. To accomplish this, we would randomly choose some subset from these four input features, along with the corresponding BMI values as training examples, that is, our ‘training set.’ We would then build several decision trees using these subsets as inputs or features for each tree while labeling them against the BMI value, that is, the output variable or target label that we want our model to predict accurately when faced with new data points.

•Consider that you have a large set of images classified into two categories, cats and dogs, that you want to classify each time new images are presented. Of course, this could be done using other supervised learning algorithms, such as SVM. However, due to their complexity, they may not necessarily yield top accuracy scores. Here, random forest proves its worthiness by its ability not only to quantitatively analyze pixel values but also to qualitatively examine shape patterns within pixels across multiple cat–dog image instances, enabling greater accuracy at classifying the images.

Random forests do have some drawbacks. They can overfit the data, which means they learn too much from the noise and outliers in the data and fail to generalize to new data. They can also be unstable, which means small changes in the data can lead to large changes in the structure of the tree. To overcome these problems, random forests use two techniques: bagging and feature selection.

Bagging refers to bootstrap aggregation, which means sampling the data with replacement and creating multiple decision trees from these samples. Each decision tree is trained on a different subset of the data, so they are likely to have different errors and biases. By combining these trees, we can reduce the variance of the predictions and improve the accuracy. The combination can be obtained by voting for classification tasks or averaging for regression tasks. For example, if we have 10 decision trees and 7 of them predict diabetes and 3 predict no diabetes, we can use majority voting and assign diabetes as the final prediction.

Feature selection means randomly selecting a subset of features (variables) to split the data at each node of the decision tree. This reduces the correlation among the trees and increases the diversity of the ensemble. For example, if we have 100 features and we select 10 features at each node, we can create different trees that use different combinations of features to make predictions.

[8.5Linear Classifiers](#07_Contents.xhtml#sub-101)

Linear classifiers are a powerful ML technique used in supervised learning problems that classify new data into broad categories based on the properties of the data. Standard linear classifiers include linear SVMs and logistic regression, which use a linear decision boundary to divide data into distinct groups. The objective is to identify a decision boundary that divides the data into distinct groups and convert the output, in the case of logistic regression, to a probability between 0 and 1 using a sigmoid function. Though these methods are helpful for linearly separable data sets, kernel methods such as the kernel trick can be employed to map non-linearly separable data sets into higher dimensional spaces. Overall, linear classifiers are practical tools for classification problems. However, their efficacy can be limited by their need for linearly separable data and reliance on a single linear decision boundary.

Let us consider an example where we have a data set containing information about housing prices, such as square footage and the number of bedrooms in each house. Given their income level, we would like to use this information to predict whether someone could afford to buy one of these houses. To do this, we could use a linear classifier such as logistic regression, which would fit our data set using linear equations and generate probabilities for each observation based on its values for square footage and number of bedrooms compared with other houses in the same price range (with higher scoring observations being more likely).

This probability score could then be used to predict whether someone could buy and afford one house from our given data set with different inputted variables such as income level or zip code area, for example. Through this method, we can generate probabilities about how likely a person will be able to afford specific properties based on different criteria, which helps us make more accurate decisions about potential homebuyers’ abilities without needing explicit programming instructions.

To understand how a linear classifier works, we need to introduce some mathematical notation. Let X be a vector of d features that describe an object, such as word frequencies in an email. Let y be a categorical variable that represents the class of the object, such as spam or not spam. Let K be the number of possible classes, and let w\_k be a vector of weights for class *k*. Then, the score for class k given X is

(8.10)

*s*[*k*](*X*) = *w*[*k*]^(*T*)*X*

The dot product is a way of measuring how similar two vectors are: it is high when the vectors point in the same direction and low when they point in opposite directions. The score *s*[*k*](*X*) based on its features.

The linear classifier then assigns X to the class with the highest score:

(8.11)

*y* = *a**r**g**m**a**x*(*k*)*s*[*k*](*X*),

where argmax (k) means finding the value of *k* that maximizes s[k] (X). This means that the ­linear ­classifier divides the feature space into regions separated by hyperplanes, where each region ­corresponds to one class. A hyperplane is a generalization of a line in 2D and a plane in 3D: it is a subspace of one dimension less than the original space that splits the space into two parts. For example, in 2D, a hyperplane is a line; in 3D, a hyperplane is a plane; and in 4D, a hyperplane is a 3D space.

There are different ways of learning the weights *w*\_*k* from a set of labeled training data. Some methods are based on generative models, which try to model the joint probability distribution of X and y; some methods are based on discriminative models, which try to model the conditional probability distribution of y given X; and some methods are based on optimization techniques, which try to minimize a loss function that measures the error between the predicted and true classes.

8.5.1Advantages and Disadvantages of Linear Classifiers

The advantage of linear classifiers is that they are simple and fast to train and use, especially when the number of features is large. They can also achieve high accuracy levels for many practical problems, such as document classification or image recognition, sentiment analysis, spam detection, etc. This means that linear classifiers can handle high-dimensional data efficiently, without requiring much computational resources or memory.

Another advantage is that they are easy to interpret and explain. The linear function that defines the decision boundary of a linear classifier can be written as a weighted sum of the features, where the weights indicate the importance or relevance of each feature for the classification task.

Linear classifiers are not only fast, simple, accurate and interpretable, but also flexible and adaptable. They can be extended and modified to suit different types of data and problems. For example, linear classifiers can be combined with non-linear transformations or kernels to handle data that is not linearly separable. Linear classifiers can also be regularized or penalized to prevent overfitting or underfitting, by adding a term to the objective function that controls the complexity or smoothness of the linear function. Linear classifiers can also be integrated with other ML ­techniques, such as ensemble methods, boosting, bagging, etc., to improve their robustness and diversity. They can also be adapted to different learning scenarios, such as online learning, ­active learning, semi-supervised learning, etc., by updating their weights incrementally or selectively based on new data or feedback.

However, linear classifiers also have some limitations. For example, they cannot capture complex non-linear relationships between features and categories, and they may be sensitive to outliers or noise in the data. Therefore, linear classifiers may not work well for problems that require more expressive models, such as image recognition, natural language generation, etc.

8.5.2Learning the Weights of a Linear Classifier

There are different methods to learn the weights of a linear classifier from a set of labeled training data. Some of these methods are generative models, which try to model the joint probability distribution of the features and the categories, and some are discriminative models, which try to model the conditional probability distribution of the categories given the features.

Examples of generative models:

Linear discriminant analysis (LDA): This method assumes that the features follow a Gaussian distribution within each category, and tries to find a linear projection that maximizes the separation between categories.

Naive Bayes classifier: This method assumes that the features are conditionally independent given the category, and tries to estimate the probability of each feature value for each category using frequency counts.

Examples of discriminative models:

Logistic regression: This method assumes that the score for each category is a logistic function of the feature values, and tries to maximize the likelihood of the observed data using gradient descent or other optimization techniques.

Perceptron: This method iteratively updates the weights based on the errors made on the training data, until no errors are made or a maximum number of iterations is reached.

Support Vector Machine (SVM): This method tries to find a hyperplane that separates the categories with a maximum margin, using quadratic programming or other optimization techniques

8.5.3Linear Discriminant Analysis

Linear discriminant analysis (LDA) is a method that aims to find a linear projection of a high-dimensional feature space onto a lower-dimensional space that maximizes the separation between different categories of data.

It is based on two assumptions: first, that the features follow a Gaussian distribution within each category; and second, that the covariance matrices of the features are equal across all categories. These assumptions imply that the data is linearly separable, meaning that a linear decision boundary can accurately separate the different categories.

LDA works by finding a set of linear discriminants, which are directions in the feature space that best separate the different categories. LDA does this by maximizing the ratio of between-class variance to within-class variance, which is also known as Fisher’s criterion. This ratio measures how well the projected data points are clustered by category and how far apart they are from each other.

Let us consider an example of two-dimensional data points belonging to two different categories. When we plot the data points on a two-dimensional plane, we can see that there is no straight line that can completely separate the two categories. However, if we apply LDA to this data, we can find a linear discriminant that projects the data points onto a one-dimensional line. On this line, we can see that the projected data points are more separated by category than on the original plane.

LDA is a widely used method for supervised learning that seeks to categorize data points into distinct groups according to their characteristics. An advantage of LDA lies in its straightforwardness and computational effectiveness. Estimating the mean and covariance of each class is the only requirement for LDA, which can be accomplished effortlessly using matrix operations. Next, it maps the data onto a lower-dimensional space to optimize the distinction between different classes. By reducing the dimensions and complexity of the problem, it becomes more expedient and effortless to solve.

To exemplify this benefit, let us contemplate a case of facial recognition. Assume we possess a data set comprising photographs of faces attributed to distinct individuals, and our objective is to determine the identity of each person depicted in the images. An approach to performing this task involves utilizing the unprocessed pixel values of each image as characteristics and then employing a classifier such as logistic regression or SVM. However, this strategy has several limitations. Initially, the quantity of factors is exceedingly vast, equivalent to the amount of pixels in every image. As a result, the issue becomes complex in terms of dimensions and requires significant processing resources. Furthermore, the unprocessed pixel values could fail to encompass the fundamental attributes of each face, such as its shape, color, texture, and so on. This exacerbates the issue, rendering it both cacophonous and intricate.

LDA can address these limitations by converting the original pixel information into a more significant and condensed representation. LDA accomplishes this by calculating the average and variance of each class (each individual’s face) based on the training data. The mean is a statistical measure representing the arithmetic average of each person’s face, while the covariance quantifies the extent to which each pixel deviates from the norm. The statistics encompass the primary attributes of each face, including its shape, color, texture, and so forth. Subsequently, LDA identifies a linear mapping that optimizes the distinction between classes by projecting the data into a space with fewer dimensions. This indicates that the projected data points are closer to the mean of their own class than the means of other classes. This simplifies the problem’s classification as the classes are more clearly defined and have less overlap.

The lower-dimensional space discovered by LDA is commonly called the discriminant space because of its ability to differentiate between distinct classes. The dimensionality of this space is equivalent to the number of classes subtracted by one. For instance, when our data set consists of 10 individuals, LDA will map the data onto a 9-dimensional space. The reduced feature space is significantly smaller than the original, which may include hundreds or millions of dimensions depending on the image resolution. This dramatically reduces the computing expense and intricacy of the task. Latent Dirichlet allocation (LDA) is a straightforward and effective method that can enhance the accuracy and efficiency of supervised learning tasks.

An advantage of LDA is its ability to address multicollinearity, which arises when certain variables exhibit a strong correlation, leading to instability and redundancy within the model. These factors can result in overfitting, limited ability to apply knowledge to new situations, and imprecise assessments of the significance of features. LDA addresses this problem using the pooled covariance matrix, a weighted mean of the covariance matrices particular to each class. The covariance matrix quantifies the extent to which each attribute exhibits variation about one another and their respective contributions to the separation of classes.

Another advantage of LDA is its ability to effectively handle scenarios when the number of features far exceeds the number of training samples. This phenomenon frequently occurs in data sets with a high number of dimensions, such as photos or text, where there exists a multitude of potential features to extract from the data but an insufficient number of data points to effectively learn from. LDA is suitable for this circumstance as it decreases the dimensionality of the data to align with the number of classes, preventing overfitting and enhancing generalization.

However, LDA has some limitations, as well. It is contingent upon certain assumptions that may not consistently apply in real-world situations. One of the underlying assumptions is that the data exhibits a Gaussian distribution characterized by a bell-shaped curve and symmetrical distribution around the mean. This assumption presupposes that the data lacks any outliers, skewness, or multimodality, all prevalent attributes in numerous data sets. Outliers have the potential to impact the mean and variance of the data, which are essential for LDA to compute the best linear discriminant..

Skewness quantifies the degree of asymmetry in the distribution of data. The skewness of the data can be either positive or negative, depending on whether the data exhibits a greater tail on the right or left side of the mean. Skewness can potentially impact the shape and position of the Gaussian curve that LDA assumes for each class.

Multimodality refers to the characteristic of data that exhibits many peaks or modes in its distribution. It suggests that the data exhibits the presence of many subgroups or clusters within each class. The presence of many modes can contradict the assumption made by LDA that each class follows unimodal Gaussian distribution.

LDA assumes that the covariance matrices of the features are equal across all categories, which means that the features have the same variability and correlation within each category. This assumption may not be realistic in some cases, where different categories may have different patterns of variation and dependence among the features.

LDA also assumes that the data is linearly separable, which means that there exists a linear boundary that can separate the data into different categories. This assumption may not hold for some complex data sets, where the data may have non-linear relationships or interactions among the features.

LDA may not perform well in high-dimensional feature spaces, where the number of features is much larger than the number of data points. In such cases, LDA may suffer from overfitting, which means that it fits too closely to the training data and fails to generalize to new data. Moreover, LDA may face computational challenges due to the large size of the covariance matrices and the eigenvalue decomposition involved in the algorithm. In such cases, other methods such as PCA may be more suitable.

8.5.4Naive Bayes Classifier

Naive Bayes classifier is a simple but powerful ML technique that can be used for classification tasks. It consists of two parts, namely, naive and Bayes.

Naive: It is so-called because it makes a simplifying assumption that the features used to predict the outcome are independent of each other, meaning that they do not influence or depend on each other in any way. This assumption is often unrealistic in real-world scenarios, but it allows the algorithm to be fast and easy to implement. For example, suppose we want to classify a fruit as either an apple or an orange based on its color, shape, and taste. A naive Bayes classifier would assume that these three features are independent of each other and that each one contributes equally to the probability of the fruit being an apple or an orange. So, if we observe a red, spherical, and sweet fruit, the classifier would multiply the probabilities of each feature given the class and compare them to decide which class is more likely. In this case, the fruit would be classified as an apple, since red, spherical, and sweet are more likely to occur in apples than in oranges. However, this assumption of independence may not always hold true in reality.

Bayes: It is based on the application of Bayes’ theorem, which states that the probability of an event A given another event B is equal to the probability of B given A multiplied by the probability of A divided by the probability of B. In other words, P(A|B) = P(B|A) \* P(A) / P(B).

In the context of classification, the event A is the category or class that we want to assign to an instance, and the event B is the set of features or attributes that describe the instance. For example, if we want to classify an email as spam or not spam based on its subject and sender, then A is the spam or not spam label, and B is the subject and sender information. The naive Bayes classifier tries to estimate the probability of each category given the features, P(A|B), and then chooses the category with the highest probability as the prediction.

However, estimating P(A|B) directly from the data can be difficult, especially if there are many features and categories. Therefore, the naive Bayes classifier makes a simplifying assumption that the features are conditionally independent given the category. This means that the probability of observing a certain combination of features given a category is equal to the product of the probabilities of each feature given that category.

For example, if we assume that the subject and sender are independent given the spam or not spam label, then P(subject and sender | spam) = P(subject | spam) \* P(sender | spam).

Using this assumption, we can rewrite Bayes’ theorem as follows:

P(A|B) = P(B|A) \* P(A) / P(B)

            = P(feature1 | A) \* P(feature2 | A) \*... \* P(featuren | A) \* P(A) / P(B)

We can estimate P(feature1 | A) and P(A) from the frequency counts of each feature value and category in the training data. For example, if we have 100 emails in total, 40 of them are spam and 60 are not spam, and 20 spam emails have the word ‘free’ in their subject while 10 not spam emails have it, then P(spam) = 40/100 = 0.4 and P(free | spam) = 20/40 = 0.5. We can also estimate P(B) by summing up the probabilities of all possible categories given B. For example, if we want to calculate P(free), we can use the following formula:

P(free) = P(free | spam) \* P(spam) + P(free | not spam) \* P(not spam)

            = 0.5 \* 0.4 + 0.1 \* 0.6 = 0.26

Once we have all these probabilities, we can plug them into Bayes’ theorem and compare the probabilities of different categories for a given instance. For example, if we want to classify an email with subject ‘free trial offer’ and sender ‘john@example.com’, we can calculate the following probabilities:

\= P(free trial offer and john@example.com | spam) \* P(spam) / P(free trial offer and john@example.com)

\= P(free trial offer | spam) \* P(john@example.com | spam) \* P(spam) / (P(free trial offer | spam) \* P(john@example.com | spam) \* P(spam) + P(free trial offer | not spam) \* P(john@example.com | not spam) \* P(not spam))

\= 0.5 \* 0.01 \* 0.4 / (0.5 \* 0.01 \* 0.4 + 0.1 \* 0.05 \* 0.6) = 0.25

\= P(free trial offer and john@example.com | not spam) \* P(not spam) / P(free trial offer and john@example.com)

\= P(free trial offer | not spam) \* P(john@example.com | not spam) \* P(not spam) / (P(free trial offer | spam) \* P(john@example.com | spam) \* P(spam) + P(free trial offer | not spam) \* P(john@example.com | not spam) \* P(not spam))

It leverages Bayes’ theorem to calculate the posterior probability of each candidate hypothesis and selects the one with the highest posterior probability. 8.5.4.1Bayes’ Optimal Classifier

Bayes’ theorem is used to calculate conditional probability. The same is used to determine the maximum a posteriori (MAP). The general question that arises is “What can be the most probable hypothesis?” or “What can be the most probable classification for a new instance?”. To answer these questions, Bayes’ optimal classifier is used.

Let the training set be represented as D and the test set be represented as V. Let v[i] ϵ V be an instance of the test data set *V*. The optimal classification for the new instance v[i] using Bayes’ optimal classifier is determined as

(8.12)

$\\left. \\begin{matrix} {\\arg\\max} \\\\ {v\_{i} \\in V} \\\\ \\end{matrix}\\sum\\limits\_{h\_{j} \\in H}P\\left( v\_{i} \\middle| h\_{j} \\right)P(h\_{j} \\middle| D) \\right.$

Consider three hypotheses h[1],h[2] ,h[3] with posterior probabilities 0.45, 0.3 and 0.25, respectively, where h[1] belongs to the positive class and h[2] and h[3] belongs to negative class. Since the posterior probability of h[1] is high, h[MAP] a new instance x is recognized as x ϵ h[1].

*P*(*h*[1]|*D*)=0.45;*P*(positive|*h*[1])=1;*P*(negative|h[1])=0

*P*(*h*[2]|*D*)=0.3;*P*(positive|*h*[2])=0;*P*(negative|*h*[2])=1

*P*(*h*[3]|*D*)=0.25;*P*(positive|*h*[3])=0;*P*(negative|*h*[3])=1

     $\\left. \\sum\\limits\_{h\_{i} \\in H}P\\left( {\\text{positive}\\left| h\_{i} \\right.} \\right)P(h\_{i} \\middle| D) = 0.45 \\right.$

     $\\left. \\sum\\limits\_{h\_{i} \\in H}P\\left( {\\text{negative}\\left| h\_{i} \\right.} \\right)P(h\_{i} \\middle| D) = 0.55 \\right.$

However, from Bayes’ optimal classifier, it can be determined as

$\\left. \\begin{matrix} {\\arg\\max} \\\\ {v\_{i} \\in V} \\\\ \\end{matrix}\\sum\\limits\_{h\_{j} \\in H}P\\left( v\_{i} \\middle| h\_{j} \\right)P(h\_{j} \\middle| D)\\Rightarrow\\begin{matrix} {\\arg\\max} \\\\ {v\_{i} \\in V} \\\\ \\end{matrix}\\left( {0.45,0.55} \\right) = 0.55 \\right.$

Bayes’ optimal classifier suggests that the new instance x belongs to the negative class.

8.5.4.2Bayesian Belief Networks

The naive Bayes classifier assumes that for the target value given, all the variables or attributes are conditionally independent, whereas Bayesian belief networks allow conditional independence over a subset of variables. A Bayesian belief network or simply Bayesian network provides the probability distribution over a set of variables.

Let X = (X[1], X[2],∙∙∙, X[n] ) denote a set of random variables where each X[i] ϵ V (X[i]). A Bayesian network is a directed acyclic graph that specifies a joint distribution over X as a product of conditional distributions on each node. It is represented as

(8.13)

$\\left. P\\left( {X\_{1} = x\_{1},X\_{2} = x\_{2},\\cdots,X\_{n} = x\_{n}} \\right) = \\prod\\limits\_{i = 1}^{n}p(x\_{i} \\middle| \\text{parents}\\left( x\_{i} \\right)) \\right.$

Consider a simple Bayesian network ([Fig. 8.10](#16_Chapter8.xhtml#fig8-10)).

![](Images/f8-10.jpg)

[Figure 8.10](#16_Chapter8.xhtml#fig-8-10)  Example of a simple Bayesian belief network

For a Bayesian network, there exist two components – a graphical structure to show the conditional independence assumptions and probability values for each variable given its parents. The directed edges represent the direct dependence. An absence of an edge between any two variables represents conditional independence.

If the graph is assumed as only three nodes A, B and C with no edge at all, it indicates that all the variables A, B and C are conditionally independent. In such case, the marginal independence is defined using joint probability distribution (cross-product rule of probability) as

P (A,B,C) = P (A)P (B)P (C)

Consider the Bayesian network where B and C are conditionally independent given A ([Fig. 8.11](#16_Chapter8.xhtml#fig8-11)).

![](Images/f8-11.jpg)

[Figure 8.11](#16_Chapter8.xhtml#fig-8-11)  Bayesian network where B and C are conditionally independent

P (A,B,C) = P(B|A)P(C|A)P (A)

For example, X has installed an alarm in his house to detect any theft that occurs in his absence. The alarm sometimes responds even if a pedestrian passes through the house. Y and Z are the neighbors of X and they assured him that they will call when the alarm rings ([Fig. 8.12](#16_Chapter8.xhtml#fig8-12)).

Thus, the Bayesian belief network is a directed acyclic graph representing the joint distribution. Inference or reasoning in this network enables efficient computation of the appropriate conditional probabilities.

8.5.4.3Expectation Maximization Algorithm

Expectation maximization (EM) and Bayesian belief networks (BBNs) are both powerful frameworks in the field of probabilistic modeling and statistical inference. EM is an iterative method used for finding maximum likelihood or MAP estimates of parameters in statistical models, where the model depends on unobserved latent variables. BBNs, on the other hand, are a type of probabilistic ­graphical model that represent a set of variables and their conditional dependencies through a ­directed acyclic graph. The relationship between EM and BBNs lies in the fact that EM can be used as a ­computational approach to perform efficient parameter estimation in complex BBNs, especially when dealing with incomplete data sets.

A data set contains two sets of variables, namely, observed and unobserved. The observed variables are those that are directly measured. The unobserved or hidden variables are those that are inferred from the observed variables. The hidden variables are also called latent variables. A model defined over a data set that has both observed and unobserved variables is said to be a latent variable model.

The EM algorithm can be used for many purposes like for predicting the missing values in the data set, find the local maximum likelihood parameters, etc.

Steps

Input: Incomplete data

Step 1: Initialization: Initialize all parameters with initial values. Then provide the incomplete data. We assume that the data comes from a probability distribution.

Step 2: Expectation: Guess the values of the missing data based on the observed data.

Step 3: Maximization: Complete the data generated in the Expectation step to update the values of the parameters.

Step 4: Check for Convergence: If the values are not converged, go to Step 2 and repeat until convergence occurs.

Assume that there are two coins, C1 and C2. The probability of getting heads with C1 is θ[1] and the probability of getting heads with C2 is θ[2] We have to find the values of θ[1] and θ[2] by performing various experiments.

Let each coin be tossed 10 times and we choose to repeat the experiment 5 times. The outcome for each coin in every trail is given in [Table 8.19](#16_Chapter8.xhtml#tab8-19).
