13.4.1Popular Python Packages

A package is a folder that contains several modules, which are files that contain Python code. A package can also have sub-packages, which are folders inside a package. To use a package, we need to import it or its modules. Some of the most common packages in Python are:

•pandas: This package provides data structures and tools for data analysis. It allows us to manipulate, filter, group, aggregate, and visualize data in tabular or multidimensional formats. It also supports reading and writing data from various sources, such as CSV, Excel, SQL, and JSON.

•NumPy: This package provides numerical computing tools for Python. It allows us to work with arrays, matrices, linear algebra, random numbers, statistics, and more. It also supports broadcasting, vectorization, and integration with other packages, such as pandas and Matplotlib.

•matplotlib.pyplot: This package provides plotting and visualization tools for Python. It allows us to create various types of graphs, such as line plots, bar charts, histograms, scatter plots, and pie charts. It also supports customization of colors, styles, labels, legends, axes, etc.

•sklearn: This package provides ML tools for Python. It allows us to perform tasks such as classification, regression, clustering, dimensionality reduction, feature extraction, model selection, and evaluation. It also supports various algorithms, such as linear models, decision trees, support vector machines, neural networks, etc.

•seaborn: This package provides statistical data visualization tools for Python. It builds on top of matplotlib.pyplot and pandas to create attractive and informative plots. It also supports categorical data analysis, distribution analysis, correlation analysis, regression analysis, etc.

•TensorFlow: This package provides deep learning tools for Python. It allows us to build and train neural networks using tensors, which are multidimensional arrays of data. It also supports various operations, such as activation functions, loss functions, optimizers, metrics, etc. It also supports GPU acceleration and distributed computing.

•IPython: This package provides an interactive shell for Python. It allows us to execute Python code interactively and dynamically. It also supports features such as syntax highlighting, auto-completion, debugging, profiling, magic commands, etc. It also integrates with other packages, such as NumPy and matplotlib.pyplot.

[Table 13.1](#21_Chapter13.xhtml#tab13-1) lists the popular Python packages.

[Table 13.1](#21_Chapter13.xhtml#tab-13-1) Popular packages of the Python language

 
| S. No || Package name || Features |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 || pandas || Data structures and tools for data analysis |
| 2 || numpy || Numerical computing tools for Python |
| 3 || matplotlib.pyplot || Plotting and visualization tools for Python |
| 4 || sklearn || Machine learning tools for Python |
| 5 || seaborn || Statistical data visualization tools for Python |
| 6 || TensorFlow || Deep learning tools for Python |

13.4.2Installing Packages using Anaconda Navigator

Installing packages through Anaconda Navigator is easy and convenient. Here are the steps to be followed:

1.Launch Anaconda Navigator from your Start menu or desktop shortcut.

2.Select the environment in which you want to install the package ([Fig. 13.2](#21_Chapter13.xhtml#fig13-2)). You can create a new environment by clicking the “Create” button at the bottom of the list.

3.Click on the “Home” tab and then on the “Install” button next to the package name. You can search for a package by typing its name in the search box. (Example: sklearn)

4.Wait for the installation to complete. You can see the progress and status of the installation in the “conda” tab.

5.To verify that the package is installed, you can open a terminal (Spyder) or a Jupyter notebook in the same environment and import the package.

13.4.3Opening Spyder from Anaconda Navigator

Spyder is an integrated development environment (IDE) for Python that comes with Anaconda Navigator. To open the Spyder terminal from Anaconda Navigator, you need to follow these steps:

1.Launch Anaconda Navigator from your Start menu or desktop shortcut. You should see a window with several icons for different applications, such as Jupyter Notebook, RStudio, VS Code and Spyder ([Fig. 13.1](#21_Chapter13.xhtml#fig13-1)).

2.Click on the Spyder icon. You should see a button that says “Launch” below the icon. If you have multiple versions of Spyder installed, you can choose which one to launch from the drop-down menu next to the button.

3.Click the “Launch” button and wait for Spyder to open. You should see a window with four panes: the editor, the console, the variable explorer, and the help viewer.

4.To open a terminal in Spyder, go to the menu bar and click on Tools > Open a Terminal. Alternatively, you can use the keyboard shortcut Ctrl+Alt+T (Windows) or Cmd+Alt+T (Mac).

5.A new tab with a terminal prompt ([Fig. 13.3](#21_Chapter13.xhtml#fig13-3)) should appear in the console pane. This terminal can run commands, install packages, and interact with the Python environment.

![](Images/f13-3.jpg)

[Figure 13.3](#21_Chapter13.xhtml#fig-13-3)  Spyder terminal

A brief explanation of some of the main menus of the Spyder terminal is given below:

•File: This menu allows users to create, open, save, close, print, and run Python files. It also has options to switch projects, restart the kernel, and quit Spyder.

•Edit: This menu lets the user edit the code, such as undo, redo, cut, copy, paste, delete, comment, indent, format, and refactor. It also has options to find and replace text, go to a specific line or definition, and manage bookmarks.

•Source: This menu provides tools to analyze and execute the code, such as code completion, linting, debugging, profiling, testing, and running cells. It also has options to show or hide the outline explorer, the code analysis pane, and the code folding indicators.

•Run: This menu allows the user to run the current file or a selected configuration in different ways, such as in a new dedicated console, in an external system terminal, or with command-line arguments. It also has options to configure the run settings, such as the working directory, the environment variables, and the interpreter.

•Debug: This menu lets users debug the code using breakpoints, conditional breakpoints, watches, and commands. It also has options to show or hide the debugger toolbar and the variable explorer.

•Consoles: This menu provides access to different types of consoles for interactive coding, such as Python consoles, IPython consoles, and system terminals. It also has options to connect to an existing kernel, open a particular console (such as a Qt or Spyder), and manage the console settings.

•Projects: This menu allows users to create, open, close, delete, and import projects. A project is a way of organizing files and settings for a specific task or purpose. It also has options to edit the project properties, such as the name, location, dependencies, and PYTHONPATH.

•Tools: This menu offers various tools and utilities for enhancing the user experience, such as preferences, keyboard shortcuts, online help, an internal console, a dependency manager, a module explorer, and online documentation. It also has options to update Spyder and report issues.

•View: This menu enables the user to customize the appearance and layout of the Spyder terminal. It can show or hide toolbars and panes (such as editor, console, help), zoom in or out of the text size, toggle fullscreen or windowed mode (for macOS), and switch between preset layouts.

•Help: This menu provides access to different sources of information and support for the Spyder terminal. It has options to show the tutorial (for beginners), Spyder documentation (for advanced users), FAQ (for common questions), and the About dialog box (for credits and license).

13.4.4Basic Data Types in Python

Python has five standard data types:

•Number

•String

•List

•Tuple

•Dictionary

Python variables do not need explicit declaration to reserve memory space. The declaration happens automatically when you assign a value to a variable. The equal to (=) sign is used to assign values to variables. The operand to the left of = is the name of the variable and the operand to the right of = is the value stored in the variable.

For example:

\>>> var1 = 24

\>>> var2 = 28.72

\>>> var3 = "Machine Learning"

\>>> type(var1)

Out\[38\]: int

\>>> print(var1)

24

\>>> type(var2)

Out\[39\]: float

\>>> print(var2)

28.72

\>>> type(var3)

Out\[40\]: str

\>>> print(var3)

Machine Learning

Python variables can be easily typecast from one data type to another by using the data type name as a function (actually a wrapper class) and passing the variable to be typecast as a parameter. However, not all data types can be transformed into another; for example, String to Integer/Number is impossible.

\>>> var2 = int(var2)

\>>> print (var2)

28

\>>> type (var2)

Out\[42\]: int

13.4.5The for and while Loops and the if-else Statement

The for loop

Syntax:

for i in range(<lowerbound>,<upperbound>,<interval>):

    print(i\*i)

For example, to print the squares of all integers from 1 to 4.

for i in range(1,5):

    print(i\*i)

1

4

9

16

for i in range(1,20,5):

    print(i)

1

6

11

16

The while loop

Syntax:

while < condition>:

    <do something>

For example, to print the cubes of all integers from 1 to 3.

i = 1

while i < 4:

    print(i\*i\*i)

    i = i + 1

1

8

27

The if-else statement

Syntax:

if < condition>:

    <do something>

else:

      <do something else>

For example, to print the squares of a number if it is negative. If it is a positive number, then print the number.

i = -5

if i < 0:

    print(i\*i)

else:

    print(i)

25

13.4.6Writing Functions

Syntax:

def functionname(parametername,…):

    (function\_body)

For example, for a function to calculate the factorial of an input number n.

def factorial(n):

    fact = 1

    for i in range(1,n+1):

        fact = fact\*i

    return(fact);

k = factorial (4)

print (k)

24

13.4.8Using Spyder to Write Python Programs

We will use the Spyder terminal to write all our ML programs. The Spyder terminal ([Fig. 13.3](#21_Chapter13.xhtml#fig13-3)) is a tool that allows users to write and run Python programs in an interactive environment. It consists of two main panes: the editor pane and the console pane. The editor pane, located on the left-hand side of the terminal, is where users can write Python code using various features such as syntax highlighting, code completion, and debugging. The console pane, located on the right-hand side of the terminal, is divided into two sub-panes: the plot pane and the I/O pane. The plot pane, located at the top-right corner of the terminal, is where users can see the graphical output of their Python programs, such as charts, graphs, and images. The I/O pane, located at the bottom-right corner of the terminal, is where users can see the terminal output of their Python programs, such as print statements, errors, and warnings. The I/O pane can also be used to enter terminal inputs for the Python programs, such as command-line arguments or user inputs.

[13.5Data Operations on the Iris Data Set](#07_Contents.xhtml#sub-153)

The Iris data set is a classic that contains information about three different species of iris flowers: setosa, versicolor, and virginia. Each species has 50 observations of four features: sepal length, sepal width, petal length, and petal width, all measured in centimeters. The statistician Ronald Fisher introduced the data set in 1936 as an example of linear discriminant analysis.

This data set is available from various sources, such as the UCI Machine Learning Repository, Kaggle, scikit-learn, and more. It may have different formats, such as CSV, JSON, pickle, or Python objects, depending on the source.

To download the data set for free, we can use one of the following methods:

•From the UCI Machine Learning Repository: Go to [https://archive.ics.uci.edu/ml/datasets/Iris](https://archive.ics.uci.edu/ml/datasets/Iris) and click “Data Folder.” Then download the file “iris.data” which contains the comma-separated values of the data set. Optionally, download the file “iris.names,” which includes the description of the data set.

•From Kaggle: Go to [https://www.kaggle.com/uciml/iris](https://www.kaggle.com/uciml/iris) and click “Download (4 KB)”. Then unzip the file “iris.zip,” which contains the CSV file “Iris.csv” with the data set.

•From scikit-learn: Use the Python library scikit-learn, which provides a function to load the Iris data set as a Python object. To do this, import the module sklearn and call the function load\_iris().

13.5.1Read the Iris Data Set and Display the First Five Rows

\# This line imports the pandas library and gives it the alias pd

import pandas as pd

\# This line reads a CSV file named iris.csv and stores it in a variable called data

data = pd.read\_csv("iris.csv")

\# This line assigns new names to the columns of the data

data.columns = \['Sepal\_Length','Sepal\_Width','Petal\_Length','Petal\_Width','Class'\]

#This line displays the first five rows of the data

display (data.head())

The above program is a Python script that uses the pandas library to load and manipulate the data set contained in iris.csv. The program first imports the pandas library as pd, which is a common alias for pandas. Then, it uses the pd.read\_csv() function to read the iris.csv file and store it in a variable called data. The data variable is a pandas DataFrame, which is a two-dimensional data structure that can store data in rows and columns. The program then assigns new names to the columns of the DataFrame using the data.columns attribute. The new names are Sepal\_Length, Sepal\_Width, Petal\_Length, Petal\_Width, and Class. These names are more descriptive and follow the Python naming convention of using underscores instead of spaces. Finally, the program uses the display() function to show the last five rows of the DataFrame. The display() function is a built-in function, which is an interactive environment for running Python code. It can show the DataFrame in a tabular format with colors and borders. The display (data.head()) function shows the first five rows of the DataFrame.

| 2 || 4.6 || 3.1 || 1.5 || 0.2 || Iris-setosa |
| 3 || 5.0 || 3.6 || 1.4 || 0.2 || Iris-setosa |
| 4 || 5.4 || 3.9 || 1.7 || 0.4 || Iris-setosa |

[13.6Finding Outliers](#07_Contents.xhtml#sub-154)

def find\_outlier(ds,col):

quart1 = ds\[col\].quantile(0.25)

quart3 = ds\[col\].quantile(0.75)

IQR = quart3 – quart1 #Inter-quartile range

low\_val = quart1 – 1.5\*IQR

high\_val = quart3 + 1.5\*IQR

ds = ds.loc\[(ds\[col\] < low\_val) | (ds\[col\] > high\_val)\]

return ds

We want to write a function to find the outliers in a data set: def find\_outlier(ds, col). This function takes a data set (ds) and a column name (col) as input parameters. It returns a subset of the data set that contains only the outlier values in the given column. Outliers are defined as values that are more than 1.5 times the interquartile range (IQR) away from the first or third quartile. The IQR is the difference between the 75th percentile (quart3) and the 25th percentile (quart1) of the column values. The first quartile is calculated by calling the quantile() method on the column with 0.25 as the argument. The third quartile is calculated by calling the quantile() method on the column with 0.75 as the argument. The lower bound for outliers (low\_val) is computed by subtracting 1.5 times the IQR from the first quartile. The upper bound for outliers (high\_val) is computed by adding 1.5 times the IQR to the third quartile. The loc() method is used to filter the data set by selecting only the rows where the column value is less than low\_val or greater than high\_val. The filtered data set is returned as the output of the function.

[13.7Removing Outliers](#07_Contents.xhtml#sub-155)

def remove\_outlier(ds,col):

quart1 = ds\[col\].quantile(0.25)

quart3 = ds\[col\].quantile(0.75)

IQR = quart3 – quart1 #Inter-quartile range

low\_val = quart1 – 1.5\*IQR

high\_val = quart3 + 1.5\*IQR

df\_out = ds.loc\[(ds\[col\] > low\_val) & (ds\[col\] < high\_val)\]

df\_out.dropna(axis=0, how = 'any')

return df\_out

The program is a function that takes two arguments: a data set (ds) and a column name (col). The function aims to remove the outliers from the given column of the data set using the interquartile range (IQR) method. The function performs the following steps.

It calculates the first quartile (quart1) and the third quartile (quart3) of the column values using the quantile() method. It computes the IQR as the difference between the third and the first quartiles. It defines the lower and upper bounds for the outliers as 1.5 times the IQR below and above the first and third quartiles, respectively. It filters out the rows of the data set that have column values within the lower and upper bounds using the loc() method and assigns them to a new DataFrame (df\_out). It drops any rows that have missing values in any column using the dropna() method. It returns the new DataFrame (df\_out) that contains only the non-outlier values of the given column. [Table 13.2](#21_Chapter13.xhtml#tab13-2) lists various functions related to removing rows.

[Table 13.2](#21_Chapter13.xhtml#tab-13-2)Various functions related to removing rows

 
| S.No || Function || Explanation |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 || data = data.drop\_duplicates() || Removing duplicate rows |
| 2 || data = data.dropna(axis = 0, how = 'all') || Removing all rows where the values of any columns are NaN |
| 3 || data = data.dropna(axis = 1, how = 'all') || Removing all columns where the values of any rows are NaN |
| 4 || data = data.dropna(axis = 0, how = 'any') || Removing all rows where the values of any columns are NaN |
| 5 || data = data.dropna(axis = 1, how = 'any') || Removing all columns where the values of any row are NaN |

[13.8Imputing Null Values](#07_Contents.xhtml#sub-156)

def impute\_nullvalues(ds,col):

hp\_mean = np.mean(data\[col\])

imputedrows = data\[data\[col\].isnull()\]

imputedrows = imputedrows.replace(np.nan, hp\_mean)

#Then the portion of the data set not having any missing row is kept apart.

missval\_removed\_rows = data.dropna(subset=\[col\])

\# Then join back the imputed rows and the remaining part of the data set.

data\_mod = pd.concat (\[missval\_removed\_rows, imputedrows\])

\# data\_mod = missval\_removed\_rows.append(imputedrows, ignore\_index=True)

return data\_mod

After removing the outliers, we can work on replacing the null values in a column with the mean value of that column using the function, impute\_nullvalues(ds, col). This function takes a data set (ds) and a column name (col) as arguments. It returns a modified data set where the missing values in the column are replaced by the mean of the non-missing values.

First, it calculates the mean of the non-missing values in the column using NumPy: hp\_mean = np.mean(data\[col\]). Then, it creates a subset of the data set where the column has missing values using pandas: imputedrows = data\[data\[col\].isnull()\]. Next, it replaces the missing values with the mean value using pandas: imputedrows = imputedrows.replace(np.nan, hp\_mean). Then, it creates another subset of the data set where the column does not have missing values using pandas: missval\_removed\_rows = data.dropna(subset=\[col\]). Finally, it concatenates the two subsets to form the modified data set using pandas: data\_mod = pd.concat (\[missval\_removed\_rows, imputedrows\]).

Alternatively, it can also use the append() method to join the two subsets: data\_mod = missval\_removed\_rows.append(imputedrows, ignore\_index=True). It returns the modified data set as the output of the function: return data\_mod.

[13.9Capping the Outlier Values](#07_Contents.xhtml#sub-157)

def cap\_outlier(ds, col):

outliers = find\_outlier(ds,col)

quart1 = data\[col\].quantile(0.25)

quart3 = data\[col\].quantile(0.75)

IQR = quart3 – quart1 #Getting the value of IQR

outliers.loc\[:, col\] = 1.5\*IQR # Capping the outlier values with 1.5 times IQR value…

outlier\_removed\_rows = remove\_outlier(data,col)

data\_mod = pd.concat (\[outlier\_removed\_rows, outliers\])

#data\_mod = outlier\_removed\_rows.append(outliers, ignore\_index=True)

return data\_mod

This function takes a data set (ds) and a column name (col) as inputs. It returns a modified data set where the outliers in the given column are capped. Capping means replacing the outlier values with a certain threshold value. This can help reduce the effect of outliers on the analysis of the data.

outliers = find\_outlier(ds, col)

This line calls another function to find the outliers in the column.

quart1 = data\[col\].quantile(0.25)

This line calculates the first quartile of the column, which is the median of the lower half of the data.

quart3 = data\[col\].quantile(0.75)

This line calculates the third quartile of the column, which is the median of the upper half of the data. IQR = quart3 - quart1. This line calculates the interquartile range (IQR), which is the difference between the third and first quartiles.

outliers.loc\[:, col\] = 1.5\*IQR

This line replaces the outlier values with 1.5 times the IQR value, which is a common way to cap outliers.

outlier\_removed\_rows = remove\_outlier(data, col)

This line calls another function to remove the rows that contain outliers from the original data set.

data\_mod = pd.concat (\[outlier\_removed\_rows, outliers\])

This line concatenates (joins) the data set without outliers and the capped outliers into a new data set.

data\_mod = outlier\_removed\_rows.append(outliers, ignore\_index=True)

This line is commented out, which means it is not executed. It is another way to join the two data sets, but it would ignore the original index of the rows. return data\_mod. This line returns the modified data set as the output of the function.

[13.10Splitting the Data into Training and Testing Data](#07_Contents.xhtml#sub-158)

Splitting the data into training and testing data is a common practice in ML. The main reason for this is to evaluate the performance and generalization ability of the model. The training data fits the model parameters, while the testing data measures how well the model can predict new and unseen data. By splitting the data, we can avoid overfitting, where the model learns too much from the training data and fails to generalize to new data.

The advantages of splitting the data are as follows:

•It allows us to estimate the accuracy and error rate of the model on new data, which is essential for choosing the best model and tuning its hyperparameters.

•It helps us detect and prevent overfitting, leading to poor performance and unreliable predictions.

•It enables us to compare different models and algorithms based on their test results, which can help us to select the most suitable one for our problem.

•It provides us with a way to validate our assumptions and hypotheses about the data and the model, which can improve our understanding and interpretation of the results.

\# Splitting the data into Traing and Test data

X\_train, X\_test, Y\_train, Y\_test = train\_test\_split(X\_scaled, Y, test\_size = 0.2, random\_state = 42)

\# The parameter, test\_size sets the ratio of test data to the input data to 0.2 or 20% and random\_state sets

\# the seed for random number generator

This program uses the train\_test\_split() function from the sklearn.model\_selection module to split the data into training and testing sets. The function takes four arguments: X\_scaled, Y, test\_size and random\_state. X\_scaled is the input data that has been scaled to have zero mean and unit variance. Y is the output data or the target variable. test\_size is a float value between 0 and 1 that specifies the proportion of the data to be used as the testing set. In this case, test\_size is set to 0.2, which means that 20% of the data will be used for testing and the remaining 80% will be used for training. random\_state is an integer value that sets the seed for the random number generator that shuffles the data before splitting. By setting random\_state to a fixed value, such as 42, we can ensure that the same split is reproduced every time we run the program. The function returns four values: X\_train, X\_test, Y\_train and Y\_test. These are the input and output data for the training and testing sets, respectively.

[13.11Training and Evaluating the Model](#07_Contents.xhtml#sub-159)

We must train and evaluate the model in ML to ensure it performs well on new and unseen data. Training the model involves finding the optimal parameters that minimize the loss function on a given training data set. Evaluating the model consists of measuring the model’s performance on a separate validation or testing data set that was not used for training.

The advantages of training and evaluating the model are as follows:

•Training the model allows us to learn from the data and discover the patterns or relationships that can be used for prediction or inference.

•Evaluating the model allows us to assess how well the model generalizes to new data and avoid overfitting or underfitting problems.

•Training and evaluating the model can help us compare different models or algorithms and select the best one for our task or problem.

•Training and evaluating the model can help us improve the model by tuning the hyperparameters, adding regularization, or using more data.

\# Training the logistic regression model

model = LogisticRegression()

model.fit(X\_train, Y\_train)

\# making predictions on the test set

Y\_pred=model.predict(X\_test)

\# Evaluating the model performance

from sklearn.metrics import accuracy\_score, confusion\_matrix, classification\_report

print (accuracy\_score(Y\_test, Y\_pred)) # 1.0

print (confusion\_matrix(Y\_test, Y\_pred)) # \[\[1 0 0 0\] \[0 9 0\] \[0 0 11\]\]

print (classification\_report(Y\_test, Y\_pred))

The above program is an example of how to use logistic regression to classify data into three classes. The program performs the following steps:

1.It imports the LogisticRegression class from the sklearn.linear\_model module and creates an instance of it called model.

2.It uses the fit method of the model to train it on the training data, which consists of two arrays: X\_train and Y\_train. X\_train contains the input features for each sample, and Y\_train contains the corresponding class labels (0, 1 or 2).

3.It uses the predict() method of the model to make predictions on the test data, which is another array called X\_test. The predictions are stored in an array called Y\_pred.

4.It evaluates the model performance by using various metrics from the sklearn.metrics module.

5.It imports the accuracy\_score, confusion\_matrix, and classification\_report functions and prints their results.

The accuracy\_score() function returns the fraction of correct predictions, which is 1.0 in this case. The confusion\_matrix() function returns a matrix that shows how many samples were correctly or incorrectly classified by each class. The diagonal elements represent the true positives, while the off-diagonal elements represent the false positives and false negatives. The classification\_report function returns a text report that summarizes the precision, recall, f1-score and support for each class. Precision is the ratio of true positives to all predicted positives, recall is the ratio of true positives to all actual positives, F1-score is the harmonic mean of precision and recall, and support is the number of samples in each class.

[13.12Regularization Techniques that Prevent Overfitting](#07_Contents.xhtml#sub-160)

Regularization techniques are methods that modify the learning algorithm or the model to reduce the complexity and prevent overfitting. Regularization techniques can help avoid overfitting by adding constraints or penalties to the model parameters, such as shrinking them towards zero or limiting their magnitude. Some examples of regularization techniques are L1 and L2 regularization, dropout, early stopping, and data augmentation.

Different factors, such as the performance gap between the training and validation sets, the model’s complexity, the data’s size and quality, and the domain knowledge of the problem, can indicate the regularization technique to be used.

Ridge and LASSO are both regularization techniques that help prevent overfitting in linear regression models. Here is a Python program that demonstrates these regularization techniques:

\# Import necessary libraries

import numpy as np

import pandas as pd

from sklearn.linear\_model import Ridge, Lasso

from sklearn.model\_selection import train\_test\_split

from sklearn.metrics import mean\_squared\_error

\# Load the dataset

data = pd.read\_csv('data.csv')

print(data.shape)

data.head()

\# Checking for any null values in dataset

data.isnull().sum()

\# Split the dataset into training and testing sets

X\_train, X\_test, y\_train, y\_test = train\_test\_split(data.drop('target', axis=1), data \['target'\], test\_size=0.2, random\_state=42)

\# Ridge Regression

ridge = Ridge(alpha=0.5)

ridge.fit(X\_train, y\_train)

\# Lasso Regression

lasso = Lasso(alpha=0.5)

lasso.fit(X\_train, y\_train)

\# Evaluate the models

ridge\_pred = ridge.predict(X\_test)

lasso\_pred = lasso.predict(X\_test)

ridge\_mse = mean\_squared\_error(y\_test, ridge\_pred)

lasso\_mse = mean\_squared\_error(y\_test, lasso\_pred)

print("Ridge MSE:", ridge\_mse)

print("Lasso MSE:", lasso\_mse)

Output:

\# Ridge MSE: 0.034

\# Lasso MSE: 0.041

In this program, we first import the necessary libraries. Then we load the data set and split it into training and testing sets using the train\_test\_split function. We then create the ridge and LASSO regression models with the alpha value set to 0.5. We fit these models to the training data and predict the target values for the test set. Finally, we evaluate the models using mean squared error (MSE) and print the results.

The output of the ML program indicates that the ridge regression model has a lower mean squared error (MSE) than the LASSO regression model. This means that the ridge model has a better fit to the data and is less likely to overfit than the lasso model. The ridge model penalizes the coefficients of the features by adding their squared values to the loss function, while the LASSO model penalizes them by adding their absolute values. The LASSO model can shrink some coefficients to zero, resulting in feature selection, but it can also introduce bias and variance. The ridge model preserves all the features, but it can also reduce their impact on the prediction. Therefore, the choice of the regularization parameter (alpha) is crucial for both models, as it determines the trade-off between bias and variance. A cross-validation technique can be used to find the optimal alpha value that minimizes the MSE for both models.

[13.14Implement Logistic Regression](#07_Contents.xhtml#sub-162)

\# Python Program to Implement Logistic Regression

\# First, we import necessary libraries

import numpy as np

import pandas as pd

from sklearn.model\_selection import train\_test\_split

from sklearn.linear\_model import LogisticRegression

from sklearn import metrics

import seaborn as sn

\# Load the dataset

\# Data set does not contain the harder and hence the header is given here

col\_names = \['pregnant', 'glucose', 'bp', 'skin', 'insulin', 'bmi', 'pedigree', 'age', 'label'\]

data = pd.read\_csv('diabetes.csv', header=None, names=col\_names)

print(data.shape)

data.head()

\# Checking for any null values in dataset

data.isnull().sum()

\# Assigning dependent and independent variables

feature\_cols = \['pregnant', 'insulin', 'bmi', 'age', 'glucose', 'bp', 'pedigree'\]

x=data\[feature\_cols\]

y=data.label

\# splitting the dataset into Training and Testing Dataset

x\_train, x\_test, y\_train, y\_test = train\_test\_split(x,y, test\_size=0.2, random\_state=5)

display(x\_train.shape, y\_train.shape, x\_test.shape, y\_test.shape)

\# Fitting the Model (Logistic Regression)

model=LogisticRegression(solver= 'lbfgs', max\_iter=1000)

model.fit(x\_train, y\_train)

y\_pred=model.predict(x\_test)

\# Evaluation Metrics

conf\_mat=metrics.confusion\_matrix(y\_test, y\_pred)

print('Confusion Matrix:', conf\_mat)

Accuracy\_score=metrics.accuracy\_score(y\_test, y\_pred)

print('Accuracy Score:', Accuracy\_score)

print('Accuracy in Percentage:', int(Accuracy\_score\*100), '%')

conf\_mat=pd.crosstab(y\_test, y\_pred, rownames=\['Actual'\],

colnames=\['Predicted'\])

sn.heatmap(conf\_mat, annot=True)

The above program is an example of how to implement logistic regression. The program performs the following steps:

1.First, it imports the necessary libraries, such as NumPy, pandas, sklearn, metrics and seaborn, which provide various functions and tools for data manipulation, model building, evaluation and visualization.

2.It loads the data set from a csv file, which contains information about diabetes patients. The data set has nine columns, which are named as pregnant, glucose, bp, skin, insulin, bmi, pedigree, age, and label. The label column indicates whether the patient has diabetes (1) or not (0).

3.The program prints the shape of the data set, which is (768, 9), and displays the first five rows using the head() method. Then, it checks for any null values in the data set using the isnull().sum() method, which returns zero for all columns, indicating that there are no missing values.

4.After that, it assigns the dependent and independent variables for the logistic regression model. The dependent variable is the label column, which is stored in y. The independent variables are the other eight columns, which are stored in x. The program selects only seven of them as feature columns, which are pregnant, insulin, bmi, age, glucose, bp and pedigree. These are the variables that are used to predict the label.

5.Next, it splits the data set into training and testing sets using the train\_test\_split() function from sklearn. The test size is set to 0.2, which means that 20% of the data will be used for testing and 80% for training. The random state is set to 5, which means that the data will be shuffled in a fixed way before splitting. The function returns four arrays: x\_train, x\_test, y\_train and y\_test, which are the features and labels for the training and testing sets, respectively.

6.The program displays the shapes of these arrays using the shape attribute. Then, it fits the logistic regression model using the LogisticRegression() class from sklearn. The solver parameter is set to lbfgs, which is an algorithm for optimizing the model parameters. The max\_iter parameter is set to 1000, which is the maximum number of iterations for the solver to converge. The program creates an instance of the class called model and calls the fit() method on it with x\_train and y\_train as arguments. This trains the model on the training data.

7.Next, it makes predictions on the testing data using the predict() method of the model with x\_test as argument. This returns an array of predicted labels called y\_pred.

8.Finally, it evaluates the performance of the model using various metrics from sklearn. It calculates and prints the confusion matrix using the confusion\_matrix() function with y\_test and y\_pred as arguments.

The confusion matrix shows how many true positives (TP), true negatives (TN), false positives (FP) and false negatives (FN) were predicted by the model. It also calculates and prints the accuracy score using the accuracy\_score() function with y\_test and y\_pred as arguments. The accuracy score is the ratio of correctly predicted labels to the total number of labels. It also prints the accuracy score in percentage by multiplying it by 100 and converting it to an integer. It also creates a cross-tabulation table of actual and predicted labels using pandas’ crosstab() function with y\_test and y\_pred as arguments. It then plots a heatmap of this table using seaborn’s heatmap() function with annot=True as argument. This shows how well the model predicted each class.

It also calculates and prints the accuracy score using the accuracy\_score() function, which shows how many predictions were correct out of all predictions. It converts the accuracy score to percentage by multiplying it by 100 and rounding it to an integer. import pandas as pd

from sklearn.model\_selection import train\_test\_split

from sklearn.svm import SVC

from sklearn.metrics import classification\_report

from sklearn import metrics

import seaborn as sn

from IPython.display import display

\# Next, we need to load our data set into a pandas DataFrame.

\# This data set will be used for training our SVM model.

\# Load data set

col\_names = \['pregnant', 'glucose', 'bp', 'skin', 'insulin',

'bmi', 'pedigree', 'age', 'label'\]

data = pd.read\_csv('diabets.csv', header= None,

names=col\_names)

print(data.shape)

data.head()

\# Checking for any null values in data set

data.isnull().sum()

\# Assigning dependent and independent variables

feature\_cols = \['pregnant','insulin', 'bmi', 'age','glucose','bp', 'pedigree'\]

x=data\[feature\_cols\]

y=data.label

\# Once we have loaded the data set, we need to split it into training and testing sets. # We will be using 70% of the data for training and 30% for testing.

x\_train, x\_test, y\_train, y\_test = train\_test\_split(x,y, test\_size=0.3, random\_state=5)

display(x\_train.shape, y\_train.shape, x\_test.shape,y\_test.shape)

\# Preprocessing data with StandardScale

from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler

sc = StandardScaler()

x\_train=sc.fit\_transform(x\_train)

x\_test=sc.transform(x\_test)

\# Create SVM instance and fit to training data

model= SVC(kernel='rbf',random\_state=0)

model.fit(x\_train, y\_train)

svc\_prediction=model.predict(x\_test)

print('svc\_prediction: ', svc\_prediction)

\# Evaluation metrics for 'rbf' kernel

conf\_mat\_rbf = metrics.confusion\_matrix(y\_test, svc\_prediction)

print('SVC \[kernel - rbf\]')

print('Confusion Matrix: \\n', conf\_mat\_rbf)

accuracy\_score\_rbf = metrics.accuracy\_score(y\_test, svc\_prediction)

print('Accuracy Score: ', accuracy\_score\_rbf)

print('Accuracy in Percentage: ', int(accuracy\_score\_rbf \* 100), '%')

print(classification\_report(y\_test, svc\_prediction))

\# Visualization of confusion matrix for 'rbf' kernel

conf\_mat\_rbf\_vis = pd.crosstab(y\_test, svc\_prediction, rownames=\['Actual'\], colnames=\['Predicted'\])

sn.heatmap(conf\_mat\_rbf\_vis, annot=True).set(title='SVC \[rbf\]')

\# Fitting the model (SVM) using 'linear' kernel

model\_linear = SVC(kernel='linear', random\_state=0)

model\_linear.fit(x\_train, y\_train)

svc\_prediction\_linear = model\_linear.predict(x\_test)

print('svc\_prediction\_linear: ', svc\_prediction\_linear)

\# Evaluation metrics for 'linear' kernel

conf\_mat\_linear = metrics.confusion\_matrix(y\_test, svc\_prediction\_linear)

print('SVC \[kernel - linear\]')

print('Confusion Matrix: \\n', conf\_mat\_linear)

accuracy\_score\_linear = metrics.accuracy\_score(y\_test, svc\_prediction\_linear)

print('Accuracy Score: ', accuracy\_score\_linear)

print('Accuracy in Percentage: ', int(accuracy\_score\_linear \* 100), '%')

print(classification\_report(y\_test, svc\_prediction\_linear))

\# Visualization of confusion matrix for 'linear' kernel

conf\_mat\_linear\_vis = pd.crosstab(y\_test, svc\_prediction\_linear, rownames=\['Actual'\], colnames=\['Predicted'\])

sn.heatmap(conf\_mat\_linear\_vis, annot=True).set(title='SVC \[linear\]')

[13.18Implement Steepest Descent](#07_Contents.xhtml#sub-166)

\# Python implementation of Steepest Descent algorithm

\# Import required libraries

import numpy as np

from scipy import optimize

\# Define the objective function

def objective(x):

    return (x\[0\]\*\*2 + x\[1\]\*\*2)

\# Define the gradient of the objective function

def gradient(x):

    return np.array(\[2\*x\[0\], 2\*x\[1\]\])

\# Define the steepest descent algorithm

def steepest\_descent(x0, objective, gradient, max\_iter=100, tol=1e-6):

  

    # Define initial values

    x = x0

    iter\_count = 0

  

    # Iterate until convergence

    while iter\_count < max\_iter:

        # Compute the gradient at the current point

        grad = gradient(x)

        # Compute the step size using line search

        alpha = optimize.line\_search(objective, gradient, x, -grad)\[0\]

         # Compute the new point by taking a step in the direction of the negative gradient

        x\_new = x - alpha\*grad

      

        # Check for convergence

        if np.linalg.norm(x\_new - x) < tol:

            break

      

        # Update the point and iteration count

        x = x\_new

        iter\_count += 1

  

    # Return the solution and number of iterations

    return x, iter\_count

\# Define the initial point

x0 = np.array(\[1, 2\])

\# Run the steepest descent algorithm

x\_opt, iter\_count = steepest\_descent(x0, objective, gradient)

\# Print the results

print('Optimal solution:', x\_opt)

print('Number of iterations:', iter\_count)

The above program is an implementation of the steepest descent algorithm, which is a method for finding a local minimum of a differentiable function. The program consists of the following steps:

1.It imports the NumPy library for numerical computations and the SciPy library for optimization tools.

2.It defines the objective function that needs to be minimized. In this case, it is a simple quadratic function of two variables: f (x) = x\[0\]\*\*2 + x\[1\]\*\*2. The objective function takes a NumPy array as input and returns a scalar value as output.

3.It defines the gradient of the objective function, which is a vector that points in the direction of the steepest ascent of the function. The gradient is computed by taking the partial derivatives of the objective function with respect to each variable: grad(x) = \[2\*x\[0\], 2\*x\[1\]\]. The gradient function also takes a NumPy array as input and returns a NumPy array as output.

4.It defines the steepest descent algorithm, which is a function that takes four arguments: x0 (the initial point), objective (the objective function), gradient (the gradient function), and optionally max\_iter (the maximum number of iterations) and tol (the tolerance for convergence). The algorithm works as follows. It initializes the current point to x0 and sets the iteration count to zero. It repeats the following steps until either the iteration count reaches max\_iter or the change in the point is less than tol. It evaluates the gradient at the current point and stores it in a variable called grad. It uses the line search function from SciPy to find an optimal step size that minimizes the objective function along the direction of the negative gradient. The line search function returns a scalar value called alpha. It updates the current point by subtracting alpha times grad from it. This moves the point closer to a local minimum of the objective function. It increments the iteration count by one. It returns the final point and the number of iterations as a tuple.

5.It defines an initial point to start from. In this case, it is a NumPy array with values \[1, 2\].

6.It calls the steepest descent algorithm with the initial point, objective function, and gradient function as arguments. It stores the returned values in two variables: x\_opt (the optimal solution) and iter\_count (the number of iterations).

7.It prints out the optimal solution and number of iterations to show the results.

Output:

Optimal solution: \[0. 0.\]

Number of iterations: 1

[13.21Implement Naive Bayes](#07_Contents.xhtml#sub-169)

Naïve Bayes is an ML algorithm that is used for classification tasks. It is based on Bayesian probability theory and assumes that the features are independent of each other. To implement this algorithm in Python, we first need to import the necessary libraries. We will use the scikit-learn library, which provides a naïve Bayes implementation. Here is the code to import the library:

\# Import necessary libraries

from sklearn.datasets import make\_classification

from sklearn.model\_selection import train\_test\_split

from sklearn.naive\_bayes import GaussianNB

from sklearn import metrics

\# Generate synthetic data set for demonstration

X, y = make\_classification(n\_samples=1000, n\_features=5, n\_classes=2, random\_state=42)

\# Split the data set into training and testing sets

X\_train, X\_test, y\_train, y\_test = train\_test\_split(X, y, test\_size=0.3, random\_state=42)

\# Create a Gaussian naive Bayes classifier instance

nb\_classifier = GaussianNB()

\# Train the naive Bayes classifier

nb\_classifier.fit(X\_train, y\_train)

\# Make predictions on the test set

y\_pred = nb\_classifier.predict(X\_test)

\# Calculate and print accuracy

accuracy = metrics.accuracy\_score(y\_test, y\_pred)

print(f'Accuracy: {accuracy:.2f}')

\# You can also print other metrics like precision, recall, and F1-score if needed

[13.22Implement Single\-Layer Perceptron Learning Algorithm](#07_Contents.xhtml#sub-170)

Here’s a Python program to implement the single-layer perceptron learning algorithm:

\# Importing necessary libraries

import numpy as np

\# Defining the single layer perceptron learning algorithm function

def perceptron\_learning(training\_data, targets, learning\_rate, epochs):

    # Initializing the weights and bias

    weights = np.zeros(training\_data.shape\[1\])

    bias = 0.0

    # Iterating for the given number of epochs

    for i in range(epochs):

        # Iterating over the training data

        for j, x in enumerate(training\_data):

            # Calculating the predicted output

            y\_predicted = np.dot(weights, x) + bias

            # Updating the weights and bias based on the error

            if targets\[j\]\*y\_predicted <= 0:

                weights += learning\_rate \* targets\[j\] \* x

                bias += learning\_rate \* targets\[j\]

    # Returning the learned weights and bias

    return weights, bias

\# Testing the function with sample data

training\_data = np.array(\[\[0, 0\], \[0, 1\], \[1, 0\], \[1, 1\]\])

targets = np.array(\[-1, -1, -1, 1\])

learning\_rate = 0.1

epochs = 10

weights, bias = perceptron\_learning(training\_data, targets, learning\_rate, epochs)

print("Learned weights:", weights)

print("Learned bias:", bias)

Output:

Learned weights: \[0.2 0.1\]

Learned bias: -0.20000000000000004

In this program, we first import the NumPy library, which is used for mathematical operations. We then define a function called perceptron\_learning(), which takes in the training data, targets, learning rate, and number of epochs as inputs. Inside the function, we initialize the weights and bias to zero and iterate over the training data for the given number of epochs. For each iteration, we calculate the predicted output, update the weights and bias based on the error, and continue until convergence. Finally, we return the learned weights and bias.

To test the function, we use sample data consisting of four input vectors and their corresponding target outputs. We set the learning rate and number of epochs to 0.1 and 10, respectively. We then call the perceptron\_learning() function with the sample data and print the learned weights and bias.

[13.23Implement Radial Basis Functions](#07_Contents.xhtml#sub-171)

Here’s a sample Python code to implement radial basis functions:

import numpy as np

\# Define the radial basis function

def rbf(x, c, s):

    return np.exp(-1 / (2 \* s\*\*2) \* (x-c)\*\*2)

\# Generate sample data

x = np.linspace(-5, 5, 100)

y = np.sin(x)

\# Define the centers and standard deviation of the radial basis functions

centers = np.linspace(-5, 5, 9)

sigma = 0.5

\# Create the design matrix

X = np.zeros((len(x), len(centers)))

for i in range(len(x)):

    for j in range(len(centers)):

        X\[i,j\] = rbf(x\[i\], centers\[j\], sigma)

\# Solve for the weights

w = np.linalg.solve(np.dot(X.T, X), np.dot(X.T, y))

\# Predict using the model

y\_pred = np.dot(X, w)

\# Plot the results

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

plt.plot(x, y, label='True function')

plt.plot(x, y\_pred, label='Predicted function')

plt.legend()

plt.show()

Output:

![](Images/712-1.jpg)

This code defines the radial basis function (RBF) as a Gaussian function with a center c and standard deviation s. It then generates sample data x and y and defines the centers and standard deviation of the RBFs. The design matrix X is created by applying the RBF to each data point and center, and the weights w are solved for using linear regression. Finally, the model is used to predict y\_pred and plot the results.

[13.24Implement Linear Classifier](#07_Contents.xhtml#sub-172)

Linear classifier: scikit-learn’s SGDClassifier

Bayesian classifier: scikit-learn’s GaussianNB

K-NN classifier: scikit-learn’s KNeighborsClassifier

Note: Linear classifier and linear regression are different. Linear classifier is an ML algorithm used for classification tasks, which means it is used to predict a discrete value (yes/no, 0/1). Linear regression, on the other hand, is an ML algorithm used for regression tasks, which means it is used to predict a continuous value (price, temperature). The main difference between the two is that linear classifier uses a threshold to determine the output, while linear regression does not.

\# Linear classifier Python program using scikit-learn's SGDClassifier

\# Import necessary libraries

from sklearn.linear\_model import SGDClassifier

from sklearn.metrics import accuracy\_score

from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler

import pandas as pd

data.head()

[13.27Implement Linear Discriminant Analysis](#07_Contents.xhtml#sub-175)

Linear discriminant analysis (LDA) is another dimensionality reduction technique that is used to reduce the number of features in a data set by projecting the data onto a lower dimensional space. It is implemented in Python using the scikit-learn library.

Here is an example of a Python program for LDA:

\# Import necessary libraries

import numpy as np

from sklearn.discriminant\_analysis import LinearDiscriminantAnalysis

\# Create some sample data

X = np.array(\[\[1, 2\], \[2, 3\], \[3, 4\], \[4, 5\]\])

y = np.array(\[0, 0, 1, 1\])

\# Create an instance of the LDA model

lda = LinearDiscriminantAnalysis()

\# Fit the model to the data

lda.fit(X, y)

\# Use the model to predict the class of the new data

X\_test = np.array(\[\[1, 1\], \[2, 2\], \[5, 5\]\])

y\_pred = lda.predict(X\_test)

\# Print the predicted classes

print(y\_pred)

Output:

 \[0 0 1\]

In this program, we first import the necessary libraries – NumPy and LinearDiscriminantAnalysis from the sklearn library. Then, we create some sample data in the form of an array X and its corresponding labels y. We create an instance of the LDA model, fit it to the data, and then use it to predict the class of new data. Finally, we print the predicted classes.

[13.28Implement Locality Preserving Projection](#07_Contents.xhtml#sub-176)

Locality preserving projection (LPP) is a dimensionality reduction technique that is used to reduce the number of features in a data set by preserving the local structure of the data. It is implemented in Python using the scikit-learn library.

Here is a Python program for LPP with explanations and comments:

import numpy as np

from sklearn.neighbors import NearestNeighbors

def LPP(X, n\_components):

  

    Locality Preserving Projection (LPP)

  

    Parameters:

    X (array-like, shape (n\_samples, n\_features)): Input data.

    n\_components (int): Desired dimensionality of output data.

  

    Returns:

    X\_lpp (array-like, shape (n\_samples, n\_components)): Projected data.

  

    # Step 1: Compute the affinity matrix W

    n\_samples, n\_features = X.shape

    knn = NearestNeighbors(n\_neighbors=n\_samples, algorithm='auto').fit(X)

    \_, indices = knn.kneighbors(X)

    W = np.zeros((n\_samples, n\_samples))

    for i in range(n\_samples):

        xi = X\[i\]

        xi\_neighbors = X\[indices\[i\]\]\[1:\]

        for j in range(n\_samples):

            xj = X\[j\]

            xj\_neighbors = X\[indices\[j\]\]\[1:\]

            if j in indices\[i\]:

                W\[i, j\] = 1

            elif j in indices\[indices\[i\]\]:

                W\[i, j\] = 0.5 / (np.linalg.norm(xi - xj) \*\* 2)

            else:

                W\[i, j\] = 0

  

    # Step 2: Compute the graph Laplacian L

    D = np.diag(W.sum(axis=1))

    L = D - W

  

    # Step 3: Compute the eigenvectors of L

    eigenvalues, eigenvectors = np.linalg.eig(L)

  

    # Step 4: Choose the eigenvectors corresponding to the n\_components smallest eigenvalues

    indices = np.argsort(eigenvalues)\[:n\_components\]

    X\_lpp = eigenvectors\[:, indices\].real

        return X\_lpp

The LPP function takes in an input data array of shape (n\_samples, n\_features) and a desired output dimensionality, n\_components. It returns the projected data array X\_lpp of shape (n\_samples, n\_components). The LPP algorithm consists of four steps:

1.Compute the affinity matrix W: For each sample xi in X, find its n\_samples nearest neighbors in X using sklearn.neighbors.NearestNeighbors. For each pair of samples xi and xj, compute their affinity weight W\[i, j\] as follows:

•If xj is one of xi’s nearest neighbors, set W\[i, j\] \= 1.

•If xj is one of the nearest neighbors of one of xi’s nearest neighbors (xj is a second-order neighbor of xi), set W\[i, j\] = 0.5 / ||xi - xj||^2, where ||.|| denotes the Euclidean distance.

•Otherwise, set W\[i, j\] \= 0.

2.Compute the graph Laplacian L: Compute the diagonal matrix D whose i\-th diagonal element is the sum of the i\-th row of W. Compute L = D - W.

3.Compute the eigenvectors of L: Compute the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of L.

4.Choose the eigenvectors corresponding to the n\_components smallest eigenvalues: Sort the eigenvalues in ascending order and choose the eigenvectors corresponding to the n\_components smallest eigenvalues. Return the matrix whose columns are these eigenvectors as X\_lpp.

[13.29Implement Logic Gates without Perceptron Model](#07_Contents.xhtml#sub-177)

Here is a Python program for logic gates that includes explanations and comments:

\# Logic gate program

\# Define the AND gate function

def and\_gate(input1, input2):

    if input1 == 1 and input2 == 1:

        return 1

    else:

        return 0

\# Define the OR gate function

def or\_gate(input1, input2):

    if input1 == 0 and input2 == 0:

        return 0

    else:

        return 1

\# Define the NOR gate function

def nor\_gate(input1, input2):

    if input1 == 0 and input2 == 0:

        return 1

    else:

        return 0

\# Define the XOR gate function

def xor\_gate(input1, input2):

    if input1 != input2:

        return 1

    else:

        return 0

\# Test the logic gate functions

print("AND gate:")

print(and\_gate(0,0)) # Output: 0

print(and\_gate(0,1)) # Output: 0

print(and\_gate(1,0)) # Output: 0

print(and\_gate(1,1)) # Output: 1

print("OR gate:")

print(or\_gate(0,0)) # Output: 0

print(or\_gate(0,1)) # Output: 1

print(or\_gate(1,0)) # Output: 1

print(or\_gate(1,1)) # Output: 1

print("NOR gate:")

print(nor\_gate(0,0)) # Output: 1

print(nor\_gate(0,1)) # Output: 0

print(nor\_gate(1,0)) # Output: 0

print(nor\_gate(1,1)) # Output: 0

print("XOR gate:")

print(xor\_gate(0,0)) # Output: 0

print(xor\_gate(0,1)) # Output: 1

print(xor\_gate(1,0)) # Output: 1

print(xor\_gate(1,1)) # Output: 0

This program defines four logic gate functions: AND, OR, NOR, and XOR. Each function takes two inputs and returns a binary output based on the specific logic of the gate. The program also includes tests for each gate to verify their functionality.

[13.30Implement Logic Gates with Perceptron Model](#07_Contents.xhtml#sub-178)

Python implementations of logic gates (AND/OR/NOR/XOR) using perceptron-based methods can be achieved using a combination of linear algebra and activation functions. The perceptron-based methods use a linear combination of inputs and weights to produce an output. The output is then passed through an activation function to produce the desired output. XOR cannot be implemented using a single-layer perceptron because it is a non-linear function. XOR requires two layers of perceptrons to produce the desired output. The first layer is used to produce the linear combination of inputs and weights, and the second layer to produce the non-linear output.

To implement an AND gate using perceptron-based methods, we can assign weights and biases to the inputs in such a way that the perceptron produces a positive output only if both inputs are positive. For example, we can set the weights to 1 and the bias to -1.5. This ensures that the output is positive only if both inputs are positive.

Here is a Python program for implementing an AND gate using perceptron-based methods:

def perceptron\_AND(x1, x2):

    w1, w2, bias = 1, 1, -1.5

    output = x1\*w1 + x2\*w2 + bias

    if output > 0:

        return 1

    else:

        return 0

\# Example usage

print(perceptron\_AND(0, 0)) # Output: 0

print(perceptron\_AND(0, 1)) # Output: 0

print(perceptron\_AND(1, 0)) # Output: 0

print(perceptron\_AND(1, 1)) # Output: 1

Here is a Python program for implementing an OR gate using perceptron-based methods:

def perceptron\_OR(x1, x2):

    w1, w2, bias = 1, 1, -0.5

    output = x1\*w1 + x2\*w2 + bias

    if output > 0:

        return 1

    else:

        return 0

\# Example usage

print(perceptron\_OR(0, 0)) # Output: 0

print(perceptron\_OR(0, 1)) # Output: 1

print(perceptron\_OR(1, 0)) # Output: 1

print(perceptron\_OR(1, 1)) # Output: 1

To implement a NOR gate, we can simply invert the output of the OR gate using the NOT operator. For example:

def perceptron\_NOR(x1, x2):

    return not perceptron\_OR(x1, x2)

\# Example usage

print(perceptron\_NOR(0, 0)) # Output: 1

print(perceptron\_NOR(0, 1)) # Output: 0

print(perceptron\_NOR(1, 0)) # Output: 0

print(perceptron\_NOR(1, 1)) # Output: 0

Finally, to implement an XOR gate using perceptron-based methods, we need to use multiple perceptrons. One way to do this is to use two perceptrons to implement the AND and OR functions, and then combine their outputs using another perceptron.

Here is a Python program for implementing an XOR gate using perceptron-based methods:

def perceptron\_XOR(x1, x2):

    and\_output = perceptron\_AND(x1, x2)

    or\_output = perceptron\_OR(x1, x2)

    return perceptron\_AND(not and\_output, or\_output)

\# Example usage

print(perceptron\_XOR(0, 0)) # Output: 0

print(perceptron\_XOR(0, 1)) # Output: 1

print(perceptron\_XOR(1, 0)) # Output: 1

print(perceptron\_XOR(1, 1)) # Output: 0

[13.31Handwritten Classification using CNN](#07_Contents.xhtml#sub-179)

Here is a Python program for handwritten classification using CNN:

import tensorflow as tf

from tensorflow import keras

from tensorflow.keras import layers

\# Load the MNIST data set

(x\_train, y\_train), (x\_test, y\_test) = keras.datasets.mnist.load\_data()

\# Preprocess the data

x\_train = x\_train.astype("float32") / 255

x\_test = x\_test.astype("float32") / 255

x\_train = x\_train.reshape((x\_train.shape\[0\], 28, 28, 1))

x\_test = x\_test.reshape((x\_test.shape\[0\], 28, 28, 1))

y\_train = keras.utils.to\_categorical(y\_train, 10)

y\_test = keras.utils.to\_categorical(y\_test, 10)

\# Define the CNN model

model = keras.Sequential(

    \[

        layers.Conv2D(32, (3, 3), activation="relu", input\_shape=(28, 28, 1)),

        layers.MaxPooling2D(pool\_size=(2, 2)),

        layers.Conv2D(64, (3, 3), activation="relu"),

        layers.MaxPooling2D(pool\_size=(2, 2)),

        layers.Flatten(),

        layers.Dense(10, activation="softmax"),

    \]

)

\# Compile the model

model.compile(loss="categorical\_crossentropy", optimizer="adam", metrics=\["accuracy"\])

\# Train the model

model.fit(x\_train, y\_train, epochs=5, batch\_size=64, validation\_split=0.1)

\# Evaluate the model on the test set

test\_loss, test\_acc = model.evaluate(x\_test, y\_test)

print(f"Test accuracy: {test\_acc}")
